Our research delves into extensive cosmic-ray anisotropies recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory from 2004 to 2018, covering 98% of the sky with 95% confidence, and detecting local excesses in 15% of regions. The findings show that regions with excess anisotropies are primarily associated with energy thresholds above 40 EeV and right ascensions between 18 and 24 hours. Additionally, we observed that 25% of excess regions display steady-state and increasing intensity trends over time. Calculations using an air-shower simulation suggest that the lack of equally significant local excesses in right ascensions implies that the average length of cosmic-ray paths is at least 12.6 gigameters. The discovery of persistent and increasing intensity trends in local excesses may indicate the presence of an intermediate-scale component alongside the globally dominant GCR component in cosmic-ray spectra. Finally, the significance of local excesses diminishes when considering smaller areas of focus and lower energy thresholds, and we discuss potential implications for the study of point sources of cosmic rays. The findings are consistent with, yet also extend the scope of our previous research, and we intend to continue monitoring and refining these findings in future observations. It's observed that the relationship between the universe's scale factor and a fundamental time variable causes the Hamiltonian operator to become singular at the Big Bang and at infinity. However, for any finite time, the Hamiltonian is well-defined and Hermitian, allowing us to investigate the motion of Dirac particles. These particles experience pre-geometric creation, produced in abundance at the universe's inception, but destroyed in vast numbers as the universe evolves towards infinity. In contrast, in a flat and eternal universe, particles are constantly created and destroyed in equal measures. Our analysis reveals that the Hamiltonian's existence depends on the sign of the Hamiltonian of the universal motion, offering a new perspective on the creation of particles. This work offers a novel method for investigating the behavior of particles in relativistic quantum systems and provides a potential means of observing the effects of pre-geometric particle creation. Over the past decade, Detection of Tumor Infiltrating Lymphocytes (TIL) has emerged as a crucial factor in understanding cancer development and evaluating the effectiveness of targeted therapies. Advancements in digital pathology have facilitated the use of TIL as a prognostic indicator, albeit its analysis is labor-intensive, requiring pathologists to evaluate hundreds of slides per week. To mitigate the shortage of skilled pathologists and increase accessibility to TIL analysis, we have developed an innovative training pipeline that utilizes federated learning to categorize TIL on large-scale hospital networks. Our approach leverages decentralized interoperability to facilitate training on diverse histopathology datasets, allowing multiple hospital networks to collaborate without divulging their underlying data. Through the implementation of federated learning, we have created an effective training pipeline that enables robust TIL analysis capabilities on various hospital dataset collections, including datasets from our institution and external sources, encompassing over 100,000 images. Our method has yielded outstanding results, boasting state-of-the-art performance rates for training and testing on individual and combined hospital datasets, achieving categorical accuracy rates of 70%, 63%, and 64% respectively for the detection of TIL. This accuracy surpasses that of conventional centralize training methods, demonstrating the immense potential of our federated learning framework for the development of robust and generalized histopathology models. Furthermore, our method exhibits enhanced generalization and outperforms baseline models, showcasing the efficacy of federated learning in the analysis of tumor cells. To facilitate the training of these models on hospital datasets, we have created an open-source Pathology Federated Learning Platform, allowing easy collaboration and training of models across hospital institutions. Our platform offers a comprehensive suite of features, including data pre-processing, model training, and testing, thereby streamlining the analysis of TIL on hospital dataset collections. Our method has exemplary utility in the analysis of tumor cells for its capacity to educate models on hospital datasets without divulging their underlying data, thereby enabling hospital institutions to collaborate and educate models collectively. To our knowledge, this is the first application of federated learning to the analysis of tumor cells, and our method exhibits exemplary potential for the education of models across hospital collections. Our open-source platform is available at https://github.com/cde-education/pathology-federated-learning, allowing for the reproduction of our results and continued development of Pathology Federated Learning platforms. A quadruped robot's movement dynamics are highly influenced by its body architecture design. Current control methods typically separate state estimation and control for navigation and balance. However, this approach can result in suboptimal performance due to simplified state models. Existing reinforcement learning techniques have achieved notable success in navigation and balance control, but these methods are generally designed for specific robot configurations. A recent method, Evolve Pathway Creator (EPC), involves an evolutionary search to create an optimal state model tailored to a specific quadruped robot configuration. In this research, we combine EPC with a reinforcement learning technique to create a universal approach for quadruped movement. The evolutionary pathway creator is first used to create an optimal state model for a given robot configuration through a series of simulations. This model can then be applied to a reinforcement learning method for seamless control of navigation and balance. The effectiveness of this approach was verified using various simulations and experiments with a physical robot prototype, where we successfully obtained diverse state models for different configurations and achieved improved performance in navigation and balance control. Additionally, this method allows for the creation of state models independent of the robot's pose and velocity, enabling the use of evolutionary optimization for efficient search and high performance in motion control. The resulting models from this method also demonstrate high fidelity and can be applied to other related robot configurations, where we achieved a 30% average improvement in balance control for a humanoid robot and a 15% average improvement in navigation for a hexapod robot. These results indicate that the evolutionary pathway creator enables the creation of optimal state models for diverse quadruped and multi-legged robots. The approach presented here offers a universal and efficient method for movement control of these types of robots. Related video: Reinforcement Learning with Evolutionary Pathway Creator, YouTube. The central region of the spiral galaxy NGC~7213 exhibits an intense X-ray emission originating from its supermassive black hole. This phenomenon has been studied using the High Energy Transmission Grating on board the Chandra X-ray Observatory, revealing multiple emission lines from iron and nickel atoms. Their observed widths and shifts suggest that high-speed gas is present, flowing in a direction towards the black hole. This gas is likely heated to a temperature of around 0.2 keV by ongoing accretion processes. A smaller component of hot gas, heated to a temperature of approximately 0.15 keV, also exists and is likely being driven by radiative processes. This study further investigates the role of a warm breeze in similar AGN systems. It proposes that this warm breeze, characterized by an electron flux of $2\times 10^{43}$~s$^{-1}$ and a temperature of around 0.2 keV, is powering the extended emission in NGC~7213. A model incorporating this warm breeze is shown to be consistent with the observed data and may provide a universal mechanism for the large-scale gas flows often seen in low-brightness AGN systems. This warm breeze could also be responsible for the Fe XXVI and Fe XXV emission lines' excessive production compared to typical AGN systems in the galaxy. A warm breeze with similar properties is also present in the galaxy Mrk~79, as evidenced by an X-ray edge in its soft X-ray spectrum. This warm breeze may be a fundamental component of low-brightness AGN systems and is likely an essential factor in understanding the large-scale gas dynamics in such environments. It is further predicted that future telescopes such as the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope will be able to observe this warm breeze directly. In addition, it is expected that the telescope will be able to resolve the galaxy into its individual stellar components using the star-forming UV emission from iron atoms. These resolutions will provide critical information for understanding the complex wind and breeze systems in NGC~7213 and similar galaxies. It is also anticipated that the telescope will be able to obtain a direct, binned spectrum of iron atoms within a 0.1 arcsecond by 0.1 arcsecond region, as well as an unresolved spectrum of the galaxy using the Low Energy Transmitter on board the telescope. This will enable the discovery of a warm breeze in numerous galaxies. In contrast to current findings, it is expected that the telescope will be able to observe this warm breeze in a much larger number of galaxies

This research proposes a novel model-free approach to reconfigure nonlinear optimal controllers by utilizing two distinct reinforcement learning techniques. Initially, a novel action space transformation method is introduced, enabling the utilization of existing nonlinear control designs despite significant parameter changes. Secondly, a novel two-phase reinforcement learning framework is developed, with an information gathering phase followed by a performance enhancement phase. The first phase employs an actor-critic algorithm to establish a model-free approximation of the optimal policy, while the second phase implements a more targeted reinforcement learning approach to refine the results. The performance of this novel strategy is evaluated through simulation and practical tests involving an aircraft pitch control system and a high-speed spacecraft's linearization system. Compared to existing model-free methods, our approach yields superior results with reduced sample efficiency. The associated challenges and potential avenues for further research are also discussed. Satellite imagery plays a vital role in understanding the ever-changing Earth dynamics. To fully leverage this information, researchers and scientists require accessible and potent satellite image processing platforms capable of analyzing diverse datasets across various scales. Currently, existing solutions fall short due to their limited built-in features and inability to process multiple images simultaneously. To address this gap, we present EarthNets, a highly scalable framework designed for planetary monitoring that supports processing of multiple images and integrates a range of machine learning models. Built on top of CloudSat-IO, a cloud-native image processing service, EarthNets enables seamless analysis of satellite imagery via a cloud-based API. We showcase its capabilities by applying it to different tasks, such as land cover classification, change detection, and synthetic image generation, outperforming traditional methods in efficiency and accuracy. Additionally, we highlight the benefits of using a cloud-based service like EarthNets, allowing multiple researchers to collaborate and process images electronically, as demonstrated in our demo video. To facilitate widespread adoption, we make EarthNets available as an open-source service. Users can submit requests and track jobs via https://earthnets.io. This complex system is often modeled as an extension of the Landau--Ginzburg--Parisi functional, incorporating rod orientation and directional velocity into the framework. These models can be further analyzed through a technique called phase renormalization, allowing for the exploration of active nematics' behavior and its connection to established theories of active matter. This research investigates how the rod's directional velocity affects the system's response to disturbances, reveals the presence of vibrations in active nematics, and confirms a relationship between the rod's velocity and directional persistence, as predicted by a specific theory of active nematics. Furthermore, we discovered that there exists a critical relationship between the rod's velocity and the system's elasticity, characterized by a power law. Additionally, we examined the impact of fluctuations on this critical relationship and discovered that as the rod's velocity surpasses a particular threshold, the system's elasticity diminishes in a power law manner as a result of these fluctuations. This paper introduces ReAD, a framework that focuses on detecting irregular movements and situations within time series data. ReAD identifies unusual areas within time series by analyzing the changes in their linear relationships. The linear connections between different time points are evaluated using a selected metric, and their variations are mapped onto a metric space called Anomaly Space. The anomalies within Anomaly Space are then highlighted as irregular areas within the original time series. The efficacy of ReAD is demonstrated through its applications on traffic analysis and autonomous driving. The framework is available on GitHub under the term "Academic Free", allowing for free use in academic and commercial applications. Further information on ReAD can be found on our website at ridad.ugent.be. The framework is available at https://github.com/RIDAD-UGent/ReAD. The cross-section for pion production in electron scattering at high energies incorporates a complex component describing the interaction via pi0 gamma and pi +/- e- channels. A crucial aspect involves the vector shape factor F_V(V), linked to the electromagnetic form factor of the pion. This work tackles the challenge of extracting F_V(V) through a data-driven approach using cross-section measurements from experiments such as SAID and HRS, focusing on the energy range 1-2 GeV. The resulting shape factor reveals a noticeable distinction between this work and previous calculations using diverse mathematical representations. Utilizing our shape factor, the pion production cross-section aligns more closely with corresponding measurements. Additionally, the proposed shape factor improves the agreement between theoretical and experimental cross-section values, specifically at energies 1.06 and 1.70 GeV. Corresponding calculations of the muon anomalous magnetic moment (g-2) reveal a shape factor prediction by CENNS that minimizes discrepancies with the latest Particle Data Group results. Specifically, our proposed shape factor yields (g-2) theory = 0.046(3) 10^-8, in contrast to (g-2) theory = -0.093(1) 10^-8 obtained with a different pion shape factor. This improvement indicates that our study reduces the discrepancy between theoretical and experimental g-2 values by roughly 500 times. Consequently, our work demonstrates that the proposed shape factor is compatible with current constraints on the muon g-2, awaiting potential direct tests in contemporary muon colliders or reevaluations of existing experiments. Nevertheless, our study reveals that even with stringent theoretical assumptions about the pion interaction, the proposed shape factor accounts for the majority of the discrepancy between the theoretical and experimental muon anomalous magnetic moment values. Mindful of the limitations and uncertainties inherent in our extraction, the proposed shape factor, expressed as F_V(V) = 1 + [8.16 +/- 0.16 + 2.03 +/- 0.10(V/GeV)] * 10^-3, will facilitate further research and discussions, potentially leading to advancements in the shape factor and our understanding of the pion electromagnetic form factor. The relationship between a galaxy's mass in stars and its surrounding halo mass has been a subject of investigation, particularly as it relates to galaxy evolution and its potential impact on the stellar mass function. For galaxies of a certain mass, those with round shapes tend to have more mass in stars, whereas those with elliptical shapes have less mass in stars. By tracking the evolution of this relationship over time, it has been found that, for a given mass in stars, galaxies become more elliptical with age. This age-dependent transformation may be linked to a common origin, as the relationship holds true when galaxies are grouped by their ages. Furthermore, it has been observed that the most massive elliptical galaxies have less mass in stars than expected, based on their masses and shapes. This result persists when considering the thermal energy released by radio active feedback, which would increase the ratio of stellar mass to halo mass. The data suggest that massive elliptical galaxies experience a suppression of their overall mass compared to their initial mass, likely as a result of gas removal and spherization processes. The resulting picture is one of galaxies constantly changing in both shape and size, leading to diverse galaxy types. The present study's findings also imply that the most massive elliptical galaxies may be formed through a combination of merger events and gas stripping, rather than a single major merger event. The effect of this suppression on the stellar mass function has been assessed, showing that massive elliptical galaxies have less mass in stars, which could account for the slope change at high masses in the stellar mass function. The implication of these results on galaxy evolution and the stellar mass function will be further explored. The analysis presented uses data from multiple observations, including the Cancer survey and the Local Volume galaxy catalog, for a total of 959 galaxies, which were then grouped and analyzed based on their ages. The analysis relied on spectroscopic data, which were used to determine the mass of stars and the shape of galaxies, using specific equations and techniques. The result is a comprehensive understanding of the evolution of galaxies over time. The study's findings also highlight the importance of considering galaxy morphology and evolution together, rather than separately. The study's leading author mentioned that ongoing and future surveys, such as the Panorico project, will provide more data, allowing for further investigation of the shape and evolution of galaxies. The ultimate goal is to understand the complete life cycle of galaxies, using extensive and sensitive observational techniques. Recent space-based photometric surveys have opened up new opportunities for
studying the effects of atmospheric aerosols on astronomical observations. Just
like ocean waters, these aerosols impact light passing through the atmosphere,
making them visible through unique patterns in photometric data. Researchers are
using this information to create new methods for measuring aerosol levels in
terms of units compatible with satellite-based measurements. They propose an
approach based solely on photometry, without integration or model-dependent
estimations, and validate this method by comparing it to established measurements
of Total Aerosol Optical Depth, a standard unit for tracking aerosol activity.
This method has numerous applications and can enhance existing space-based missions
by providing new aerosol data, potentially used in conjunction with other
measurements. As an example, this technique could be employed in the upcoming
HESS2 Collaboration project, where tracking aerosols will be crucial for
monitoring dust levels during the development of the Square Kilometre Array. The
project aims to understand how heavily pulsed radio signals from distant galaxies
will be affected by atmospheric aerosols and dust. The proposed method has been
tested using data from the Gaia mission, and although it may need to be refined for
further accuracy, it demonstrates potential for providing essential aerosol
information. This will be essential for project planning in the HESS2 mission and
could be a vital tool for monitoring aerosol levels in the future. The proposed
method has also been compared to other existing approaches for utilizing stellar
photometry and has shown that it agrees well with other measured aerosol values. 
This includes treating stars as calibrated optical filters to measure the 5500 Angstrom wavelength, and then matching this value to established aerosol measurements. The new approach has demonstrated that aerosol activity can be accurately predicted using stellar photometry, and this will be a key component for monitoring aerosol levels in the future. The proposed method has also shown that aerosol activity is linked to the variability in stellar colors, rather than just the overall brightness of the stars. This means that even if the overall brightness of the stars changes, the variability in their colors can still be used to track aerosol levels. The team also explored the potential for using radial velocity measurements, which could provide precise information about the overall brightness of the stars, and thus the aerosol levels. However, this would require simultaneous imaging and spectroscopic data, and would need to be verified through further testing. We present GGLasso, a comprehensive Python package for solving the generalized graphical lasso problem. Given a matrix stack representing incomplete multivariate data and a precision matrix theta, the objective is to estimate theta under the graphical lasso regularization framework. GGLasso supports various modes, including block diagonal and arbitrary structural prior distributions on theta's blocks. To address the issue of missing values, the library incorporates three methods: complete case, imputation, and iterative procedures. GGLasso is compatible with scikit-learn and offers a range of state-of-the-art optimization algorithms, such as SPARS, Newton-regularized gradient descent, and Quasi-Newton. Additionally, the library features a graphical interface for visualizing and interpreting the results, including posterior sample means and credible intervals for theta's blocks, as well as node and edge significance levels. The package is designed for application in multivariate analytical chemistry, while also being versatile enough to handle general structural equity problems on matrices. You can install GGLasso via pip install gglasso or clone the GitHub repository at https://github.com/chemstats/GGLasso to customize and contribute to the package. In this document, we outline the mathematical framework, highlight the library's functionality and provide a user guide for executing key examples. Furthermore, we examine the performance of GGLasso through benchmarking tests. We culminate by illustrating a real-world application of GGLasso in the context of GCxN data. The X-ray emission from low-mass young stellar objects (YMYSOs) like TW Hydrae can be used to gauge the strength of any photoevaporation that may be occurring from their accretion disks. According to photoevaporation theory, X-rays can strip electrons and ions from the disk, ultimately yielding a characteristic 0.5-keV plasma signal. Conversely, magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) disk breeze models suggest that ionized gas from the disk can rise into the stellar atmosphere, potentially producing a higher-temperature plasma signal. TW Hydrae, a 10-million-year-old YMYSO with prominent X-ray emission, serves as our study's primary subject, allowing us to compare photoevaporation and MHD breeze scenarios. Analyzing TW Hydrae's corona through high-angular resolution radio observations, which can identify the strength and location of any plasma emission, will help differentiate between these two models. In this study, we use realistic simulations of TW Hydrae's accretion disk and surrounding atmosphere to model its X-ray emission and radio visibility under both photoevaporation and MHD breeze scenarios. As radio telescopes like the Next Generation Very Large Array achieve high-angular resolution, they will be capable of detecting any hot gas from the accretion disk, potentially revealing whether photoevaporation or MHD breeze models best describe TW Hydrae's behavior. In our mock observations with an NGVLA at its highest angular resolution (10") for both models, we find that any hot gas from photoevaporation should be within 100-1000 radial kilometers of the disk, whereas MHD breeze plasma can be found at higher altitudes (>10 radial kilometers). Consequently, models based on TW Hydrae may distinguish between these two general theories of disk photoevaporation and MHD breeze. Artificial neural networks have dominated competition results in various game-based tournaments, such as Go and StarCraft, thanks to their inherent ability to approximate complex functions. Despite their success, neural networks are difficult to interpret and modify. This difficulty poses a significant challenge in applying neural networks to other fields, such as computer vision and engineering, where understanding and modifying model behavior is crucial. In these domains, a more interpretable and modifiable model based on knowledge rules is often preferred over a neural network. This study combines neural networks with a knowledge-based rule-based system to create a more interpretable model. The system allows for the search and optimization of neural network weights based on predefined rules, effectively searching the neural network's solution space. This approach leverages the strengths of both models, enabling results that would be impossible for either the neural network or rule-based system to achieve alone. As proof of concept, we applied this model to the task of designing antenna components using the AntDS system, which was originally designed for metal hammering and pottery. After translating the antenna components' parameters into AntDS's attribute-based language, we searched the neural network's solution space to create optimized designs. Our results indicate that AntDS can achieve golden-standard results, surpassing the current state-of-the-art design methods for antenna components. Additionally, our research demonstrates the feasibility of applying this model to other engineering and computer vision tasks. Future work can build upon this research by exploring additional knowledge rule-based systems and applying AntDS to visual domains. Investigations into topological insulators have accelerated the pace of solid-state physics research in the current era. Despite extensive studies on various materials with unique properties, there has been limited exploration of specific types of compounds containing multiple atoms. Therefore, it is crucial to identify novel materials with distinct characteristics through calculations that can aid in the design of advanced materials with exceptional properties. Our computational analysis using first-principles methods has discovered 124-newly identified topological insulators with extensive band gaps, which are typically not found in materials composed of four atoms and three atoms. From these findings, we focus on the potential applications of topological insulators with four-tetrahedrally coordinated cadmium (M = Cd) or mercury (M = Hg) atoms and examine their potential to host exotic Dirac/Weyl points. To determine their potential applications, we apply strain on the materials in their natural states and investigate the changes. Our research suggests that mercury-based compounds could exhibit stability as 2D layers, while being mercurium's unique bonding properties account for this phenomenon. Notably, we discovered that mercury-based compounds with a specific structure (hexagonal P63m structure) exhibit specific properties (no lattice vibration) that contribute to their stability as 2D layers. This could lead to the integration of these unique topological insulators into existing heterostructures, enabling the simultaneous manipulation of electrons and nuclei. Our study has potential applications in generating long-lasting, self-polarized quantum electrical signals. Additionally, we explore the possibility of achieving room temperature stability in mercury-based compounds by applying external pressure, which would enable their transition from 2D to 3D states, while mercury-based compounds with a different structure (P63m) remain stable across various conditions. Conversely, cadmium-based compounds are found to be stable across both of their two possible structures (P63m and P63/mmc) through the application of external pressure or at room temperature. Reinforcement learning agents can be vulnerable in certain situations. A potential threat comes from an adversary manipulating the environment to disrupt the learning process. Active research is being conducted to study and mitigate this threat. Most studies rely on direct interaction with the agent and the environment, while this research explores a situation where the agent and environment relationship remains secret. To address this challenge, we proposed that an agent could estimate the passage of time to gauge the influence of the adversary's actions. Specifically, we investigated two theoretical frameworks: one framework assumes the agent knows when the adversary interacts, while the adversary's goals are centered on slowing the agent's progress; in the second framework, the adversary's interaction is unknown, and the adversary's goal is to conceal their interaction to maximize the agent's perceived time passage. For both frameworks, we developed algorithms to estimate temporal insights and analyzed their effectiveness and limitations. Notably, we discovered that an agent can detect when the adversary interacts, and the agent can prevent the adversary's attempts to deceive them. Our research provides a starting point for addressing unforeseen situations in reinforcement learning. To further investigate this research, we created a game-like environment where a agent navigates a grid to reach the goal, and the adversary seeks to make the agent believe the distance to the goal has increased. In changing environments, reinforcement learning faces significant challenges
when trying to balance reward maximization and risk mitigation. Traditional
models assume Markovian world dynamics, but our research addresses the more
realistic case of non-stationary environments. We develop a risk-aware reinforcement
learning algorithm that adapts to and learns from the dynamics of a changing
environment, doing so without requiring pre-training of a risk assessment model.
Our method achieves this adaptation through real-time risk analysis, and is made
possible by a novel dynamic protocol we've developed for risk evaluation. We
prove that our algorithm yields performance close to that of an ideal model
that knows the risk structure in advance. Furthermore, we show that our risk
evaluation method is possible by investigating the conditions under which a risk
assessment model can be trained. Our results demonstrate that if risks change
slowly enough, a separate risk assessment model can be effectively trained,
and we validate these findings with experiments. Overall, our research enables
risk-averse reinforcement learning in constantly changing environments without
requiring a pre-trained risk model. Keywords: Reinforcement Learning, Risk-aware, Non-stationary, Adaptation, Separation, Multi-agent. </abstract>

Software development teams utilizing Bugzilla or GitHub for issue tracking often leave a digital trail that historically stored data, though rarely exploited, holds significant value for research. This wisdom can be leveraged by analyzing real-world scenarios from existing repositories to guide current practices. This paper introduces BDD-Alt, an alternative dataset for software development issue tracking, derived from publicly accessible Jira repositories. BDD-Alt serves as a supplementary resource for software development researchers, offering 13,610 tracked issues and 78,807 changes. Our research demonstrates the potential for leveraging historical data, illustrating how Jira's presence influences issue tracking patterns when compared to teams using Bugzilla or GitHub. Moreover, we highlight the effectiveness of Jira's presence in enhancing the utilization and variety of issue tracking functions. This finding suggests that implementing Jira from the outset can promote the adoption and diversity of software development practices. Our investigation also explores the correlations between software development team attributes and practical activities, as observed in the BDD-Alt dataset. This involves analyzing the influence of team size, team type, and release periods on the frequency and variety of changes. Our dataset also reveals a positive relationship between the initial issue count and the ultimate number of closed issues. Our research further examines the dynamics of issue interdependence, revealing that issues with comments or attachments tend to accumulate changes over time. Our dataset also illustrates the sequence of software development activities, showing that troubleshooting or refinement issues tend to follow foundational or feature requests. Our findings also confirm that issues with longer descriptions or comments initially tend to experience a lag before being updated. Our dataset also highlights the diversity of change operators, showing that the majority of changes rely on text modification, accompanied by the observation that larger teams display increased variety in changes. Our investigation also highlights the effectiveness of jira in enhancing the frequency and variety of software development practices when compared to teams using bugzilla or github. Our dataset can be accessed via: https://github.com/alternate-bdd/dataset. This research is a part of a larger project aimed at understanding historical issue tracking data, as explored in our conference paper at ICSE 2020, 'A Million Lines of Java: Towards Characterizing and Finding Bugs in Real-world APIs': https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04166. This research was further discussed at the 2020 IEEE Workshop on Software Testing & Analysis, as well as the 2020 ACM/IEEE International Conference on Software Engineering. This research was funded by NSF Grant #2047719, as well as an Google Research Award.

Artificial polymer generation poses a complex challenge in deep learning. A newly proposed method, called the Programming Deduction Method (PDM), tackles this issue by first identifying a precise mathematical description of a polymer structure and then generating the corresponding programming code through linear transformations. Utilizing code similarity metrics, PDM identifies functional connections between programs, enabling the deduction of new polymers from prior code versions. Experimental results indicate that PDM effectively learns abstract polymer structures, surpassing previous polymer generation methods in accuracy and outperforming program induction methods in dendrimers and ab-initio molecule generation methods in generating polymers. Additionally, PDM demonstrates a strong relationship with linear regression, enhancing its performance when combined with regression-based polymer generation methods. A key advantage of PDM lies in its capacity to generate polymers with diverse internal structures, promoting novel functional group arrangements. The method is also self-supervised, enabling it to operate without labeled data, including at an early stage of training when the majority of its atoms are non-functional, leading to more robust performance compared to prior methods. A public repository containing the method's implementation, the programming deduction method's source code, and the associated data are available for review. Experimental data can be accessed at https://github.com/LebedevPPhy/pdm and empirical results can be viewed at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1T9p7U7xk7TC9u4vQYHhGkTJ1eCk7p3pM. Recent advancements in speech enhancement through non-parallel data training techniques have achieved notable success. These methods typically involve the simultaneous transcription and enhancement of speech from audio signals. In this paper, we explore the benefits of combining speech enhancement and transcription techniques, demonstrating that concurrent processing yields superior performance compared to executing these tasks separately. To illustrate our point, we focus on a specific scenario - two patients sharing a consultation room - and show that our proposed method effectively filter out and separate the breathing sounds of both individuals. Evaluation of our model reveals improvements in transcription accuracy and speech quality metrics when both speech and transcription are processed simultaneously, as opposed to individually. We also discovered that employing a depth-wise separable convolutional neural network architecture yields superior performance in addressing the dual-patient breathing challenge. Specifically, our results demonstrate a 14.44% enhancement in transcription accuracy and a 11.95% improvement in speech quality compared to processing the speech and transcription separately, exceeding the performance of other baseline methods by 52.56%. A demonstration of our model can be found at https://youtu.be/j_OvToyhU1Y. This paper introduces a novel approach to validate the distinctiveness of signers based on dynamic signatures captured via computer vision. Unlike traditional methods that rely on static biometric data such as images or fingerprints, this research utilizes time-dependent video signatures. We propose the Intricacy Metric, a comprehensive measure that assesses uniqueness, intricacy, and consistency within these signatures. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we collected a dataset consisting of 1,500 dynamic signature samples from 100 individuals. Results indicate that each signer's signature exhibits distinct features, and the Intricacy Metric effectively evaluates their individuality. Predicting the effects of policy changes on social networks is a complex task with varying prediction periods, ranging from a few weeks to months after the intervention. Many studies utilize graph neural networks, modeling the network and node characteristics to forecast future system behavior. Given the inherent limitation of these models in accommodating differing forecast periods, we propose a unified framework that combines train and evaluation processes for multiple horizons, allowing for end-to-end learning across varying forecast lengths. To achieve this, we introduce a network transformation to expand the temporal scope, and match this with a temporal sampling strategy for node feature prediction. This is complemented by an auxiliary loss encouraging consistency across varying forecast periods. Experimental results on Twitter and Wikipedia show substantial improvements over baseline models, and also highlight the benefits of end-to-end learning over sequential model training. Further analysis explores the role of system horizon in forecasting behavior. Code and pre-trained models are available for reproduction of our results. In recent years, multiple graph neural networks have been developed in an attempt to uncover the underlying latent variables present in high-dimensional, interconnected data. However, these methods often rely on preconstructed graphs, which can be inaccurate or unavailable. In response, we introduce a novel GNN framework that utilizes a differential equation and chance processes to automatically discover both the latent variables and their associated graphs. This approach enables the learning of simultaneous latent variable models, allowing us to derive accurate graphs, even in the absence of external graph data. To evaluate our method's effectiveness, we test it on synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing its performance to established benchmark methods. Notably, our approach excels in representing the data using fewer latent variables and achieves superior graph reconstruction accuracy. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of our method through a case study that combines single-cell RNA-seq data with functional protein domains. This study demonstrates that our method can establish a consensus map of cell-type-specific latent variables and corresponding graphs, enabling the identification of distinct cell subpopulations. As a result, our approach offers a valuable framework for visually interpreting the hierarchy of latent variables present in high-dimensional, interconnected data. Iterative compressed sensing methods can efficiently recover sparse signals from underdetermined measurements. Convergence of these methods can often be proven by framing them as iterative optimization procedures. However, these methods may exhibit slow convergence rates, typically linear, for ill-conditioned problems. In contrast, a diverse set of stabilization methods can improve convergence rates and provide robustness against exceptions and parameter choices. The process of combining images from different telescopes or observations involves blending the images while accounting for the distinct point spread functions that vary in shape and size. Ideally, the resulting merged image should appear as if it was obtained with a single telescope, having a uniform point spread function. In our study, we investigate the feasibility of achieving a uniform point spread function through the residual correction of photon noise following image merging. We also examine the conditions necessary for this correction to converge, and demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of simulated images. Furthermore, we apply this technique to a set of actual images obtained through the Wide Field Camera 3 on the Hubble Space Telescope, and show that a merged image can be obtained with a consistent point spread function. This method serves as an alternative to traditional techniques for merging images, such as the Multi-Scale Gaussian Combination method. Although the technique may exhibit slower convergence for highly noisy images, it offers several advantages, including simplicity, robustness, and the ability to handle disparate image properties. Our research explores the application of these representations to model the complex shapes of biological cells. By leveraging the inherent continuity of implicit neural networks, we can represent and generate cell shapes characterized by subtle gradients and sharp boundaries. However, neural implicit representations suffer from high memory requirements due to the need to store a density value at every point in space. To overcome this limitation, we employ a learned level-of-detail technique, enabling the efficient representation of cells at varying levels of detail. Our technique enables the generation of realistic biological cell shapes by learning the underlying implicit shape functions directly from data, and offers a flexible and efficient approach to cell modeling. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we performed a user study demonstrating its capabilities in modeling and shaping cells using explicit and implicit methods. Additionally, we found no significant difference in shaping performance between the explicit and implicit methods. Two commonly employed visualizations for three-dimensional data - Cartesian and spherical coordinates - are frequently confused with being inherently three-dimensional, when in fact they are simply one-dimensional representations with implicit assumptions about their context. We argue that these assumptions are not necessarily universal and propose replacing Cartesian and spherical coordinates with more robust notions, drawing inspiration from recent advancements in reinforcement learning. We use a self-driving car scenario as a case in point, demonstrating how direction concepts can be effectively communicated and utilized without revealing the underlying spatial framework. This perspective promotes the consideration of depictions as a means to convey and utilize knowledge, rather than being inherently tied to spatial representations. We suggest exploring alternatives to the traditional depiction of space, such as utilizing direction information, and propose an experimental approach to develop a more nuanced understanding of depictions that can learn and adapt like models in reinforcement learning. In addition, we emphasize the importance of lesson extraction - transferring knowledge from areas like reinforcement learning to other domains. We provide a simple framework for lesson extraction and illustrate its potential with two depiction-related outcomes, including the integration of path-planning techniques and the incorporation of spherability concepts. The proposed ideas are meant to stimulate discussion and serve as a starting point for a deeper investigation into depictions and lesson extraction. This study employs the hard-disk model as a starting point to develop new ideas in statistical physics, particularly focusing on thermodynamic properties of macroscopic systems, where their microstates are governed by irreversible Markov processes. Since evolutionary paths in hard-disk systems are not unique, we face two main challenges. Firstly, we need to define and establish the physical integrity of the equilibrium state when multiple collision pathways exist. Secondly, we must devise a method to calculate thermodynamic properties, such as the heat capacity, from collective characteristics of individual particles. To address these challenges, we devise two theoretical frameworks. The first framework ensures physical consistency by imposing the condition of maximum entropy among all feasible collision arrangements. The second framework applies a non-increasing thermodynamic integral, a method initially explored by von Neumann, Lev Landau, and Eric Meron. Both theoretical models yield the same results, demonstrating that thermodynamic properties of hard-disk magnets can be calculated using collective properties of particles, specifically their average speeds, which are accessible through non-equilibrium simulations. By reversing the direction of collisions, we also observe a significant increase in thermodynamic properties, aligning with our theoretical predictions. The two theoretical models showcase distinct levels of predictive accuracy, with the first framework predicting exact values and the second framework estimating them to within 10% accuracy. The primary benefit of our theoretical approach lies in its compatibility with event-driven molecular dynamics, allowing for the calculation of thermodynamic properties using regular datasets collected from non-equilibrium simulations. The proposed method presents new possibilities for evaluating thermodynamic properties of systems governed by irreversible Markov processes, including those with finite collision memory, as illustrated by a case study of hard-disk systems with memory. The study's outcomes may also be extended to other types of contact systems, as well as kinetic Ising systems undergoing irreversible interactions. The method presents a practical solution for evaluating the thermodynamics of systems that are difficult to model analytically, such as those governed by event-driven Markov processes. The problem of localizing and identifying sound events is a critical issue in audio signal processing, with practical applications in areas such as audio content analysis and machine hearing. This problem is typically addressed through techniques that combine frame-level detection and localization with event identification. Our research builds on the SoundEvent 2018 dataset, focusing on improving sound event positioning and identification using a specific neural network architecture. This architecture incorporates rectangular filters and is applied to a dataset that has been enhanced through channel rotation as well as time and frequency augmentation. A simple yet effective method was employed to determine the start and end times of sound events. Experimental results indicate that our approach yields accurate detection and localization of sound events, with notable improvements achieved through data augmentation and filter rotation. Specifically, our model achieves a high mean accuracy of 0.9256 in identifying the three class categories, and demonstrates promising localization capabilities with its end-time prediction. With further refinement of its design and augmentation techniques, our model has the potential to excel in sound event positioning and identification. A comprehensive set of source code and data augmentation methods used in this research have been made publicly available on GitHub. Concurrent transmission based wireless systems have the distinct attribute of transmitting multiple signals across various frequencies or phases simultaneously. This characteristic enables them to differentiate between subcarriers with identical symbols or distinct ones, thereby enhancing efficiency and resilience in the face of interference. In this systematic review, we delve into the various applications and models of wireless systems that exploit superposition, primarily focusing on PTUS, MIMO, MRC, OFDM, and Full-Dimensional Wireless Systems. Our examination reveals that utilizing superposition in wireless transmission holds significant potential for future development, where traditional techniques may prove insufficient. Consequently, we investigate the Enumerative combinatorial method for calculating null space, which enables efficient superposition in wireless communication. Moreover, we explore the capabilities of FDWS in accommodating an increased number of concurrent transmissions and discuss its-enabling techniques. Lastly, we highlight key research areas that require further exploration and advancement. Ultimately, we aim to inspire further study in this domain through this comprehensive review and the exemplified models. A collection of spectrograms obtained from time-series data is analyzed using a random matrix theory framework. This approach enables the derivation of statistical relationships between spectrogram values and genuine signal coefficients. Consequently, this methodology serves as the foundation for developing signal evaluation methods based on spectrogram statistics. By concentrating on the characteristics of spectrogram levels, this method avoids making unnecessary assumptions about time-series structures. As such, it is applicable to a broad range of signal types, including non-stationary signals and signals for which only a limited duration is available. In addition, this method is versatile, with various signal metrics being introduced, including a simple mean squared error (MSE) metric and a more complex metric involving the k-th moment of signal amplitude spectrum (KMS) that demonstrate strong correlation with the signal's energy density and spectral characteristics, respectively. Furthermore, this method's effectiveness is validated through numerical simulations where it successfully identifies low-amplitude signals within strong noise backgrounds. Lastly, this method's applicability is further illustrated through its use in detecting continuous wave signals within radio data. This study identifies and differentiates two distinct ENSO modes - central Pacific (CP) and eastern Pacific (EP) - using observational data from 1979 to 2017. Our analysis reveals that CP events are associated with increased precipitation in the vicinity of Hawaii and reduced precipitation in the southeastern Pacific, distinguishing them from EP events that are linked to heavy rainfall in the southeastern Pacific, drought in the maritime continent, and altered precipitation patterns in the northwestern Pacific. Our results show that CP events are more likely to occur during El Ni\~no conditions, whereas EP events are associated with La Ni\~no conditions. Additionally, the seasonal distribution of CP events mirrors that of the EP mode, but with a delayed peak. Our observations also highlight the potential for CP events to exacerbate droughts in the maritime continent, whereas EP events may contribute to heavy rainfall in the southeastern Pacific. This research identifies groups of block configurations that exhibit flag-transitive symmetry within the 2-dimensional projective plane over a finite field, utilizing a systematic approach. A flag-transitive group within a projective plane corresponds to the semidirect product of its 2-dimensional vector space group with a cyclic group, and a group action that is transitive on the set of flags. A block configuration group admits a projective embedding if it is a subgroup of the projective general linear group, and we discover all such groups that provide an embedding of the projective plane with a flag-transitive group action. Furthermore, we investigate groups of block configurations that are isomorphic to the Euclidean motion group of a 2-dimensional space, and identify those that admit an embedding of the Euclidean space with a flag-transitive group action. Additionally, we provide examples of groups that admit embeddings of the projective plane and the Euclidean space, and give applications of these groups to combinatorial geometry.

This study examines electronic interactions within confined hydrogen, helium and lithium ions using a mathematical model that measures entropy based on electronic proximity in these trapped ions. Coulomb interaction strength is shown to influence this entropy, with increased interaction leading to greater disorder in the electronic configuration. In hydrogen, this entropy is always positive, but becomes negative in the presence of strong electronic confinement and inter-electron interactions. In helium and lithium ions, however, negative entropy is possible even under weak electronic confinement due to the corresponding increased effective electronic charges. In contrast, information entropies related to thermodynamic systems yield different results, with an absence of negative entropy values for all three systems. Moreover, these entropy measures predict a greater tendency for electronic collapse in hydrogen compared to helium and lithium ions. Introducing an energy scale for entropy allows us to study the behavior of these entropies as a function of electronic confinement and effective electronic charges. These findings could contribute to the understanding of electronic instability in these confined ions. requiring models to be in thorough agreement with observations of massive compact 
binaries. We introduce a novel framework for translating these gravitational models 
into a broader, mathematical structure. This allows us to identify specific issues 
arising from the binary environment, and to develop techniques for constraining the 
gravitational constant under certain theories. We illustrate the effectiveness 
of this framework using two examples - scalarized general relativity and bimetric 
gravity - and explore potential extensions to explore various models of gravity. 
Additionally, our approach holds potential for improving current methods in 
delving deeper into binary data to set further constraints on these theories. 
Key tools that our framework offers for conducting extensive binary tests include 
a universal language for describing how compact objects lose energy, and a set of 
general criteria for modeling the observed spectra of radiation from these objects. 
By reconstructing the observed spectra in this way, we can simulate observations 
of the objects as they would appear under a specific new theory of gravity. This 
approach to testing gravity enables us to better compare different models, and 
to clarify how they handle specific issues arising from the binary environment. 
Ultimately, our framework enables a more detailed and nuanced examination of 
the observed behavior of compact binary systems, and encourages further research 
into the potential limitations of current theories of gravity. Specifically, by 
modeling the observed radiation spectra, we can investigate the stability of 
models under perturbations, and gain insight into the dynamics of the system's 
orbital motion, as well as its final state. This novel perspective on testing

In this research, we integrate cut-elimination into multiplicative linear logic (MLL) by developing a dedicated proof net structure. Our approach is inspired by the work of Gaudin, Bellier, and Kesner on MLL with cut-elimination, but we replace their complex tokenisation system with a simpler net-based methodology. We introduce a proof net language that incorporates cut and demonstrate that it allows for an automated derivation of the left and right contraction laws. We also show that our framework facilitates the derivation of a key cut-elimination theorem, which has significant implications in the field of programming languages. Furthermore, we develop a proof net version of cut-elimination, which is driven by contraction management and ultimately leads to cut-elimination. We also explore an alternative method of 'cut removal', which is inspired by the work of Ehrhard and Regnier and allows for the automated derivation of the beta-eta conversion, a key principle in programming languages. We also examine a proof net version of this strategy, which is based on the beta-eta conversion and is driven by a proof net decomposition method that is distinct from the traditional proof nets used in programming languages. In addition to these contributions, we also delved into the relationship between nets and strong modulation, but this aspect is not related to cut-elimination. Regardless, we hope that our integration of cut-elimination into MLL will serve as a valuable addition to the field of programming languages and that it provides a valuable insight into the relationship between nets and programming languages. (This research is an extension of my PhD thesis.)

This research introduces an innovative approach to predicting financial time series synchronization based on cross-correlation analysis. Using sophisticated network modeling, we examine the synchronization of multiple time sequences and identify the likelihood of synchronization based on initial phase differences. To achieve this, we construct cross-recurrence plots and convert them into weighted graphs, allowing us to apply established synchronization prediction methods. Notably, our approach enables the identification of specific time intervals where synchronization is feasible and provides a quantitative measure of synchronization likelihood. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this graph topology remains consistent across various time sequence transformations, such as rescaling and embedding, thereby validating our method's efficacy. We have made the code available on GitHub for public access. Our study focuses on the synchronization of macroeconomic indices and stock market prices across different US cities and time zones, yielding promising results and guiding future practical applications. Additionally, we discuss potential practical uses of this research, including risk management and portfolio diversification, and outline future scientific objectives, such as integrating this work into the existing synchronization prediction framework and exploring new graph modeling techniques. To showcase the practicality of our approach, we present a concrete example of how to utilize synchronization likelihood to manage a portfolio of US stocks and shares, demonstrating a potential gain of 14 million euros or 16% per year. Given its predictability, synchronization presents a promising opportunity for guiding strategic investment decisions and informing financial policy-making at both individual and collective levels. To reinforce this finding, we present an in-depth analysis of the synchronization between closing prices of Apple's shares and the S&P 100 index over the course of a year, revealing a significant 99.9% likelihood of synchronization and providing a quantitative measure of synchronization likelihood. By distinguishing between the electron and spin contributions, we establish a general distribution of instantaneous interactions and derive the radial and angular distributions for both electron-vibrational and spin-vibrational interactions. We demonstrate that electron-vibrational interactions are primarily governed by the electron density, whereas spin-vibrational interactions are influenced by the spin density and the magnetic field gradient. We estimate that electron-vibrational interactions could reach levels of tens of millielectronvolts, while spin-vibrational interactions are anticipated to be substantially smaller. Our theoretical framework enables the calculation of instantaneous interactions at ultrafast time scales and contributes to a deeper comprehension of the dynamics of excited electronic and spin states. We suggest that the instantaneous nature of electron-vibrational and spin-vibrational interactions may lead to the creation of nonclassical states through the collapse of wave functions. Enhancing CTR forecasting is crucial to maximizing the impact of online promotions by predicting the most effective ways to showcase items and encouraging user engagement. Considering that visual materials play a significant role in this process, we propose an end-to-end deep learning framework that leverages this information. By using a encoder network to analyze images and incorporating the resulting embeddings into a forecasting model, we enable the system to weigh the importance of each promotion based on both visual content and historical promotion performance. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over state-of-the-art methods that only utilize historical promotion performance, resulting in improved CTR forecasting and increased user engagement. Additionally, our method allows for the automatic generation of high-quality visual materials that align with current trends and user preferences. Key findings include a 13% increase in forecasting accuracy and a 15% increase in click-through rates, accompanied by a 30% decrease in misclassified recommendations. Furthermore, our research reveals that visual material quality significantly correlates with click-through rates, providing valuable insights for designers and engineers. As a practical application, our framework is currently deployed in real-world settings, directly affecting the frontends of multiple advertising platforms. Traditional case management systems can effectively monitor the progression of individual items, but often struggle with managing collections of items that adhere to specific criteria, such as items within a specific price range. This research aims to enhance the flexibility of current case management technologies by allowing the definition of rules governing item collections. We propose an approach that utilizes a pre-built 3D surfel map to facilitate robot relocalization within a constructed environment. By surfels, we refer to small, densely-generated three-dimensional polygons used to approximate an object's surface. We suggest deriving visual features that integrate both spatial and visual information to enhance localization, as well as developing a method to calculate reprojection errors for surfel-based maps using robot pose candidates as spatial information. This methodology is demonstrated to yield effective localization results on a robotic platform equipped with an RGBD camera and without any need for pre-built 3D models. From our tests, we found that using the proposed approach, we can achieve an average relocalization rate of 81.6% within 0.5 meters from the true pose, with a median angular error of less than 10 degrees. This algorithm identifies the most typical treatment duration curve by clustering patient data and then calculating the average or most frequent care schedule from those clusters. A variation of the algorithm also includes a smoothing step to eliminate irregularities in the resulting treatment duration curves. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated using real-world data from the University Medical Center Charleston, where the algorithms successfully created a standard treatment timeline and uncovered irregularities in the data, laying the groundwork for using these typical curves to optimize emergency department operations and improve the efficiency of patient care. In multi-agent systems, the application of extensive communication and complex processing can be hindered by efficiency limitations. This research introduces an innovative method for collaborative tasks that incorporates medium access control and channel allocation. The approach enables agents to jointly plan strategies using quantized information and reduce interaction costs. We examine existence conditions for robust strategies in equilibrium, and demonstrate that these conditions are met with suitable choice of parameter values. Furthermore, the proposed method is demonstrated through simulation of a target destruction mission. Results show that the agent communication and processing load are significantly reduced, while performance remains near optimal. The key benefit of this method is its compatibility with existing wireless networks. The algorithm has been implemented and tested on a wireless robot network. Finally, the reduced computation and communication loads of the agents are visually demonstrated through the robot trajectories in a video available at the mentioned URL. This approach offers a practical means for scalable and efficient cooperative mission operations over resource-constrained networks. The key distinction of this method lies in its integration of CSMA into collaborative game dynamics, which enables efficient target destruction missions with minimal communication load and processing load, over resource-constrained wireless networks. The core idea of this method is that all agents utilize a single frequency for communication, and when a robot wants to access the channel, it employs CSMA protocol to determine whether the channel is available. If it can access the channel without interference, the robot selects a nearest target; otherwise, it moves closer to a selected target through a straightforward navigation algorithm. When the channel access is hindered by another robot, the detecting robot waits for the other robot to complete its mission before initiating its own. This approach allows for efficient collaborative missions with minimal communication load and processing load over resource-constricted wireless networks. Research has suggested a connection between local charge asymmetry and the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) in heavy-ion collisions.  To investigate this relationship, the CME's impact on the collision was examined by correlating the charge distribution with the collision's geometric properties in lead-lead collisions.  Specifically, the connections between charge asymmetry and collision orientation were analyzed with the help of the ALICE experiment's data from the Large Hadron Collider at CERN.  Statistical fluctuations and non-alignment of the collision's charges played a significant role in the analysis, particularly when examining the collision's density.  Results from both collision energies (2.76 and 5.02 TeV) indicated that the CME's influence is restricted to approximately 3-4 times its predicted value by charge dependence-based relationships.  These findings highlight the complex nature of the CME's measurement and the importance of understanding background relationships between charge and geometric properties in the analysis.  Further research with high-statistics data at lower energies is necessary to confirm the CME's existence.  This work also outlines potential areas of investigation for future studies, including the CME's interaction with the Collision-Environment Effect.  Additional data, including that collected during the Run 3 program, will be essential in clarifying the CME's physical properties and the effect's scope in the quark-gluon plasma phase. The area of cooperative automation is becoming increasingly significant as it addresses a critical issue of scaling autonomy applications efficiently: the task sequencing problem. This study presents an innovative clustering method to address this issue, taking advantage of the unique capabilities of multi-point robotic manipulators for data-driven learning. In domains with high-level task interoperability, like food preparation, ordering object sequences is essential for proper processing and execution. This challenge is amplified by the vast possibilities of object ordering for any given set, often exceeding the manipulator's degree of freedom, making direct sampling impractical. Our proposed method is a varacious technique that drives clustering to generate valid object configurations based on manipulator interaction with environment obstacles. This approach leverages the manipulator's capabilities to collect meaningful task data, clustering similar configurations efficiently. By applying this cluster-based model, we can prioritize relevant configurations, demonstrating significant sampling speedup compared to traditional random sampling methods. This technique is learned entirely using autonomous manipulator interaction, showcasing its effectiveness through application examples using a simulated manipulator in a kitchen environment. The study highlights the feasibility of this clustering model for diverse cooperative automation applications, also illustrating its potential for real-world manipulation learning. This work details the development of highly agile MOSFETs utilizing a standard CMOS process. By incorporating a set of carefully designed access regions, these transistors exhibit significantly improved threshold voltage and, on average, outperform comparable devices using alternative techniques that rely on non-yield-enhancement process steps. Notably, the inclusion of the access regions does not compromise the device's overall robustness, with the performance benefits being quantified through the measurement of the transition frequency, which shows an approximately 20% enhancement relative to conventional devices. Furthermore, the time and cost associated with the wafer production are reportedly minimal. We report two types of MOSFET architectures that demonstrate exceptional agility - one with a cutline length of 2 $\mu$m and the other with a cutline length of 0.2 $\mu$m - that demonstrate the potential for high-performance analog and digital applications. Additionally, we show that these MOSFETs can be integrated into a practical differential amplifier circuit, where the improved transition frequency achieves an increase of nearly 30% without undergoing additional process steps. Our research indicates that high-performance digital and analog applications can significantly benefit from this improved agility technology, which is produced using standard CMOS process conditions. Moreover, this technique could be the foundation for the development of next-generation power devices. By combining this technique with existing MOSFET structures, we can expect to see a substantial expansion in the applicable frequency range. One potential application could involve the development of next-generation 28nm FDSOI technology, where the improved agility could enable the utilization of the topmost gate layer at lower voltages, thus reducing leakage at that level. In contrast to conventional triple-gate or SOI CMOS technologies, our approach may offer greater cost-effectiveness and performance. Additionally, we report that high-performance LDMOS devices with significantly increased transition frequencies can be fabricated using a standard CMOS process. By incorporating a unique structure, these devices have shown to be resistant to process variations, offering a transition frequency of up to 80 GHz in a 40nm CMOS process. Our research indicates that custom-designed access regions within the LDMOS structure can lead to break-down voltage and significant gain improvements, ultimately resulting in enhanced high-power amplifier performance. This paper introduces a novel approach to measuring user source variability impact
in video search outcomes using automated test agents. Traditional user studies are
often hampered by the lengthy time required to recruit participants, while automated
test agents can instantly gather data from a range of sources. Employing
instrumentation, we analyze user behavior and assess video selection patterns
across various source types. The results indicate that search outcomes exhibit
systematic differences in accordance with the source, thereby necessitating a
more equitable ranking method. Moreover, our findings indicate that human users tend
to favor videos with higher views and engagement, underscoring the need for a fair
ranking criterion. Ultimately, this research underscores the importance of considering
systematic source biases in video search outcomes and proposes a possible solution.

We investigate the multiple time, discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process with periodic allocation, examining how system condition and initial step size impact the development of a semi-classical solution. A semi-classical solution exists whenever the system's detailed balance condition is not met. As time progresses, a semi-classical solution evolves according to a conserved quantity, regardless of the system's condition. A semi-classical solution can be obtained through a discrete-time version of the Radin-Suess time evolution formula. In the low density regime, solutions may display complex oscillatory behavior. We also observe that, in a two-point system, a semi-classical solution can be expressed as the sum of two deterministic values, each corresponding to a system where the allocation is either all on one site, or all on another site. In a three-point system, a semi-classical solution can be expressed as the sum of three deterministic values, each corresponding to a system where the allocation is either all on one site, all on another site, or all on a third site. We conjecture that this behavior may be general for multiple-point systems. We also discuss how system density might be estimated through a multiple-point system in a specific regime. As a result, systems may eventually reach a stationary state, in which the distribution of allocation is uniform. In a three-point system, this stationary state can be obtained through a multi-scale approximation method. We observe that this result may be general for multiple-point systems. Furthermore, in a three-point system, when initial step size is small enough, a semi-classical solution can be expressed as the sum of three deterministic values, each corresponding to a system where the allocation is either all on one site, all on another site, or all on a third site, and the system's behavior is determined by a system where the allocation is uniform. This research focuses on the concept of unpredictability in mobile robots that operate within a barrier-filled environment, with the goal of diverting other robots from predetermined paths. These divertor robots will operate by navigating around static obstacles, producing an uninterrupted curve pattern on the ground as they move, which will serve as a warning or obstruction tactic for the other robots to deviate from their original course. Our investigation involves examining different methods and scenarios to make this robot's path more irregular and challenging to follow, thereby enhancing its disruptive capabilities. In particular, we are exploring the effectiveness of two distinct strategies: the utilization of reference frames with shifting origins and the incorporation of oscillating motion patterns. By subjecting these systems to analysis and simulation, we have observed that even modest levels of disruption, as induced by either method, can significantly impact the other robots' ability to track their original paths. Notably, we have found that combining both approaches yields an even higher level of unpredictability, rendering the other robots highly likely to diverge from their original course. This research is expected to contribute to the development of innovative and unpredictable mobile robot systems that can effectively interfere with other robotic missions. Additionally, we envision various potential applications and extensions of this research, encompassing not only barrier robots but also unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) navigating through obstructed areas. Moreover, we anticipate that our work may also spark new perspectives on the applications of unpredictability in robotic systems within various domains. Preoperative planning in laparoscopic surgery relies on accurate co-ordinates from preoperative images to navigate the operative field during the procedure. However, smoke generated by electrocautery during the surgery often distorts the view and hinders the surgeon's visibility. Researchers have proposed a novel technique to locate and remove the influence of smoke from laparoscopic images. Building upon existing image processing methods, they developed an algorithm that utilizes the Laplacian filter to enhance and clarify smoke-affected images. Although their approach shows promise, we raise crucial questions about the reliability of relying on image processing to navigate surgical procedures. Notably, we investigate whether improving image quality can be construed as a reliable criterion for locating smoke in laparoscopic images. To this end, we assembled a dataset of laparoscopic cholecystectomy videos featuring smoke effects and introduced a task to detect and locate smoke images. Notably, we found that optimizing the algorithm solely for clear images can result in a higher success rate, but this approach may be compromised by the introduction of blurry images. Consequently, we conclude that focusing solely on improving image quality may not be an effective strategy for this specific task. Additionally, we observed that our approach achieved a new state-of-the-art performance on the established CS dataset. Furthermore, we evaluated the robustness of our model against variability in its training data and discovered that its reliance on clear images limits its applicability to real-world surgical settings. Notably, we explored the use of convolutional neural networks and proposed an iterative task to locate smoke images. Furthermore, we studied the anatomical structures in laparoscopic images and observed that our approach successfully identified and removed the influence of smoke from these images. The potential drawbacks of relying on image processing to navigate surgical procedures are also addressed.
