This research proposes a novel method to enhance machine learning-based jet classification models by introducing interpretive AI algorithms, specifically XGBoostDecisionRulesNet. The addition of interpretive AI deep learning methods has been extensively explored in visual image recognition, but remains under investigated in high-energy particle detector data analysis. By integrating an XGBoostDecisionRulesNet model with specialist variables and feature importance propagation across network layers, our approach significantly increases transparency and understanding of the machine learning system. In our study, four expert variables were selected from the Large Hadron Collider's data stream and incorporated into an XGBoostDecisionRulesNet model, which demonstrated superior performance with an accuracy of 98.5%, 97.5%, and 96.6% for three-player, two-player, and single-player scenarios respectively. Notably, our model excelled in misidentification rates, particularly in distinguishing top quarks from bottom quarks, and showcased a notable reduction in false positives for Higgs boson detection. Furthermore, our approach emanated feature importance from the root level, thereby granting clearer insights into the model's decision-making processes. In-depth examination of our model revealed that particle characteristics, including mass, charge, and decay stability, played pivotal roles in classification, thereby addressing the inherent subjectivity inherent in machine learning-based systems. Our research demonstrates that interpretive AI can significantly enhance machine learning jet classification models, resulting in more concise, comprehensible systems that can be effectively communicated to and engaged with non-expert audiences. This study offers a promising foundation for the integration of interpretative AI deep learning methods in high-energy particle detector data analysis. All model codes, variables, and data used in this research have been publicly accessible on the GitHub repository. This research can serve as a useful guideline for incorporating interpretative AI deep learning methods in jet classification models, potentially leading to enhanced transparency and understanding of machine learning systems in high-energy particle detector data analysis. In addition, the model can be adapted to various tasks, including enhanced modeling of particle interactions based on expert variables, and the utilization of interpretative AI deep learning methods in automated machine learning systems to investigate complex particle patterns. This study may also contribute to the development of transparent and machine learning-based systems that can be used in numerous applications beyond high-energy particle detection, such as machine learning-based medical diagnosis. Finally, the model can be employed as a transparent and machine learning-based system to analyze and comprehend the structure of particle interactions in theoretical particle models, thereby facilitating a more in-depth and systematic investigation of these models. For any positive integer $r$, a sequence of numbers is defined as degenerate $r$-Stirling numbers, which count the number of ways to write a positive integer as a sum of a given number of positive integers. These numbers form a polynomial-valued semi-group and have properties related to partitions of integers. When $r=1$, these numbers reduce to standard degenerate Stirling numbers, which have been studied in the past. In this work, we explore degenerate $r$-Stirling numbers in more depth and we identify a subset of degenerate $r$-Stirling numbers that form non-vanishing polynomials of the form $a^n + b^n$ for given integers $n$ and a subset of signs. These degenerate $r$-Stirling numbers are referred to as $r$-connected and we provide a number of properties and examples of $r$-connected degenerate Stirling numbers for $r=2,3$. We also make conjectures about the possible polynomials of the form $a^n + b^n$ that appear as $r$-connected degenerate $r$-Stirling numbers. In addition, we define a corresponding concept of $r$-connectedness for degenerate Stirling numbers and provide a number of examples and observations about $r$-connected degenerate Stirling numbers. This work can also be viewed as a study of the degenerate $r$-Stirling polynomial, which is a polynomial that captures the underlying structure of degenerate $r$-Stirling numbers and has a number of interesting properties. It can also be viewed as a degenerate version of the $r$-Stirling numbers that have been studied by many authors. It is hoped that this work will lead to further study of degenerate $r$-Stirling numbers and their associated polynomial. Finally, we provide in this work a number of observations and future research directions based on the connections between degenerate $r$-Stirling numbers and other areas of mathematics, such as the study of permutation patterns and integer partitions. In particular, we make conjectures about the possible appearance of "excluded" patterns in permutations that are counted by degenerate $r$-Stirling numbers and the related phenomenon of "pattern-strict" positivity. We also study the distribution of parts in permutations that are counted by degenerate $r$-Stirling numbers and make conjectures about the possible frequencies of parts. A specific connection can be observed - if a killing vector generates a momentum operator, its flow must follow a geodesic path, but this flow is typically singular at the points where the killing vector fields intersect. This implies that the momentum operators are only defined up to a multiplicative constant. As a result, they adhere to specific symmetry properties, such as being self-adjoint or complex-hermitian. This relationship is further exemplified in various spacetimes, including the (D+1)-dimensional de Sitter, AdS de Sitter, and flat spaces in D dimensions. Interestingly, a combinatorial formula exists to calculate the operators in D=3. It's demonstrated that no killing vectors exist in D=2 that can generate non-trivial momentum operators. The sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations poses a significant challenge in studying fermionic systems, particularly those exhibiting quantum spin liquids and superconductivity. A novel method using complex-valued neural networks to transform weighted data and mitigate the sign problem has been developed. This method, tested on the Hubbard model, shows that neural networks can efficiently tackle the sign problem in an intricate system, opening up opportunities for studying complex fermionic systems. Additionally, the study investigates the limitations and potential flaws of using neural networks to address the sign problem. While this method achieves remarkable results, it is unclear whether it can be extended to longer chains due to the increasing complexity of the data. Future research will focus on developing strategies to tackle larger systems and applying the method to study superconducting and topological matter. Furthermore, the study explores the possibility of using neural networks to estimate an integral that is critical in studying the Fermi surface of the Hubbard model, thereby providing new insights into the model's physics. Overall, the study demonstrates that neural networks can be utilized to tackle the sign problem, enabling the investigation of complex fermionic systems and their physics. Verifying the integrity of program inputs typically involves an assertion language for specifying requirements and a mechanism for verifying those assertions. However, the process can be complicated by the fact that program inputs may not always be reliable, requiring assertions to be valid under all possible input scenarios before they can be trusted. In cases where this is not feasible due to performance constraints or other limitations, an alternative solution may be to establish a theoretical framework for evaluating and confirming unreliable program assertions. This framework should provide a method for determining when an assertion can be reliably confirmed, potentially using environmental factors or even random number generation to guide the process. Ultimately, the goal of this investigation is to identify and framework for handling unreliable program assertions. Potential areas of study include investigating the properties of program run-lengths, examining how to utilize dynamic program behavior for verifying assertions, and exploring the relationship between program trajectories and reliable assertions. Another possible approach considered within this investigation is that one cannot reliably confirm unpredictable program assertions. To address this possibility, the investigation also delves into how to prove the reliability of certain program behaviors, employing methods such as finite-state verification and the cutting-frame approach. Additionally, the investigation looks at how to demonstrate the reliability of predictable program behaviors, using methods such as parity functions and the use of the Nitro program-language. Finally, the investigation concludes by distinguishing between the concepts of (1) program assertions that can be reliably confirmed and (2) program frameworks. While a program framework provides a structural foundation for program behavior, as seen with the Nitro language, a program assertion provides a relational description of program behavior. This distinction is examined through the lens of two fundamental types of program structures: stacks and tree-like programs. Based on this analysis, the investigation proposes a framework for exploring the relationship between program structures and reliable program assertions. This framework can potentially be used for confirming program assertions in various technical domains, such as testing and program verification. Potential applications of this investigation include (1) developing a theory for predicting program run-lengths based on program trajectories and (2) establishing a method for confirming program assertions using program frameworks. This investigation is distinct from previous studies that have explored program structures and reliable program assertions, instead focusing on the theoretical foundations for confirming unpredictable program assertions. Despite the efforts of public health officials, unverified information continued to spread rapidly via social media platforms in China. This research investigates the propagation mechanisms of digital rumors within China's social media environment. By analyzing user engagement metrics, it is revealed that rumors spread more quickly than verified information, with an average acceleration of 20-30 days in dissemination. It is further determined that digital rumors typically require only minimal propagation drivers, with an average of six key accounts needed to reach half of China's population, revealing the potential of targeted accounts in controlling the spread of rumors. This research provides crucial insights for public health communication strategies and system design, advising against reliance on conventional methods due to the limited scope and timeliness they offer in disseminating critical information. Instead, a greater emphasis on incorporating key propagators into communication plans is proposed to boost the efficacy of public health campaigns. These metrics demonstrate that digital technology can serve as a complementary tool in enhancing the digital technology-driven disease control system, thereby improving the success rate, impact scale, and efficiency of public health campaigns. Crucially, this research points out that digital technology-assisted public health campaigns may require supplementary measures to address concerns over user privacy and information security when handling sensitive medical information online. To address these concerns, this research proposes the incorporation of core propagators into campaign designs, thus enabling the dissemination of essential information to a greater number of people and boosting the efficacy of digital technology-assisted public health campaigns. Additionally, this research suggests that digital technology can be utilized as a means of augmenting existing disease control systems to accelerate the release of information and enhance real-time risk communication, thus serving as a versatile tool in enhancing digital technology-driven disease control systems. Dimensionality reduction techniques are widely used in hyperspectral image analysis to enhance processing efficiency, but their effectiveness varies significantly depending on the imaging environment. Spectral dimensionality reduction methods, such as principal axis transformation, can outperform traditional principal component analysis by minimizing data loss and improving classification accuracy. Our research investigates the applications of spectral dimensionality reduction in hyperspectral pixel categorization and evaluates its performance across different environments in terms of data loss, computational complexity, and classification accuracy. The results indicate that spectral dimensionality reduction is a highly effective technique for hyperspectral pixel categorization, offering improved classification accuracy and reduced computational complexity, although its performance may be influenced by the quality of the images and the corresponding targets. Our findings also highlight the potential risks of over-reducing dimensions in spectral data, which can negatively impact classification accuracy. Additionally, we observe that spectral dimensionality reduction tends to generate more targeted spectral targets than principal component analysis, further underscoring its efficacy for hyperspectral pixel categorization. Our research contributes to the ongoing discussion on spectral dimensionality reduction and guides future developments in this area. The proposed methodology is poised to further enhance the processing efficiency and accuracy of hyperspectral image analysis. Starting with the RPA equations, a new iteration of parquet theory is developed 
by utilizing a graphical transformation that enables the direct reorganization of 
equations without necessitating the breaking down and recombining of terms. 
This approach is demonstrated through the example of obtaining the vertex correction 
expression for the polarization function, which is shown to be equivalent to the 
standard parquet theory formulation. The new framework facilitates the smooth 
integration of various approximations, as seen in the explicit inclusion of the 
local interaction within the \(2\perp 2\) approximation. The structure of the iterated 
equations is analyzed, and a Hamiltonian perspective on the parquet theory is 
proposed, which includes the concept of a 'Hamiltonian surface' and'stability 
points'. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the \(2\perp 2\) approximation falls 
within a region of 'asymptotic stability'. The framework's versatility is 
demonstrated through the application to the study of a model system with a 
two-dimensional dispersion relation. The results obtained, including the full 
parquet polarization function and the interaction-induced shift of the Fermi surface 
radius, are presented and discussed. The new framework is expected to be a useful 
tool in the systematic investigation of various approximations within parquet 
theory. The code used for the numerical calculations is publicly available at 
https://git.lpm.org.ph/LPM-Code-parquet-parquet/-/tree/main.README.md.

This work is a more general theory which includes the standard parquet theory as a 
special case, and it is shown that the standard parquet theory can be applied to 
systems with non-constant interaction, whereas the symmetric parquet theory can 
only be applied to systems with constant interaction. However, the standard parquet 
theory may also be applied to systems with constant interaction by treating the 
constant interaction as a non-constant one parameter family of interactions. 
Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the standard parquet theory is equivalent to 
a certain limit of the symmetric parquet theory. The standard parquet theory is 
also shown to be a special case of a larger class of theories known as the 
'Hamiltonian viewpoint on parquet theory'.

The objective of this research is to investigate how music's informational content
has changed over time. We based our study on the Western music repertoire from
1600 to 2010, using a sophisticated mathematical approach that measures musical
structures according to diversity of patterns within a song. This approach enables
the comparison of musical works from different eras on an equal basis. We tested
the hypothesis that musical informational content has increased over time by
analyzing features such as melody, harmony, and rhythm, as well as the overall
pattern complexity of songs in terms of their overall shape. We also examined the
correlation between musical informational content and significant historical and
socio-cultural events, such as the invention of the steam engine and radio, and
found that these advancements led to further development in musical informational
content. Our results demonstrate a positive trend, supporting the theory that
musical informational content has indeed increased over time. Moreover, we found
that musical informational content reached a peak around the mid-20th century and
has since stabilized. We validated the accuracy of our approach by applying it
to literary texts, which showed a consistent and steady increase in informational
content throughout the lifespan of a single author. These findings make a case
for the application of complexity theory to cultural phenomena, and provide a
framework for further research in the evolution of musical informational content
in the future. We make our dataset of musical features and analytical tools
available to the public, enabling researchers to continue exploring the topic.

A standard strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences within a period as part of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of simplicity, it has a significant drawback: the number of parameters to estimate exceeds the amount of available data, resulting in ill-conditioned statistical calculations. To overcome this issue, we introduce a new approach that reduces the parameters to a minimal set, effectively transforming the model into a well-conditioned one. This technique involves distributing parameters evenly across the distribution's domain, resulting in a model with only two parameters. We then derive closed-form expressions for key statistics, enabling efficient maximum likelihood estimations. Compared to traditional methods, our approach offers improved accuracy when estimating the extreme value distribution's parameters, as demonstrated by simulation data and case studies involving rainfall and wave data. Furthermore, we introduce a metric to assess model quality and demonstrate the superiority of our method over other methods for specific types of data. The benefits of our approach are showcased through applications to rainfall and wave data, illustrating its ability to provide accurate estimates and accurately predict extreme events. The methods presented address a long-standing limitation of the Poisson process model, enabling its use in practical applications with limited data. The authors make available a comprehensive package of software for users to reproduce the results and apply the methods to their own extreme event data. The code is documented and distributed on GitHub under the name ppbtb. Additionally, the figures and relevant data are shared on the Zenodo platform according to the corresponding figures. The paper is structured to facilitate understanding of the methods and results, with the first section introducing the Poisson process model, followed by a description of the new approach, and then presenting simulations, case studies, evaluations, applications, and finally concluding with future research directions. The primary data collected and analyzed in this study comprise time series of extreme events, with accompanying time labels that reflect changes in parameters, with specific consideration for climatic data provided by Meteo-France. The secondary data collected involved reproducing the results using various methods, with particular examination of our approach on rainfall and wave data, and the tertiary data consisted of sharing the results, code, and data as per the recommended guidelines. The main data used in this study can be accessed through the HSkin website, while climatic data was obtained from Meteo-France, and the wave data from NOC. The theoretical foundations underpinning our Poisson process model are rooted in the works of Smith, and our approach for simulating extreme events builds upon the developments by Heffernan

In Offline Reinforcement Learning, a pre-trained Q-function is refined using batch RL without continued interaction with the environment. However, if the data used for this process is contaminated with corrupted samples, the resulting policy will be suboptimal for the unsupervised tasks it needs to perform. Building on the concept of robust finite state conditional expectation models, we introduce the concept of corruption-resilient Q-functions and develop a method to generate such functions that can withstand corrupted data in RL without requiring knowledge of the corruption mechanism. We further establish that traditional offline RL methods cannot guarantee optimal performance in the presence of corrupted data, but we propose a modified batch RL approach, called 'CleanRL', which is capable of achieving near-optimal offline performance even with corrupted data. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using a synthetic grid world and a real-world dataset. Further details are available on our project website: https://sateeshnambala.github.io/CRQL. Our code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/sateeshnambala/CRQL. It has been tested on RL environments on GitHub. Our project website also includes a project video: https://youtu.be/6B_0B-9H1hQ. In addition, we examined the role of tunneling rates in controlling engine behavior, and observed that these rates can be used to switch the engine between active and dormant states.

Building on the concept of determinism in finite automata, researchers have expanded the idea into various sequential machines. A recent theoretical framework, known as resynchronizability, extends this principle to various types of machines. A resynchronizable machine can be reset to its initial state after a certain sequence of transitions, which may involve the consumption of additional input symbols.  In the case of term automata, where output values are generated at each transition, determining whether a machine is resynchronizable is a more complex issue.  In this paper, researchers investigated the unidirectional variant of resynchronizability, or more specifically, whether a term automaton can be reset to its initial state after a preceding sequence of left-to-right transitions.  By developing a linear algebra approach, they showed that deciding unidirectional resynchronizability is indeed a decidable problem.  Furthermore, the framework was extended to cover various practical applications, including automatic code optimization and programming translation tasks.  To demonstrate the practical value of their results, they conducted empirical tests using real-world programming tasks.  Notably, they were able to successfully employ the proposed algorithm to improve the performance of the Valgrind memory error detector.  In summary, the study contributes to the ongoing expansion of the resynchronizability concept while also presenting tangible applications of the underlying theoretical results. 

Keywords: resynchronizability, term automata, unidirectional variant, decidability, linear algebra, programming translation, Valgrind memory error detector.

Several important mathematical operations, such as matrix multiplication and polynomial multiplication, can be viewed as a broader class of generalized convolutions. We provide a novel, direct formula for the $n$-fold generalized convolution of two sequences, which enables more efficient computation than traditional brute-force methods, particularly when employing multi-threaded or parallel frameworks. We demonstrate the applicability of this finding to key operations in linear algebra and number theory, also outlining additional potential uses. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of applying our findings to develop novel algorithms for solving systems of linear equations and factoring integers. While some of these challenges remain unsolved, our analysis suggests that the proposed method could yield an improvement in computational complexity, at least under specific conditions. We illustrate the effectiveness of this approach through concrete examples, showcasing its potential for faster execution and greater memory efficiency than existing solutions. Specifically, we reveal that even basic applications of our technique can outperform the multi-threaded brute-force approaches, including existing algorithms for matrix multiplication, polynomial evaluation, and other tasks. These results are further substantiated by our findings, also presented in this paper, on the optimal sorting of vectors in parallel. We investigate several specific scenarios, such as when the sequences involved or their significant elements are symmetric, which leads to new directions for generalized convolution. We explore these directions, providing direct formulas for them and illustrating the common thread between our $n$-fold generalized convolution and important operations in programming, such as string matching and the construction of permutations. Ultimately, we envision our research as a contribution to broadening the understanding of generalized convolutions, while also highlighting their potential applications to the critical problems of sorting and finding patterns in parallel. It is plausible that the proposed direct formulas can be adapted to address these challenges. We provide a theoretical upper limit for the potential improvement in computational complexity, which suggests that the proposed method could yield a $O(n)$ factor improvement over existing solutions for some problems. However, we acknowledge that this may not be the entire potential improvement, as some existing parallel algorithms might already enjoy better complexity than others. We aim to encourage researchers to investigate the widespread applications of $n$-fold generalized convolution, while also encouraging the development of new parallel algorithms through inspiration from our direct formulas. We envision our research as a contribution to expanding the horizon of parallel algorithms, while also illustrating the potential links between $n$-fold generalized convolution and important problems in programming, applications, and theoretical computer science. We provide a comprehensive list of problems and challenges that we investigate, which revolve around the generalized convolution

Our research indicates that GJ 229B's spectral characteristics are consistent with those of other T-dwarfs, contradicting prior claims linking it to white dwarfs through binary systems. Instead, our findings solidly establish GJ 229B's status as a spectral T-dwarf companion born from the same stellar material. Additionally, our research highlights GJ 229B's likely low surface gravity, making it a unique, cool object. Although GJ 229B's characteristics are somewhat ambiguous, our analysis aims to resolve doubts surrounding this enigmatic dwarf and provides a baseline for future observations, which we hope will further clarify its status and allow it to join the growing ranks of objects requiring low-systematic error spectra for extensive study in the fields of planetary and stellar evolution. Predictive models are employing data science to track the spread of COVID-19, relying on various sensing methods to gather information about individuals. The application of mobility data-based models has been a significant focus area - assuming an individual's movements follow a random pattern in space and a consistent routine in time. However, these models do not accurately reflect real-world mobility patterns and do not account for situations where close physical contact occurs. To address this gap, a novel framework is presented that uses wearable sensors to capture proximity data, which can be used to develop predictive models for COVID-19 transmission. The outcome of incorporating this data is an enhancement of up to 44% in the models' predictive ability. The framework's implications are discussed for using wearable data to create sophisticated models that assist in controlling the spread of infectious diseases. Additionally, the potential for using the sensing infrastructure to support safe public transportation is explored, along with the development of digital vaccination certificates and safe interaction indicators for a healthy society transition. The urban bus system is taken as a case study, and analyses using actual data from Boston and Miami are presented to demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in identifying the timing and conditions under which safe public transportation is feasible. The code and datasets are publicly available for reproduction of the results. The findings offer an approach for navigating the mobility and sensing compromises associated with a well-mixed environment that minimizes exposure risks. The framework contributes to a corpus of knowledge that enables reliable express testing and data-driven experimentation for a safe urban transportation launch during an outbreak. The outcome also empowers health and transportation officials to make informed decisions about mobility and public transportation strategies for pandemic management. The methodology is adaptable for utilization on any urban bus system, and the framework provides an generalized approach for applying proximity data in supporting the re-opening of mobility systems during an outbreak. The outcome also demonstrates the feasibility of implementing an express testing and safe interaction framework on a well-mixed urban bus system resulting in a 44% improvement in predictive ability. The implementation is discussed for a urban bus system, and the datasets and code are publicly available for reproduction of the results. The safe public transportation launch has been initiated, and the urban bus system has been made accessible to the general public. Push has been the dominant engine in the Speedcube Open, the premier tournament for 3x3x3 solvers. To gain a deeper understanding of Push solving techniques, researchers examined the end-influence, measuring the frequency of each possible final configuration given the last cube rotation. This analysis enabled classification of moves into high-impact events and those with little effect. Using this framework, researchers split Push moves into "wall-pushing" or "corner rotation," revealing predictable outcomes of some pushers. This knowledge was leveraged to develop an automatic move verification system, allowing for efficient generation of high-quality puzzles. As a result, researchers constructed 100 million unique puzzles in under 100 hours, including the densest yet known cube configuration. A corresponding puzzle generator for 4x4x4 was also proposed, paving the way for further exploration of general n-dimensional cubes. These findings could provide valuable insight into the nature of cubic geometry. Additionally, researchers demonstrated that their approach, while initially designed for Speedcube research, can be adapted for other domains, such as protein folding, by referencing the Space Open. The data collected from Push Open could be linked to the structure of certain proteins, facilitating a new perspective on understanding these molecules. The experimental setup, comprised of a specialized gamma-ray detector and an octupole magnetic spectrometer, allows for the simultaneous measurement of beta and charged particles as well as the transmission of gamma rays. This innovative approach, combined with sophisticated simulation tools, enables a detailed examination of the Hoyle state's decay behavior and confirms that its primary mode of decay is through two gamma rays at 7.12 MeV. The achieved level of accuracy is remarkable, with an error margin of just 0.13 percent, and the results can be accurately explained using theoretical simulations with a high level of agreement. The experiments were conducted with 12.13 MeV bombarded targets of 12C and 16O at the research facility. The findings provide strong support for the Hoyle state's initial assignment as a 0+ state and confirm its distinctive nuclear structure. Additionally, the experiments investigate the nuclear interactions between 16O and 12C at extremely low densities, revealing that nuclear forces weaken significantly in dense environments. The research paves the way for further investigations into the Hoyle state's behavior in dense environments and the underlying mechanisms of nuclear interactions. Moreover, the technique could have various applications in medical, industrial, and astronomical research due to its versatility and the ability to adapt to a wide range of detection windows. The research is a groundbreaking combination of experimental techniques and the innovative use of available equipment to study nuclear structure and behavior in unique conditions. The research has significant implications for understanding the underlying mechanisms of nuclear structure and has the potential for a wide range of applications in medical treatment, industrial analysis, and astronomical research due to its versatility and the ability to adapt to a wide range of detection windows. This study examines the intricacies of tables within research papers to validate factual information and discover supporting evidence, particularly in fields like healthcare and social sciences. To achieve this, we introduce a novel dataset consisting of 246 tables selected from research articles published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association. We utilize a table analysis framework to extract and understand the semantic meaning of these tables, comprising cells organized into rows and columns, often containing data marked as headers, footers, and captions. We define two primary tasks: proof discovery, which identifies table cells containing relevant evidence, and fact validation, which confirms the accuracy of specific information presented in tables. We evaluate system performance through automated metrics and human annotation, ultimately presenting our results and methods as a task contribution to SemEval-2021. Specifically, we address SemEval-2021 Task 9: SEM-TAB-FACTS within subgroup 1, focusing on the full dataset, to showcase the importance of joint learning between table rows and the effectiveness of combining heading and cell embeddings in achieving top-ranked performance across both tasks. Additionally, we present an illustrative case study highlighting our system's capabilities in understanding and navigating the content of research tables. Experimental findings demonstrate that our approach outperforms baseline systems in tasks involving table cells and fact validation, ultimately demonstrating the potential for joint learning models in addressing these challenges. Notably, our table analysis framework yields satisfactory results, even in scenarios of limited training data, emphasizing its utility in real-world scenarios involving diverse fields of study. Finally, we gather and release additional human annotations to support the understanding of research tables, providing context for future work within this domain. The data used in this study can be accessed at https://github.com/darobin/SEM-TAB-FACTS/tree/master/data and our table analysis framework at https://github.com/darobin/SEM-TAB-FACTS/tree/master/table_analysis. The code supporting our joint learning model can be found at https://github.com/darobin/SEM-TAB-FACTS/tree/master/code. (From Abstract)

This paper delves into the intricate nature of numbers within quantum physics, 
investigating how quantum mechanics' underlying principles translate into 
phrases that convey a sense of subtlety and hidden realities in physics. 
Specifically, the manuscript examines the paradoxical phi, quantum entanglement, 
the multifaceted properties of the Pauli matrices, and the composite nature of 
particles like electrons, electrons in molecules, and atoms. It also touches 
on Möbius numbers, an odd aspect of quantum topology, and the discrete, numerical 
building blocks of space called quasicrystals. Ultimately, the manuscript 
contemplates the intricate code of numbers that underlies the universe, 
positing that this intricate nature may hold clues for unlocking new 
breakthroughs in quantum research. Additionally, the manuscript includes a 
reflection on the mathematical tools used to analyze quantum systems, 
suggesting that these tools hold value beyond the realm of quantum physics 
alone. As such, the manuscript offers a hopeful perspective on the potential 
for human insight that can be derived from exploring the intricate numbers 
within and surrounding quantum physics. (From the introduction)

A graph G is considered fully measurable if every vertex v of G has a unique path to every other vertex in G. The minimum number of vertices needed to measure entire graph G is known as its metric dimension and is denoted by md(G). To improve efficiency, researchers have developed a simplified version of fully measurable graphs, removing the requirement for unique paths and instead using the minimum number of vertices needed to distinguish between every pair of paths in G. This new property of graph G is called SMD(2), or shortened metric dimension of order 2, and is demonstrated with various examples and by establishing certain bounds for SMD(2) in terms of graph parameters N, the number of vertices, and D, the diameter of G. Specifically, it is shown that SMD(2) of G is greater than or equal to 3 if D is 1, greater than or equal to 2N/3 if D is less than or equal greater than 2, greater than or equal to N/2 + 1 if they have cycle number C, and equal to N if they have a Hamiltonian path or cycle. Moreover, it is shown that SMD(2) of certain graphs such as hypercube Qn and complete graphs Kn is equal to N, and that SMD(2) of n-disjoint cycles graph Cn is equal to N/2 and O(n^(1/3)). As such, it is proposed that the lower bound for SMD(2) of graph G could be md(G) and potentially even better. These findings are further validated in the context of shortest path metric graphs. On the other hand, it is shown that SMD(2) of graph G can be md(G) plus one, and established certain conditions under which this equality holds for certain graph parameters. These results are validated in the context of trees T. To facilitate these findings, a simplified approach to calculating the metric dimension of graph G based on its diameter D is introduced, and the associated algorithms are proposed and demonstrated. This approach leads to a general upper bound of SMD(2) of graph G, particularly md(G) + (D + 1)(2N - (D + 1)) / (D + 2), and the associated algorithms are tested and validated with various examples and graph parameters. These results are further refined in the context of trees T. To improve efficiency, an iterative approach to calculating the metric dimension of graph G is introduced, and the associated algorithms are proposed and demonstrated.

Building upon Sechler's equation, our findings expand the scope of applications under specific non-uniform rainfall and boundary conditions. We have formulated exact solutions for two-dimensional cases with diverse boundary scenarios and, by taking certain limits, obtained new formulas for analyzing groundwater levels. Furthermore, our approach is exemplified through numerical examples that demonstrate its practical utility. Unlike existing methods, our formulations are free from restrictive assumptions regarding the homogeneity of the aquifer and the extent of rainfall influence, offering greater flexibility in modeling applications. Deep learning models' reliability in making decisions under uncertain or disputed information has not been adequately explored, particularly when certain assumptions remain unclear. We introduce a novel quantifiable measure of uncertainty, quantified uncertainty, and apply it to enhance the construction of decision forests, a simple yet robust classification algorithm. By representing the forest's uncertainty through a set of potentially ambiguous premises, we can acquire partially certain decision rules, and leverage specialized argumentation techniques to optimize performance. Our approach, called Indecision Forests, allows for efficient computation with a time complexity of O(nm), and offers greater control over acquired rules in comparison to other meta-learning methods. Experimental results reveal that Indecision Forests yields a consistent improvement in accuracy and a higher percentage of fully certain decision rules when operating with quantified uncertainty, in comparison to models dealing with unambiguous information. The implementation details and evaluation are made available on GitHub. Furthermore, we have introduced a new API for reasoning under uncertainty, enabling easy integration of our method into existing projects. A comprehensive evaluation of this API on various datasets is scheduled for future publication. The proposed Indecision Forests model has demonstrated superior performance in a range of empirical tests, and its source code has been made accessible on GitHub. The model's capacity for handling complex and assumption-prone data, as seen with imageNet, has been explored, and a corresponding code repository is scheduled for release at a later date. The induced decision rules acquired through our method exhibit a noticeable advantage in terms of dependence on problematic features in comparison to other decision forests. A parameter tuning study for optimizing performance with limited labelling is planned, and preliminary evaluation suggests that Indecision Forests yields a notable improvement in accuracy using our proposed quantified uncertainty measure. A corresponding code repository will be made available upon completion of the study. Improving the transparency of Double Layered Neural Networks (DNNs) is crucial for enhancing public trust, but current methods have limited effectiveness due to constraints in their representation. In this research, we introduce a novel method that combines concept emergence analysis with Inverse Learning Push (ILP) to explain the internal concepts within DNNs in a more detailed way. In contrast to existing approaches, our ilpCA method allows for the exploration of multiple conceptual networks within a feature map. By merging ilpCA with ILP, we can reveal how these concepts evolve across different layers and time sequences. As a result, our ilpCA method enables the discovery of clearer explanations for DNN models, surpassing the current state-of-the-art performance by 5% to 20% depending on the dataset. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that conceptual networks often exhibit stationary points where inputs result in the same output, indicating that these concepts may serve as a stable foundation for data representation. Additionally, our ilpCA method facilitates the creation of precise clarifications for DNN models, resulting in an average increase of 87% to 93% in accuracy when evaluated using the AUC metric. To validate the effectiveness of our ilpCA method, we conducted an in-depth analysis of various image classification and segmentation datasets, as well as medical image diagnosis, and observed similar outcomes in these studies. Consequently, our ilpCA method provides a highly transparent and detailed explanation of DNN models, surpassing the current approaches and merging the strengths of concept analysis and ILP to clarify the complex concepts within DNN models. The source code for this research is available at https://github.com/hjkmkdl/ilpCA. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are highly regarded for their balance of accuracy and computational efficiency in node classification tasks. However, they are susceptible to overfitting, particularly when working with densely connected graphs. Several countermeasures have been proposed to address this issue, but they often neglect the graph's structural importance in the learning process. This paper argues that these methods come at the cost of disregarding the graph's topological features. To remedy this, we present GCN-IL, a novel improvement method based on Influence Learning that effectively counteracts overfitting while preserving the graph's structural influence. By offering a comprehensive evaluation, we showcase the superiority of our method in comparison to existing solutions. Furthermore, we investigate the optimal hyperparameter settings using a search strategy. By studying the performance in unsupervised and semi-supervised settings, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method in enhancing model generalization, particularly when working with undirected graphs. This is further substantiated by our code availability on GitHub. By addressing the graph's structural influence in the learning process, we take a significant step towards creating models that are both accurate and interpretable. This research contributes to the advancement of GCN-based models in addressing the long-standing issue of overfitting in these models. Additionally, it opens doors for further exploration into the graph's structural influence in the learning process. From a theoretical standpoint, we establish the connection between the graph's structural influence and the eigenvalues of its Laplacian, eigenvalues that are widely recognized and extensively studied. This research presents an opportunity for further theoretical analysis and the development of new improvement methods. A novel yield index, referred to as the Portfolio Yield Index (PYI), is introduced. This yield indicator reflects the overall return expectation of a portfolio or security, being calculated as the weighted average of individual security yields based on market values. Unlike existing price-based indicators, PYI accounts for market capitalization in its calculation. One of PYI's distinctive characteristics is its dynamic nature, where the weighted average returns decrease as larger-cap stocks generate lower returns. This distinction gives rise to a PYI sub-index known as the Large Cap PYI (LC-PYI), which is calculated based solely on the returns of larger-cap securities. Consequently, the LC-PYI typically tracks a lower return expectation compared to the PYI. Cross-sectional dispersion analysis reveals a significant and positive correlation between the broad PyI and liquidity, but also detects a substantial and positive correlation between the LC-PYI and larger market capitalization. Researchers also utilize PyI-based factors in practical investment tests, which demonstrate that this indicator can facilitate profitable trading strategies in both US and Chinese equity markets. One specific strategy generates notable returns of 11.6% and 9.7% monthly in the US and Chinese markets, respectively, while maintaining reasonable volatility. Notably, the US strategy also exhibits effective risk-adjustment metrics, including a Sharpe Ratio of 3.17 and a Sortino Ratio of 5.83. These empirical findings clearly demonstrate the practical implications of understanding the cross-sectional dispersion of portfolio yields. In addition, the cross-section of PyI-based factors serves as a reliable indicator of return expectations, providing valuable insights for investment decisions. Finally, researchers also explore the practical utility of the PyI-based factors in context of the well-established Fama and French models. One specific test reveals that the PyI-based factors contribute significantly to the existing models' explanatory power, with the joint model yielding impressive R-squared metrics of 0.83 in the US and 0.79 in the Chinese markets. An econometric model of society, incorporating elements of interdependent decision-making, reveals that a long-term equilibrium is achieved when nations prioritize the well-being of all, as measured by the Genuine Social Product (GSP). This is demonstrated through numerical examples, highlighting the significance of international cooperation in addressing global challenges like climate change. Nation-states can establish a climate agreement by collaborating, even when individual gains are limited, as making nations benefit financially from cooperation enables them to achieve a more equitable global climate deal. This is illustrated using a simple climate model, showing the benefits of pairing climate cooperation with other benefits of cooperation. Specifically, nations are more likely to commit to a 2°C Paris Agreement temperature limit when they prioritize the well-being of all, as measured by the GSP. This is comparable to the effect of making nations financially stable and secure in their relationships. Additionally, nations are more likely to meet the agreed-upon limits on greenhouse gas emissions when they prioritize the well-being of all, as measured by the GSP. This is achieved through increased levels of global climate cooperation, as opposed to the lack of cooperation. Mechanisms for promoting a long-term climate equilibrium include educating nations about the importance of interdependence and global well-being and designing decision-making models that prioritize the well-being of all, as measured by the GSP. These mechanisms can help achieve a more equitable global climate deal. Numerical examples investigating the effects of different parameters on the likelihood of global climate action are discussed. These examples reveal that a high level of global climate interaction and a focus on the well-being of all, as measured by the GSP, are essential requirements for achieving a more equitable global climate deal. The infrared mass of the $K$ meson, $M_{K,irr}$, is determined to be between $283$ MeV and $337$ MeV, and the scale factor over the current mass, $R_{K}$, ranges from $0.85$ to $1.25$. Furthermore, the minimum mass for mesons $B$ and $B_s$, $M_{B}(irr)$, is between $5351$ MeV and $5853$ MeV, and the scale factor over the current mass, $R_B$, could be $0.91$ to $1.13$. These analyses suggest that the proposed $S$ scalar can effectively resolve the discrepancy in the $K$ system masses within a range that also accounts for constraints from flavor changing neutral currents and for both left-handed and right-handed components of the $S$ scalar's interaction with fermions, even at a mass scale of $M_{\text{Scale}} > 100$ TeV, where the scalar's properties align with the expectations of natural flavor conservation in the vectorlike complementarity limit. The introduced model also provides a plausible solution to the $K$ and $B$ meson mass anomalies within two distinct cases of the vectorlike complementarity limit. The analyses suggest that the scalar's properties will leave notable signatures in upcoming experiments, such as those at the SuperKEKB and LHC, particularly in its decays into $KS$ and $B_s$ channels. The completeness of the vectorlike complementarity limit may also be tested by measuring the ratio of the $K$ to $B_s$ meson decay rates into the $KS$ channel. The model proposes several notable interactions among Standard Model particles, as well as between $S$ and Higgs bosons and mesons $K$, $B$, and $B_s$. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a widely diagnosed neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by excessive restlessness, inattention, and impulsiveness. ADHD's accurate diagnosis has historically been challenging, especially differentiating it from other mental health issues. Advances in brain-imaging technology, particularly resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), have enhanced our understanding of ADHD's neurobiological roots by monitoring regional brain interactions. However, identifying the most informative brain areas and correlations is essential for optimizing imaging biomarkers' diagnostic effectiveness. Recent research employed rs-fMRI data and machine learning algorithms to improve ADHD diagnosis. Notably, a deep learning approach was used to differentiate ADHD patients from healthy controls, showcasing the significance of multi-feature information in diagnosing accuracy. Compared to other methods focusing solely on optimal regions, this study integrated and combined data from various brain areas, achieving improved results. Consequently, this work underscores the merit of multi-feature classification in diagnosing ADHD and highlights the potential for future advancements in ADHD diagnosis through multi-feature data. Additionally, this study's findings emphasize the necessity to control for variables like age and medication when collecting rs-fMRI data to isolate pure ADHD symptoms. These conclusions were drawn from an extensive, publicly-available dataset containing information on 625 individuals with ADHD and 672 healthy controls. Establishing a diagnosis of ADHD requires comprehensive assessment by mental health professionals, and this work aims to contribute to this process with data-driven, non-invasive imaging techniques. These findings may have implications for understanding pure ADHD symptoms but should not be used as the sole basis for diagnosing the disorder. Future research can build on these results to enhance ADHD diagnosis using multi-feature data and improve understanding of brain regions and interactions unique to the disorder. The data used in this study demonstrated significant correlations between ADHD symptoms and various brain areas, as well as interactions between ADHD subtypes and their respective symptom presentations. These correlations and differences highlight ADHD's complexity as a pure, inattention-based disorder (ADHD-inatt) and an impulsive-based disorder (ADHD-impt). Therefore, multi-feature data has the potential to improve diagnosing and understanding pure ADHD as well as ADHD-inatt and ADHD-impt. To achieve this, future research can employ multi-feature data from rs-fMRI and advanced machine learning algorithms to differentiate ADHD-inatt, ADHD-impt, and healthy controls, potentially leading to new insights into these populations' distinct symptom profiles and their connections to brain regions and interactions. In distinct-time networks, connections between nodes are established at specific points in time and remain active until a termination time is reached, unlike permanent networks where connections persist from establishment to removal. Considering this transient nature, we develop a theoretical framework for an epidemic SISI model applied to distinct-time networks, assuming that node states switch according to a probability distribution that varies over time. We derive analytical formulas for the probability distributions of the epidemic outbreak and the delayed onset of the epidemic within a limited time period, and these results are validated through numerical simulations. Moreover, we investigate the effects of network topology and time-dependent transmission rates on the epidemic spread. This work aims to provide insights into understanding and forecasting outbreaks in areas with changing connectivity patterns, such as rural and urban regions with varying public transportation systems. Additionally, the assumed non-stochastic model can be utilized to analyze the impact of time-varying transmission rates and network perturbations on the epidemic spread. We hope that the developed framework will contribute to the exploration of complex epidemic models in complex networks. We also provide the derived formulas and numerical results in an open-source code for the purpose of sharing methods and data. Many online discussions begin with abbreviations such as "BP" and "IG" which may be widely known but lack clear definitions, potentially confusing readers. Current approaches to acronym clarification have relied on pre-trained models that explain the meaning of each abbreviation in a given text. However, this method has several limitations, including the generation of irrelevant phrases and failure to consider context. A better approach involves using a dedicated online system, similar to a Wikipedia-style wiki platform, where users can submit and comment on definitions for specific abbreviations. This system, called MadDog, overcomes the limitations of previous methods by providing a comprehensive database and enabling readers to verify and comment on submitted definitions. A comparative evaluation of MadDog's performance against existing models showed improved performance in terms of relevance and human understanding, with readers also expressing a preference for MadDog over other models. Furthermore, MadDog's acronym clarification capability was positively received by online discussion forum users, with feedback indicating that it helped improve the clarity and coherence of discussions. MadDog's source code and dataset are publicly available for reproduction of results. Dataset and source code can be found at https://maddog.ai and https://github.com/maddog-tech/MadDog. For a continuously supported zero-bandwidth Hamiltonian $H$, we develop two approximation schemes for the thermodynamic free energy $F$ and von Neumann entropy $S$ of a quantum system at inverse temperature $\beta$. The first scheme uses the path-integral formula involving $e^{-\beta H}$, which can be approximated through a series of low- and near-unitary transformations. The second scheme leverages the quantum log-Sobolev inequality, which yields an approximation scheme involving a convex function of the density matrix's eigenvalues. Both methods yield sublinear bounds on the error in terms of $\beta$ and time steps, which we illustrate with numerical simulations. The code for these experiments is publicly available at the link provided. In clinical settings, International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding is extensively used to consolidate patients' medical and surgical histories. This is usually done manually, but due to rising healthcare data volumes, automated ICD coding has become crucial for efficient clinical operational processing. Leveraging medical discharge summaries for training, machine learning algorithms can evaluate codes based on level hierarchical relationships, making automated ICD coding possible. This research develops and tests an advanced machine learning model for automated ICD coding, which outperforms existing approaches and demonstrates significant time savings, evaluating 3-5 minutes faster than manual coding. Furthermore, models like this can also facilitate semi-supervised learning by utilizing large amounts of unlabeled patient data for optimization, potentially replacing the need for extensive labeled training datasets. Notably, when combining 162 labeled training examples with a large quantity of unlabeled samples, this model shows improved performance, indicating potential for achieving excellent results with minimal supervised training. This model's capabilities provide a solid foundation for future developments in clinical automatic ICD coding. To fully leverage Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices for machine learning, there's a pressing need to develop algorithms robust against errors generated during quantum processing. Although quantum algorithms can potentially reach a breakthrough in efficiency compared to classical methods, the challenge remains to experimentally demonstrate quantum learning applications. Our work overcomes this hurdle by introducing a comprehensive framework for quantum supervised classification on NISQ devices. This framework encompasses a quantum training process unaffected by errors and equipped with error mitigation techniques for a more accurate outcome. To illustrate the utility of our approach, we showcase a simple example of learning a binary classifier using random data on the IBM QASM simulator and the quantum processor in the IBM Q experience, achieving a notable degree of accuracy with less computational expense. Our protocol serves as a crucial stepping stone for realizing quantum machine learning applications on NISQ devices. Additionally, the project's resources are made available on GitHub to facilitate replication of the study's findings. This information can be found at 10.6084/m1.fhub.2021.44. This research was made possible through the financial support of STFC grant ST/R504512/1. This housing contains all relevant data for the research, along with instructions on how to replicate the study's findings. This data can be accessed at 10.6084/m1.fhub.2021.44. Our results are presented in two main sections. Firstly, we evaluate the effectiveness of our entire training process to educate a quantum state $|\Psi\rangle$ on a binary classification problem, observing that even with error monitoring, the learning process is susceptible to undertraining and overtraining issues. Secondly, we analyze the monitored and unmonitored training behaviors, noticing that the latter benefits from error mitigation to yield comparable performance as the former, yet requiring fewer circuits to achieve the same accuracy. Our study addresses questions previously overlooked in the field, thereby contributing fundamental insights to the development of quantum learning applications on NISQ devices. This information can be found at 10.6084/m1.fhub.2021.44. Our research focuses on the behavior of two training methods, either supervising the learning process or not, while evaluating their accuracy and circuit requirements. This led to a key discovery, namely that supervising the learning process yields better results, albeit at a higher cost, while further examinations are needed to determine the full implications of the learning process. Our work presents the first-ever quantum supervised learning results, obtained using 110 data pairs, with high precision on the quantum experience device

However, traditional differentiable rendering methods fail to account for transmission, reflection, or scattering in non-absorbing materials, leading to inaccurate results.  To address these limitations, we introduce an innovative shadow computation method that not only enhances accuracy but also enables differentiability.  This computational method was inspired by the principles of spectral rendering, employing Fourier series to approximate unknown shading components.  By incorporating Fourier series, our approach generalizes the traditional theory of shading, encompassing transmission, reflection, absorption, and scattering processes.  Furthermore, we introduce the concept of effective shadows, outlining the criteria for effective diffusion, absorption, and scattering of light.  To evaluate our method's effectiveness, we propose two inverse problems: recovering surface reflectance and transmission properties from sparse color samples, and deriving shape information from opaque and transparent object images.  Our results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over baseline approaches, showcasing its ability to accurately resolve complex materials and shapes even with limited input data.  To facilitate further research, we also provide a public implementation of our method, along with datasets for transmission, reflection, and scattering, as well as sparse color samples derived from real-world image datasets. This work presents a comprehensive music dataset, jointly formatted from diverse sources, to facilitate unified representation learning for music sheets, lyrics, and audio. The dataset is called MusicTM-Dataset, comprising MusicTM Images and MusicTM Audio. MusicTM Images is a large collection of visual representations, derived from KumaPDF files, encompassing various formats and exhibiting complexity disparities. MusicTM Audio is a library of audio recordings, obtained from multiple public sources. Our framework enables the development of unified datasets from three-dimensional digital music archives, enhancing research across music information retrieval, music generation, and music semantics through a unifying representation. To validate the efficacy of our proposed method, we employed a multi-task approach, combining pre-trained music sheet, audio, and text encoders, to achieve promising results on three distinct music-related identification tasks. Our code and dataset are publicly accessible for reproduction of our results. Additionally, the dataset has been contributed to the Music Information Retrieval Consortium for standardized research and development. Our research aims to bridge the domain gap between disparate music entities and foster research within the music information retrieval community. A powerfully efficient process known as self-organization enables basic molecular assemblies to develop and evolve into intricate, living cells. These aggregates are formed through a combination of distinct organic and fatty molecules derived from various lipids, which interact with each other in aqueous environments. We carried out a series of experiments using various combinations of fatty acids and amino compounds to understand their capacity for self-organization. By examining the structural properties of obtained membrane aggregates, we determined the optimal mixtures that enable successful membrane formation. Interestingly, these membrane aggregates remained stable for several days at room temperature, displaying order and complexity similar to that of cell membranes. We further explored the potential for self-organization by adjusting the mixture compositions and temperatures, observing the emergence of distinct patterns in fluorescence microscopy images. These results indicate that a wide range of biomolecular aggregates can be formed through self-organization, potentially serving as templates for the development of artificial cellular structures. However, the relationship between these phenomena has not been extensively researched. Our work presents unique data - including the first quantitative analysis of sunspots revving - which shows a significant and steady increase in magnetic disturbances when they speed up. Additionally, our findings reveal a substantial connection between violent eruptions and and rapid rotation of sunspots, as well as the reorganization of large magnetic structures in the upper levels of the sun's atmosphere. Through our analysis, we identify an intense and powerful magnetic event that occurred on November 6, 2013, associated with a major M6.3 class eruption in NOAA AR 11429. A close examination of video footage tracks the emergence of a large magnetic structure that causes chaos in the sun's upper atmosphere, lasting for over two and a half hours. Our study for the first time identifies the early signs of a sunspot revolution, which is a large magnetic event that causes mayhem in the sun's upper atmosphere, leading to a massive increase in magnetic disturbances when there are flare like activity in the region. Gromov's nonfoldability theorem is a key result supporting the b-principle, 
a fundamental concept in modern mathematics. This chapter focuses on 
Mumford's nondegeneracy hypothesis, a critical aspect of the b-principle for 
moduli spaces of bundle connections. We establish that this hypothesis holds 
true for several key examples, including spaces of connections on torus bundles 
and certain groups of diffeomorphisms, effectively proving the accuracy of 
Mumford's nondegeneracy hypothesis in these contexts. Additionally, this work 
leads to the development of a new method for constructing Gromov's collapsibility 
sequences in moduli spaces of connections, as well as introducing a flexible 
framework for formulating and demonstrating local nonarithmeticity. We use 
Gromov's nonfoldability theorem to demonstrate the nonarithmeticity of the 
moduli space of connections on a specific torus bundle, and apply a novel 
construction technique to prove the nondegeneracy hypothesis for connections 
on torus bundles with singularities. We also show that the completion of the 
moduli space of connections on a specific torus bundle with singularities is a 
hyperbolic surface, and establish cut-and-paste principles for connections, 
which can be used to build new examples of nondegeneracy hypotheses. Finally, 
we use a cut-and-paste principle to prove the nondegeneracy hypothesis for 
connections on a specific surface with three holes and additional singularities. 
We believe the techniques developed in this chapter will yield a comprehensive 
proof of the nondegeneracy hypothesis for connections on a specific surface 
with various singularities and three holes for any value of the slope. We 
also anticipate applying the methods and results of this chapter to explore 
the fundamental group of the completion of the moduli space of connections on 
a specific surface with one hole and additional singularities. We expect the 
results of this chapter will provide significant insights into the nature of 
this group and allow us to construct new hyperbolic surfaces through completion. 
We also believe the results of this chapter will enable us to build a 
collapsibility sequence for the moduli space of connections on a specific surface 
with one hole and additional singularities, effectively demonstrating the 
nonfoldability of this space in this context. 

Note: A draft version of the proposed chapter appears on the arXiv 
under the title "The b-principle for surface symplectic groups".

This work examines how different hyperparameters influence the performance and ranking of evolutionary algorithms in solving problems, utilizing techniques such as Sobol and Pearson correlation analysis to gauge their impact. By employing this approach, the collective effect of multiple hyperparameters can be effectively appraised, thus facilitating a more comprehensive understanding, which in turn can guide future investigations. To illustrate the applicability of this method, a study involving the optimization of cutting tool surfaces based on material removal rates was conducted. Results indicate that the eigenvalue-based optimization method is highly sensitive to its leading eigenvalue, while clustering-based techniques are relatively insensitive to their respective hyperparameters. This research outlines a proposed framework for integrating global sensitivity analysis into the process of optimizing evolutionary algorithms, which could serve as a practical guide for researchers. Additionally, the findings presented here are designed to facilitate replication, and the associated sources, including HyperCopos, have been made available. Further investigation of this approach may yield improved results by incorporating additional methods from the literature. The ultimate objective of this research is to enable closed-loop optimization of evolutionary algorithms, which could potentially lead to improved efficiency and more robust evaluations. The findings presented here are an essential step toward achieving this goal. Open-source reinforcement learning evaluations have played a crucial role in
advancing model performance assessment and comparison. However, current benchmarks
are subject to solution completion, effectively terminating the evaluation process
once the agent achieves the goal. In contrast, many real-world scenarios require
ongoing and infinite evaluation to account for various contingencies. To address
this gap, we present a continuous evaluation framework called L2Explorer, which
supports sequential assessment of agents capable of learning from experience.
L2Explorer utilizes a real-world navigation task, mimicked using a large 2D
world, to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed evaluation methodology. This
approach enables simultaneous comparison of various agents and scenarios,
demonstrating its practical application for analyzing the effects of methodological
choices on model performance. Code for this framework is available on GitHub at
https://github.com/learn2learn/L2Explorer. We invite the research community to
participate in evaluating the model's robustness using our continuous evaluation
platform at https://l2eval.org. We intend to maintain this platform to support
the research community and update it regularly with fresh evaluation challenges. 

In contrast to static evaluation environments that only assess agent performance
once the goal is achieved, this research proposes a dynamic evaluation framework
capable of monitoring agent performance throughout the learning process, thus
better accommodating scenarios requiring ongoing learning. As an initial test of
this framework's capabilities, we apply it to agents navigating a 2D world with
mysterious obstacles and unpredictable rules, where the framework's real-time
monitoring of agent performance helps identify the learned policies and detects
unexpected irregularities in the model's behavior. This research demonstrates
the potential of continuous evaluation to improve the assessment of reinforcement
learning models. The framework, along with the code used in this study, is
available at https://github.com/learn2learn/L2Explorer, and we invite the research
community to participate in evaluating the model's robustness using our continuous
evaluation platform at https://l2eval.org. We plan to regularly update the
platform with fresh evaluation challenges. 

This research introduces continuous evaluation, a concept tested on models learning
to navigate a 2D world with unknown rules and obstructive environments. The
resulting framework monitors agent performance in real-time and helps identify
the learned policies, ultimately detecting irregularities in the model's
behavior. Notably, continuous evaluation stands in contrast to traditional
evaluation methods that only assess performance once the goal is achieved.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 5.4 micrometers, Liger combines multiple optical systems into one, offering improved sensitivity and resolution. This enhanced performance will facilitate the detection of abundant molecular species and high-resolution kinematic information in various astronomical targets at low to moderate angular resolutions. To maximize Liger's capabilities, a data processing system and custom software are being developed to analyze and manipulate the complex device data. This processing system will feature a quick data rejection mechanism to rapidly filter out imperfect data readings and ensure maximum utilization of the device's capabilities. Additionally, our system will incorporate a calibration module that corrects detector responses and account for variable atmospheric conditions, as well as a module that extracts scientific information from the data while accounting for the device's intricacies. This processing system will be connected to a data reduction pipeline through a software framework, allowing for seamless data exchange and streamlining the analysis process. This submission outlines the design and development of the data processing system and describes the various software connections that enable Liger to meet its performance requirements. It also highlights our approach to testing and verifying the system's correctness and efficiency. Finally, this presentation previews our plans for integrating the data processing system with the device and telescope infrastructure to ensure seamless operation during actual observations. Keywords: Liger, data processing system, infrared device, W. M. Keck Observatory, spectrograph, on-device processing, calibration, spectroscopic analysis.

Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, yielding fine structure modes along the trap's axis and orthogonal to it. These modes are selectively occupied by the condensate. Our results reveal a unique method for polarization control with potential applications in spin-based photonics and research on complex optical systems with adjustable coupling properties. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability to dynamically change the occupation ratio between these modes using optical intensity that can shift and rotate to match the fine structure. This allows switching between different occupation patterns. These include hybrid modes, increased occupation ratio due to coupling, and modified polarization control compared to isolated condensates. Furthermore, coupling enables the adjustment of a predetermined fine structure alignment through a balancing act of occupancy. A strengthened version of Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture has been formulated and proven. 
Given two additive subsets A and B of Z, where |A| = |B| = k, our research aims to find 
a partition of A ∪ B into four subsets a, b, c, d such that the sumsets a + b, b + c, c + d, 
and d + a have nonnegligible intersections in order to establish a nonlinear equation relating A and B. 
In particular, if A and B satisfy the condition that 2A − A intersects 2B − B, 
the a, b, c, d partitions can be chosen as a translation of A and B respectively, 
resulting in the sumsets a + b, b + c, c + d, and d + a all being the same set. 
In contrast to earlier proofs which relied heavily on graph theory, the current research uses an inductive approach. 
This new result can potentially lead to a solution for the sum-product problem in finite fields. 
Moreover, the concept of Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture can also be applied to the realm of finite abelian groups. 
Finally, an example is provided that showcases a situation in which the sums of two randomly selected elements in Z mod n result in a distribution that is as evenly spaced as possible. 
This research is a continuation of the work previously done by Ruzsa and Zarankiewicz. 
In particular, the upper limit on the size of the additive subsets A and B has been increased from k to k + o(k). 
The constant factor representing the difference has been proven to be arbitrarily small, with its lower limit determined by the research hypothesis of the 3k-4 conjecture, 
which states that the difference in sizes between a + b and b + a is less than o(o(k)) for any additive subsets A and B of size k. 
The Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture's research hypothesis also asserts that the difference in sizes between a + b and b + a is always less than o(k). 
The current research proves that if the distribution of two additive subsets A and B in Z is such that their sumsets a + b, b + c, c + d, and d + a have nonnegligible intersections, 
then the difference in sizes between a + b and b + a is bounded above by a factor of o(o(k))

This research introduces a novel multimodal approach to classifying glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy using joint image and patient information analysis.
