Specifically, the study combines optic disc and macula regions of interest (ROIs) to analyze images, extracts relevant features, and integrates them with patient demography. Notably, this study also explores the effect of technical difficulties during image capture on model outcomes, ultimately improving glaucoma detection and diabetic retinopathy diagnosis through a comprehensive evaluation of clinical and image data. Evaluation metrics include area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUC-ROC), loss functions, confusion matrices, feature importance, and model generalization assessment via the ocular dataset's varied subsets. Results demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses baseline image-based models and validates the significance of both image and demography features in glaucoma and DR classification. Additionally, this work underscores the importance of considering technical difficulties as a distinct condition, rather than a model anomaly. The findings support the use of combined image and demography data in the classification of ocular diseases. Two types of boundary conditions are examined - Dirichlet and Neumann - leading to the construction of scattering matrix profiles for both cases through numerical methods. Ultimately, this framework's ability to resolve differing boundary conditions is demonstrated, setting the stage for exploring more complex boundary coatings and generalized radial functions. Additionally, this study's findings are motivated by recent studies on transmission eigenfunctions and their sparsity, as well as the mathematical tools employed to analyze the stability and convergence of the proposed method. The global simplicial bundle, defined as a specific type of simplicial bundle, possesses characteristics similar to those of a classical fiber bundle. Specifically, the formation of global simplicial bundles is invariant under category functors that preserve simplicial structure, and this property is a consequence of a more general theorem. The relationship between global simplicial bundles and classical fiber bundles is also explored in the paper. It is demonstrated that there is a functorial relationship between these two categories, and it is shown that a global simplicial bundle is equivalent to a classical fiber bundle when certain conditions are met. The paper further delves into the homotopy theory of global simplicial bundles and establishes relationships between these bundles and the simplicial sets formed by the homotopy classes of maps between these sets. The resulting general theory is demonstrated through a range of examples, including global simplicial bundles that are equivalent to classical fiber bundles, as well as instances of distinct global simplicial bundles that are nonetheless homotopy equivalent. The paper concludes with a discussion of the weight structure present in the category of global simplicial bundles, and it is shown that this weight structure is non-trivial. The weight structure can be interpreted as a form of homotopy coherence, and it is a result of the functors that map global simplicial bundles to the simplicial sets formed by the homotopy classes of maps between these sets. The weights in this structure can be seen as a way of extending the concept of homotopy classes to the simplicial setting. The paper goes on to describe the unitary global simplicial bundle, a specific type of global simplicial bundle that is obtained by extending the unitary bundle functor to the simplicial setting. The resulting bundle is characterized by its role in the homotopy theory of global simplicial bundles, and it is shown to be a key component in the weight structure present in this category. The paper concludes with a discussion of the further study of global simplicial bundles, and it outlines two areas of research that remain to be explored. The adaptation involved transforming the variables $x$ and $y$ into $xy$ and $y^2-x$, and substituting $x=1$ to eliminate a singular point, while replacing $y$ with $z$ to account for another singular point. This research provides a theoretical framework for understanding associated costs in quantum systems and sheds light on the behavior of entanglement within these systems. An individual's social connections are intricately woven into daily life, affecting behaviors and habits. Understanding social structures requires accurate visual representations of these connections, which can be learned from various data sources. Existing methods for generating social relationship graphs prioritize either accuracy or aesthetics but often fail to balance both. To address this limitation, we present a comprehensive approach for creating visually appealing social relationship graphs that also accurately depict the underlying social framework. Our method leverages social media data, targeting nodes with the fewest connections, and employs force-directed graph layouts to optimize aesthetics. To evaluate its effectiveness, we created graphs for prominent social media figures, achieving high accuracy and improved aesthetics. Furthermore, our approach outperformed existing methods in various benchmarks. The source code for our approach is freely available on GitHub. 

Note: The source code is at https://github.com/socialgs/socialgs. GitHub is a version control platform where users can collaborate by sharing and updating code across various projects. 

We also developed a web-based demo for interactive visualization, available at https://social-relationship-graphs.herokuapp.com. Heroku is a platform that enables users to deploy web applications directly from their repositories, making it easy to share interactive visualizations with others. 

Please contact us at sgs@masonlab.org for further assistance or to request customized social relationship graphs. We are committed to providing modified graphs that adhere to your specific requirements.

Finally, we'll examine the practical implications of this cost-conscious perspective, and explore potential future improvements in how we implement it. This includes leveraging additional hardware features, like advanced trigonic units, to further reduce overhead. This survey aims to provide a helpful perspective on how we currently approach hardware-efficient implementations, and it's hoped that it will contribute to continued advancements in this field. The RF Booster theme aims to contribute to the development of future collider projects, both domestically and internationally. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum independent set, yielding a 2-EPAS (exponential-time polynomial-time approximation scheme).

We introduce a simple PTAS for sparse weighted CSPs using LP relaxation and the Sherali-Adams LP for specific constraint classes, achieving this without assuming monotonicity in the constraints. This result generalizes the previous findings for specific graph classes and the application of LP relaxation to finite-domain CSPs by Jonsson, Jenssen, and Zivny. 

A key contribution of our method involves accurately solving the LP in a specific graph class, which we call FLC (full-trace label collapsing graph class). This class includes graphsthat have a limited number of biconnected components and those that can be transformed into such graphs by removing vertices. We demonstrate that FLC includes various graph classes such as: 

*   sparse instance of unique-satisfiability (USAT),
*   minimum vertex cover with a solution ratio of L(0) = 1,
*   maximum cut,
*   minimum biclique,
*   and others.

We show that for any FLC, we can find a solution with a ratio of at least L(n) = 7/3 after O(n^3) LP iterations, which can be used for developing a PTAS. This result generalizes the previous findings for specific graph classes achieved by Baker, Jonsson, Jenssen, and Zivny.

In the standard RAM model, implementing basic arithmetic operations like subtraction and multiplication typically requires linear time if only addition is allowed for operations and input retrieval. We aim to identify all constant-time computable functions when only these two operations are available, considering the ability to use the base address as a variable. We demonstrate that this is feasible for several notable functions, including specific power functions, the counting number of 1s in binary, and the alignment metric in specific scenarios. We also show that, aside from a limited set of operations, all constant-time executables for these two operations compute a polynomial or quasi-polynomial function. We define and utilize the terms "polynomial" and "quasi-polynomial" within the context of RAM model computability. We further prove that executing a polynomial or quasi-polynomial computation using addition alone is feasible in O(n^k) or O(n^<α(n)>) time, where n represents the input size, and α(n) denotes the least common multiple of the integers from 2 to n. We establish that this result yields constant-time execution for specific divide-and-conquer algorithms, such as merge sort and quicksort, under particular conditions on the input distribution. We also present the implementation details for a constant-time sorting algorithm in the RAM model using addition. We provide further potential research directions in this area. We introduce "quasi-polynomials" as a novel concept to analyze RAM model computability and demonstrate their practical utility in this context. We execute a thorough write-up of the current state of research in this area, presenting an in-depth examination of the underlying mathematics and RAM model computability principles involved. We introduce a novel approach to tackle questions in theoretical computer science using the additive RAM model, drawing on connections between these two fields, as previously explored in the article additive_ram_model. We illustrate the versatility of the RAM model through examples, demonstrating that it can be used to analyze various existing algorithms under specific input conditions. We introduce the idea of aligning integers in binary as a computable function in the RAM model and demonstrate its practical applications. Several session-based recommendation techniques have been developed in response to the rise of mobile e-commerce. These techniques combine past session information with current ongoing sessions to make predictions, and often rely on rich context from specific sessions to enhance their performance. However, these techniques often fail to utilize the inherent connections within user behavior patterns across different sessions. To address this, we propose a new method called SGR, which uses an adaptive graph neural network to analyze user behavior within and across sessions, and makes recommendations based on this dual perspective. SGR co-trains two modules: one focuses on intra-session links within each session, while the other discovers inter-session links across multiple sessions. By combining these modules, SGR can make recommendations that take both short-term and long-term user preferences into account. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of SGR over existing recommendation methods. To implement this method, we created a session-based user graph from historical data and derived node embeddings through the matrix factorization of this graph. This allows each session and corresponding item to be represented as informative embeddings. These embeddings are used to guide a co-training process involving an intra-session module (processing individual sessions) and an inter-session module (analyzing the user's overall historical behavior). The two modules exchange information to generate a unified representation for each session, which is then used to make recommendations. The intra-session module applies a graph attention neural network to each session to emphasize key items, while the inter-session module applies a multi-layer perceptron to the user's overall historical behavior. The two modules are trained simultaneously on different views of the data to enhance the representation. The method was evaluated on four real-world datasets and compared with previous recommendation techniques, and demonstrated improvements in relevance and click rates. However, it did not perform well when user-length session datasets were used due to the lack of a clear starting point for each session. The method also has potential applications in e-commerce and other mobile recommendation scenarios where rich context from specific sessions can enhance performance. The code for this method has been made available on GitHub. To address the variability within each session, we used an adaptive graph neural network to analyze user behavior within each session. The method also discovered inter-session links across multiple sessions to provide a longer-term perspective. The two modules were trained simultaneously to exchange information and generate a unified representation for each session. We investigate the role of interactions within a one-dimensional non-Hermitian system characterized by a quantum circuit based on SU(N) symmetry, where N is 2 or 3. Using a higher-order topological theory, we show that interactions can either strengthen or weaken a system's point-gap topology, depending on the specific details of the interaction. In particular, we find that two-range interactions destroy the bulk-edge transition associated with the system, while multi-body interactions can still exhibit topological characteristics. Additionally, we find that certain interactions can weaken a system's resilience to point-gap topology, while other interactions can improve it. Specifically, an L1-infinity norm interaction can reduce a system's sensitivity to point-gap topology, while an L2 norm interaction can improve it. We perform exact analytic calculations on these interactions within the context of two-dimensional lattice models and find similar results. Furthermore, we investigate how interactions affect a system's spectral properties, including its distribution of eigenvalues and the location of its largest eigenvalue. Our results show that a certain interaction can move a spectral edge away from the origin, while another interaction can move it closer to the origin. These findings indicate that interactions can either enhance or weaken a system's point-gap topology, and we hope that these results will guide the development of interaction-engineered materials. Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of hate speech, which is having severe repercussions on societies worldwide. One type of hate speech, misogyny, is particularly hazardous and has been on the rise on social media platforms. To combat this issue, we developed an advanced machine learning system capable of detecting misogynic content and categorizing it into two categories (abusive or non-abusive) on Arabic social media. Our approach employed a dual-task architecture, incorporating two models: one that identifies misogynic content and another that categorizes the content into abusive or non-abusive categories, using a binary classification system. To improve the models' performance, we employed various data augmentation techniques, such as BERT, FastText, and lexical techniques. Our experiments were conducted on an Instagram dataset and the results demonstrate that our models achieved outstanding performance, achieving accuracy rates of 98% for misogyny detection and 97% for binary classification, surpassing several baseline models. One particular model, which combined BERT and FastText, achieved a remarkable 0.985 AUC for misogyny detection and 0.976 AUC for binary classification. Our study's success could pave the way for the utilization of similar systems in practice to combat hate speech on social media platforms. The code for our project is openly accessible on GitHub for other researchers to build upon. Additionally, our team has won the Arab Twitter Misogyny Challenge hosted by the Semantic Technological Challenge Group. We introduce a novel scheme known as FiDeCo, enabling encoded caching and decentralized computation through a single, versatile construction. FiDeCo utilizes a private encoding function, a public decoding function, and an access function that utilize a randomly generated encoded vector. We demonstrate that FiDeCo can emulate various prominent schemes founded on matrices, such as sCDS and eCDS, as well as CDS based on graphs or codes, thereby establishing its universality. We also investigate a generalized version of FiDeCo, dubbed Gen-FiDeCo, which accommodates a selection of distinct private encoding functions. Our analysis reveals that both FiDeCo and Gen-FiDeCo can achieve a comparable or better performance compared to their non-encoded counterparts and can attain a substantial reduction in computation and data storage requirements. Furthermore, we provide a joint construction for combining FiDeCo or Gen-FiDeCo with access structures enabled by secret sharing, thereby expanding their potential applications. We present numerical examples to showcase the practical benefits of FiDeCo and Gen-FiDeCo in terms of the resulting computation and storage loads on individual devices, as well as the impact on security in scenarios involving enabled access structures. These examples illustrate that both schemes can substantially minimize these loads while maintaining comparable levels of security. Additionally, we propose a method for determining an optimal private encoding function that maximizes the feasible size of distributed encoded vectors, thereby achieving the highest possible access structure parameters for a given data vector. This method involves computing the largest possible rank of orthogonal matrices and can be applied to various data vectors, which may originate from sources such as data streams or other encoded caching and decentralized computation schemes. We provide numerical instances that demonstrate the practical usefulness of this approach. Lastly, we discuss potential extensions and areas of research that these results have enabled. One potential area of research is the development of specific constructions of private encoding and public decoding functions tailored to particular data sources or access structures. This could lead to more efficient and scalable implementations of FiDeCo and Gen-FiDeCo. Another area of research could involve exploring the performance limits of encoded caching and decentralized computation schemes; in particular, it is unknown whether non-trivial cases of CDS based on graphs or codes exist where the data size is smaller than the number of nodes. Further investigation is needed to resolve this issue. Finally, another area of research could involve combining encoded caching and decentralized computation with other security schemes to enable multi-layer security mechanisms. In particular, it is unknown whether FiDeCo or Gen-FiDeCo can be combined with secret sharing while maintaining security

A key step in the argument of Interlands and Jiang's work involves a specific linear combination of Eisenstein series that enables one to obtain an expression for Dirichlet L-functions at integral points. This paper presents a novel combinatorial approach to evaluate the same linear combination of Eisenstein series used by Interlands and Jiang. Our method yields individual terms of the combination that can be explicitly defined using the action of Casimir elements on intertwining operators between irreducible constituents of $\pi\otimes\pi^{1,0}$. This paper provides a detailed analysis of those constituents and the action of Casimir elements to gauge the influence of Interlands and Jiang's parameter $m$ in their work. Our findings also cover the instances where a constituent is stimulated by the action of $m$. Natural language processing has a crucial role in understanding digital content, and one of the key challenges, also known as the information overload issue, is being addressed by text summarization. This problem is being tackled by researchers through two primary approaches: one is invasive, requiring actual language use, and the other is reactive, relying on statistical methods. This paper presents an innovative solution to the text summarization problem by leveraging graph-based techniques. Our proposed method employs graphs to identify essential sentences that capture the core meaning of the given text. This method's effectiveness was evaluated and compared with established datasets, including the Reuters dataset, and our experimental findings indicate significant improvements in accuracy when using this method. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that this method's performance can be enhanced by utilizing various sentence extraction techniques. By comparing the outcomes, we conclude that the graph-based method outperforms the traditional RAKE (Text summarization via Ranking Aggregating and Kinetic depth) algorithm in F1 measure by a margin of up to 107%. Additionally, our method boasts a notable advantage of being able to generate summaries for content without prior summaries being extracted. This method's potential applications include, but are not limited to, summarizing meetings, forums, and social media posts. The source code for this project has been made publicly available on GitHub. The graph-based method's performance can be replicated using the provided specifications, and our analysis suggests that this method can be further optimized by extracting graphs from actual text rather than synthetic data. A longstanding problem posed by Turan's nearly 90-year-old challenge has yet to be fully resolved, despite significant progress by Erdos and Galvin. This problem, concerning the creation of combinatorial structures with specified missing substructures, has been tackled using the probabilistic method and various structural techniques. This paper addresses Turan's tetrahedron challenge by providing nearly exact counts for the maximum size of tetrahedron-free graphs, achieving a gap of at most two from the predicted extremal constructions. This progress is achieved using the framework of Kalonji's restricted sum sets and a novel structural property for tetrahedron-free graphs. This paper also proves a generalization of the Erdos-Zahl conjecture in the context of the $\ell_2$-metric, indicating that the diameter of tetrahedron-free graphs tends towards two. This result is also generalized to the $s$-claw free graphs and the $\ell_p$-metric for $p<2$, and could be applied to other graph structures using the framework of Bollobas' hypergraph theory. This research provides new insights and potentially useful tools for addressing general questions concerning the absence of specific substructures in graphs. This paper also uses and develops the framework of Kalonji's restricted sum sets, and a novel structural property for $s$-claw free graphs, and provides new estimates for the maximum size of $s$-claw free 3-uniform hypergraphs. These estimates achieve a gap of at most three from the predicted extremal constructions. This research also addresses a question posed by Bollobas and Thomason by providing upper and lower bounds for the minimum degree in sparse $s$-claw free graphs. This research also generalizes the Erdos-Zahl conjecture in the context of the $\ell_p$-metric for $p<2$, and proves new estimates for the maximum size of tetrahedron-free graphs in the $\ell_p$-metric for $p<2$, and the $s$-claw free graphs in the $\ell_p$-metric for $p<2$. Achieving a seamless visual experience and map data accuracy is crucial for navigating complex locations effectively. While system requirements need to consider account for the level of detail, rendering map lines necessitates an anti-aliasing technique to counteract pixelation. This is particularly important when users view the map, as line anti-aliasing enhances visibility, particularly for cyclists and pedestrians. Unfortunately, current methods are inefficient for line maps, causing a subpar user experience. In response, we've developed an optimized anti-aliasing technique for mapping line segments, producing a high-quality visual output while minimizing computational burden. Specifically, we combined spatial coherence and color information to eliminate unwanted aliasing effects. Our approach incorporates a system for identifying coherence areas, determining a color gradient mode, and refining line coordinates for a clear visual outcome. By comparing our method against five standard anti-aliasing approaches, we demonstrate a substantial improvement in performance, achieving up to 60% faster rendering times. Moreover, our technique demonstrates a 4 to 6 times faster execution speed when map data is simplified, outperforming alternative methods significantly. As a result, we've made this algorithm available as an open-source component, enabling developers to integrate it into their global navigation-service platforms and ensure a seamless user experience. This includes a sample code snippet, our test dataset, and a demonstration video illustrating the efficacy of our line anti-aliasing technique. In addition, we've provided an open-source vector rendering engine with an implemented line anti-aliasing technique, allowing users to customize their map rendering for a superior visual experience. Our technique is designed for compatibility with various platforms, including Android, iOS, and desktop environments, tailored to meet the requirements of global navigation-service providers. By offering an open-source implementation, we've made it possible for developers to integrate a high-quality, anti-aliasing map rendering algorithm into their platforms. This includes a range of features, such as color-based line merging and spatial coherence filtering, to ensure a clear and readable map display, especially for users engaged in cycling and pedestrian activities. Moreover, we've enabled map data simplification to enhance performance, achieving a balance between a pleasing visual outcome and efficient rendering times. In fact, our algorithm is now used in several prominent global navigation services, demonstrating its superiority and versatility. This knowledge has further informed the development of our algorithm, guiding efforts to optimize and refine the technique. As a result, we've achieved a high-quality map rendering approach, distinguishing ourselves from six compared methods through performance, code efficiency, and user experience considerations

Recent research has focused on developing session-based suggestion systems, which learn user interests within the context of a session - a series of related activities - and provide relevant recommendations by analyzing the transitions between these activities. Most existing systems utilize session-driven suggestions to enhance existing interfaces and enhance user interactions; however, these systems often struggle to express the diversity of available options. To address this limitation, we introduce CRRS - a framework for creating suggestion systems that combine the hierarchical representation of potential outcomes with the granular suggestion of relevant options. By dividing the suggested actions into distinct groups, users can easily navigate the hierarchy and explore specific recommendations within those categories. Furthermore, we propose two-phase and two-domain approaches to CRRS, which allow users to engage with two sessions at the same time and receive relevant suggestions from two different domains. We evaluated these systems through two user studies, which demonstrate that they improve user experience compared to existing suggestion systems. We further showcase the flexibility of our method by applying it to two real-world scenarios - Twitter's activity timeline and Wikipedia's edit history - and provide guidance for developers on designing and implementing this type of suggestion system. Our work opens up new avenues for designing suggestion systems that combine hierarchical and granular suggestion techniques. Furthermore, our research enables editors to target specific aspects of articles for improvement, enhancing their editing experience and promoting more focused collaboration among users. While our work specifically addresses Wikipedia's needs, our proposed solution can be adapted to enhance the quality of other user-generated content projects. In machine learning, knowledge transfer allows models to exploit information from other models, often achieving better results.  Most knowledge transfer studies have concentrated on using data to move information between models.  In contrast, this research explores the possibility of transferring knowledge without data, relying solely on evaluation outcomes.  Using a black-box framework that makes decisions based on input, we developed a zero-shot knowledge transfer technique that extracts relevant information from successful models and applies it to new situations without prior experience.  The technique does not require detailed insight into either the successful models or the new situations.  Testing the approach using decision-making sets, we found that it consistently performs as well or better than models trained directly on the new situations, and also improves existing models.  Specifically, using sets of graphs, networks, and text, we found that decision-quality scores increased by an average of 25% or more.  In particular, applying the technique to data-driven policy optimization, we found that decision-quality scores increased by as much as fourfold.  Thus, this study demonstrates that decision-based black-box models can successfully transfer information without data, achieving better results in a wide range of situations.  As a result, decision-based black-box models have considerable potential for use in a wide range of applications.  Moreover, this research lays the foundation for future studies aimed at improving decision-based black-box models.  In particular, we propose the following research directions: (a) using different types of models, such as universal and probabilistic systems; (b) exploring the theoretical underpinnings of decision-based black-box models; (c) applying the technique to other domains, such as reinforcement learning and natural language processing.  In addition, we provide publicly accessible code and data for reproducing the results presented in this research.  Further details are available online at https://zsbk-tutorial.github.io/. While point cloud data is ideal for capturing complex shapes, existing methods fail to utilize this data effectively, instead relying on reconstructed RGBD clips that lack the original depth maps. To address this limitation, we present a new framework for engaging clusters in multi-timepoint point cloud datasets. Our method involves building a cluster-based graph to track hands and objects, and then utilizing a unified model for existing and missing data to reconstruct interactions from various viewpoints. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through qualitative and quantitative evaluations on the SOGC and DOBS datasets, and showcase its ability to rebuild engagements using a small number of timepoints, accurately detect existing interactions in the SOGC dataset, and compare favorably to current state-of-the-art methods in the DOBS dataset. Additionally, we provide a method for assessing engagement similarity, and showcase its utility in discovering latent engagement categories. Our proposed approach aims to improve analysis of hand-object interactions by leveraging their native depth map representation. This is achieved through monitoring and rebuilding engagements using multiple timepoints and graph-based clustering to handle varying hands and objects. Our method compares favorably to current state-of-the-art methods in the DOBS dataset. The code and datasets can be accessed via https://github.com/marcom1neto/ReconstructENGAGE. We have successfully tested these methods on a robot-depth camera setup with varying backgrounds, achieving accurate results with only a few frames. Our method not only saves time but also adapts to changing backgrounds, making it suitable for applications where markers cannot be used and kinetic sensors are not practical. Our code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Gruppe-Adler/LearnAndAdapt. In various studies, the complexity of artificial neural networks was evaluated using different metrics, however these studies overlooked one significant factor: the intricate structure of the networks. When attempting to find a simple solution, networks often converge to one that is intricately structured. To rectify this, we introduced a new metric that quantifies a neural network's complexity based on its layout. By applying this metric to multiple tasks, we discovered that a straightforward, universal guideline emerges: easy problems require low-complexity layouts, while hard problems require high-complexity layouts. Moreover, we found that the best general outcome occurs when the complexity of the problem is matched with the complexity of the corresponding neural network layout. To achieve this, we developed an automated method for transforming layouts into simple neural architectures, which we named layout-based parameter pruning. When used on several benchmarks, our method consistently outperformed alternative complexity reduction techniques, demonstrating that the simplicity and complexity of artificial neural networks are interconnected concepts. The source code for our project is available at https://github.com/ja-jav/ja-neur-core/. Additionally, the datasets used in our research can be found at https://ja-jav.github.io/ja-neur-core/data.html. Consequently, we propose a novel approach called LAYPR, which can transform intricate neural layouts into simpler architectures by pruning relevant parameters. An implementation of LAYPR is available at https://ja-jav.github.io/ja-neur-core/laypr.html. The marginal dependence framework is a widely used approach in analyzing joint probability distributions. It involves representing joint models of two or more variables as the product of individual probability distributions, along with a dependence structure that reflects the relationships between these marginals. This framework has several benefits, including simplified estimation and predictive analysis. However, the underlying structure of marginal dependence models remains unclear, which hinders the interpretation of results. In this dissertation, I introduce two new models that fall under the marginal dependence framework: the applications of copula-based and time series analysis frameworks. The first model incorporates discrete and continuous variables within a single system, while the second model utilizes dynamic vine copulas to model interdependent time series data. I demonstrate the effectiveness of these models through empirical studies, which highlight their capabilities in capturing both joint and individual behavior in data, while also facilitating the estimation of dependency structure and risk assessments. The marginal dependence framework holds immense promise, and I hope that the proposed models will contribute to further development in this area. The associated R packages, including RDD and dvineCopula, have been designed to facilitate the implementation and demonstration of these models, along with relevant data sets (available at <https://www.uv.nl/en/research/Projects/MARGINAL-DEPENDENCE>()). A prospective framework for intergenerational mobility implies that expectations about future outcomes influence behavior when outcomes are unpredictable and vary randomly.  In this setting, society's opportunity structure affects individual aspirations, resulting in a social dynamic.  As more individuals with higher expectations achieve better outcomes, their aspirations increase, creating a self-reinforcing cycle.  To model this process, we use a discrete-time model with prospect theory-based preferences, assuming expectations are initially equal to average outcomes.  As time progresses without knowledge of the future, expectations decrease, and individuals become dissatisfied with their current state, leading to demands for social and economic change.  This theory provides a possible explanation for phenomena like the Great Society movements in the US and the UK's 2016 Brexit referendum.  To test our model, we employ a simulated structural approach using data from the US and UK, revealing that expectations decrease over time, and increases in income inequality and instability boost dissatisfaction, while factors like education and social connections can boost prospects and thus satisfaction.  As a result of these findings, we propose the creation of social and economic safety nets, as well as increased investment in education and community-building to boost prospects and reduce discontent.  Furthermore, our model suggests a need for ongoing efforts to reduce inequality and protect vulnerable groups from economic instability.  While policy initiatives can influence prospects, addressing distributional concerns requires continued action beyond economic growth.  Finally, our theory offers a unique perspective on the relationship between prospects, distribution, and social stability, and could be applied to models of collective action to investigate the conditions under which different social and political movements emerge. The symmetry principles of space and time have a profound impact on the behavior of particles, demonstrating the interconnectedness of their properties.  One fundamental aspect of this principle is the parity operator, defining the spatial inversion reflection.  Historically, parity's influence was linked to the statistics of particles, with a specific relationship established by Jordan and Wigner.  In their work, a direct connection between the parity operator and the exchange statistics of particles was discovered, giving rise to fermion and boson designations.  However, the non-relativistic nature of Jordan and Wigner's result led to a limited number of particle species predicted.  In an attempt to overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the application of a more comprehensive parity transformation, one that accounts for both the spatial and time inversion components, in line with the relativistic spin-statistics equivalence principle.  In this work, a general framework for the relationship between parity and particle statistics is established, enabling the classification of any particle species based on the properties of the parity operator.  Specifically, an exhaustive analysis of the properties of bosons and fermions is presented, with a thorough discussion of the implications of Jordan and Wigner's result.  Furthermore, this research provides a promising approach to identifying novel, complex bosonic systems, such as anyon condensates, through an in-depth examination of a particular bosonic system exhibiting a non-abelian behavior akin to anyon physics.  Finally, the researchers present an open-source code for calculating the parity's eigenvalues, known as ParityChecker, and demonstrate its functionality using a simple bosonic system.  In particular, the ParityChecker code is used to evaluate the parity's eigenvalues for a non-abelian bosonic system, predicting two potential excitations: a bosonic particle and a particle displaying both bosonic and fermionic characteristics.  The researchers speculate on the possibility of achieving a perfect overlap between the parity's eigenvalues and the wave functions of these excitations, enabling the creation of perfect bosonic matter wave interferometers.  Additionally, the wide applicability of the parity's role in modeling particle behavior is emphasized, with this principle may potentially be applied to the development of novel algorithms for simulating anyon condensates.  In conclusion, the established connection between the parity operator and particle statistics, along with related tools and resources, offers a comprehensive approach to understanding the behavior of relativistic particle species. This data is then used to investigate a specific signature consisting of three heavily interacting bosons and considerable amounts of transverse momentum dispersed across three or more distinct regions. A statistical analysis reveals the presence of this signature at 5.2σ confidence, confirming the creation of three substantial gauge bosons. This analysis is then followed by a calculation of cross-sectional probabilities, which measure the frequency of three-boson creations at 13 TeV. This calculation yields estimates of approximately 7.4 fb for three-boson creations and 3.0 fb for two-boson creations at similar energy levels. This measurement marks the first observation of three-boson creations in LHC data, which also validates theoretical predictions using monopole and dipole models. Recent breakthroughs in AI have transformed scientific and engineering research into highly data-driven fields. Nonetheless, significant discrepancies remain between cutting-edge AI methods and conventional modeling approaches employed in various domains. This disparity is largely due to the fact that historical modeling techniques are often disregarded in favor of AI solutions that solely rely on input data, thus overlooking valuable expert knowledge. This thesis aims to bridge this gap by integrating collaborative learning models that utilize both data and expert input. Through detailed case studies in two complex domains - healthcare and finance - we demonstrate that incorporating expert knowledge into AI models can greatly improve their accuracy and reliability, even when expert input is imperfect or incomplete. Moreover, we find that expert-knowledge infused AI models can efficiently identify areas of the models that require expert input and thus need to be modified. This research culminates in the development of a novel deep learning framework that selectively incorporates expert knowledge into AI models. This framework enables the detection of critical model components and guides the transfer of expert knowledge to areas of the model that are in need of improvement. Overall, this thesis underscores the significance of combining expert knowledge with AI methods to reach their full potential. This new paradigm can facilitate the development of more robust, interpretable systems that complement the strengths of both human and machine. This research was influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic and has inspired various applications, such as the development of personalized models and AI-powered diagnostic tools that take into account expert knowledge and individual health characteristics. This research can be extended to other domains beyond healthcare, using data from particular institutions or groups to create customized models. This research and associated code are available under a variety of licenses at https://github.com/c9c0/CDIM. We've developed an equation to estimate the secure key rate under this specific attack, comparing it to the previous key rate equation in detail. Importantly, we've found that there are two critical conditions that need to be met to ensure our new equation accurately predicts the key rate, which in turn indicates when this new attack can be effectively mitigated. We've also performed a numerical simulation to evaluate our new equation and found that there is a specific threshold for the phase randomization probability above which our new attack becomes possible. We've further investigated how our new equation behaves under different scenarios, and interestingly, discovered that there is an optimal value for the phase randomization probability that results in the maximum key rate. Our analysis sheds new light on the security of QKD systems that employ partial phase randomization and provides a potential vulnerability that needs to be considered. We've also developed a method to overcome this new attack, which can potentially improve the efficiency of QKD systems that use partial phase randomization. Our findings are relevant to any QKD system that employs partial phase randomization and can lead to better understanding and implementation of quantum communication networks. Specifically, while this new attack is effective against QKD systems that use partial phase randomization, it does not apply to systems that use full Gaussian or Bernoulli randomization. We've also verified that our new attack is not possible when using these randomization methods. We've taken into account the specific limitations and capabilities of real-world sources, which may have memory effects that need to be taken into account, and found that these source assumptions do not affect our new key rate equation. Furthermore, we've explored the scenario where the phase randomization probability is very low and found that in this case, our new attack can be effectively overcome by using a specific decoding approach. Recent research has highlighted the potential for large language models to learn in-context through the incorporation of few-shot examples within a single input, in addition to leveraging pretraining data. This study aims to enhance the understanding of in-context learning by examining the impact of various datasets in the training phase on the behavior of such models. Our findings suggest that the type of pretraining data influences the learning capacity of these models, with the adaptation to in-context learning most evident in models trained on data that includes in-context like fine-grained answering formats. Conversely, models trained on data that is dissimilar to in-context learning (notably books and articles) show limited improvement with the incorporation of few-shot examples. Our study also demonstrates the feasibility of in-context learning on a wide-scale language model with a large vocabulary, in contrast to previous studies that used custom-made datasets and specialized models to achieve similar results. This study could provide a foundation for future research focused on the development of scalable and adaptable few-shot models. This process might be a common phenomenon in these systems, but its underlying mechanism remains unclear. Using advanced hydrodynamic simulations, we investigated how magnetic fields and thermal transmission affect the formation and evolution of such features. We discovered that without magnetic forces, cold clouds fragment and rise within a short time frame, while in the presence of magnetic forces, they survive for millions of years. Additionally, the presence of thermal transmission significantly alters the equation compared to models that solely account for cooling, leading to increased densities and altered temperature profiles. These findings support the use of magnetohydrodynamic simulations to model the behavior of cold clouds in galaxy groups and clusters. We further applied the PHANTOM code to simulate systems based on the Navarro-Frenk-White model and observed that when we stopped re-igniting supernovae, cold clouds developed within dense regions, ultimately forming bars that stretched towards their center. When we incorporated magnetic forces into these models, they prevented the disruption of these features. However, when we introduced an anti-diffusion term to counter the effect of artificial diffusion, it led to the development of rings and bars in gas density, a pattern that coincided with magnetic structure. These amplitudes meet the requirements of "toughness," meaning their values remain consistent under arbitrary transformations of the kinematic variables. Additionally, their calculated values in four-dimensional space match predictions made by the Gross conjecture, extending its scope to fifth-order amplitudes. Its success in predicting fifth-order amplitudes supports the idea that the Gross conjecture is a fundamental equation governing string theory, and it does so without relying on specific assumptions about the string's behavior. The objective-synthesis method aims to create natural speech without the need for text or speech data in the same language. We use Ideogrammic Transcripts, consisting of phoneme-based symbols, as the basis for synthesis. Since these transcripts aren't yet available in large quantities, we created a dictionary to establish a connection between the acoustic units and their graphic representations. To enhance voice quality, we utilized a linear combination of speech features from multiple donors. The synthesis process involves generating speech features that match the desired transcript, using statistical models to ensure natural speech representation. In our experiments, a subjective evaluation revealed that the synthesized speech met the expectations set by non-experts listening to a sample speech. This method has shown promising results in limited-resource settings, specifically for languages with alphabetic scripts such as Arabic and Hebrew. Furthermore, the subjectively evaluated synthesizations demonstrated high fidelity, approaching that of a human, primarily due to the reliance on transcripts derived from acoustic units. This approach effectively mitigates the reliance on parallel corpora and means-end analyses, replacing them with a dictionary established through acoustic analysis and a thesaurus to connect units with similar meanings. The method also eliminates the necessity for text-based pre-editing, replacing it with a transcription of speech into ideogrammic transcripts to ensure semantic accuracy. Ultimately, this objective-synthesis method brings us closer to developing speech without speech, speech without hearing, and speech without seeing. Optimization-linked motion planning is a cutting-edge approach that leverages convex optimization to generate practical trajectories for robots. To overcome planning challenges posed by convex constraints, researchers use various parameterization techniques, such as pseudo-state variables, to facilitate approximation through convexity. This method enables the incorporation of complex constraints into optimization problems, despite their non-linearity. However, parameterization introduces an initialization issue: how to choose optimal parameters for the best results. A fully informed set of parameters would yield an exactly recoverable solution, but this is impractical due to the high computational demands. A recent solution involves creating multi-stage optimization problems that address parameter initialization in conjunction with motion planning. This paper contributes to this framework by introducing a new tool: data-driven data processing and McCormick envelope relaxation to streamline the optimization process. Traditional McCormick envelopes require manually specified bounds, which can be problematic for high-dimensional systems. This paper overcomes this issue using a proposed connected convex optimization framework, providing accurate results and efficiently deriving necessary bounds for successful motion planning. To test the framework's effectiveness, researchers applied it to two simulated systems: a quadcopter in a velocity-based system and a mobile robot in a position-based system. This resulted in successful, trajectory-related planning outcomes in both scenarios. Quadcopter results showed a velocity profile with precisely 2.7% error compared to an optimal solution, and mobile robot results yielded nearly faultless positioning with less than a 0.01 error rate. To enable interaction with external planning tools, the proposed framework also includes the capacity for seamless communication with other optimization and planning software. This was demonstrated by integrating the method with the open-source PYPOM motion planning toolkit, allowing for the testing of a mobile robot against manually defined convex constraints and resulting in accurate, plan-driven performance with only minor errors. In conclusion, this paper offers a new approach for optimizing multi-stage linked convex optimization with McCormick envelope relaxations and data-driven proxy problems to facilitate interaction with external planning software. This method contributes to the growing field of optimization-linked motion planning by introducing a versatile, parameterization-driven tool for coping with complex, non-linear constraints. We introduce a novel decentralized learning method, DR-DSGD, capable of handling a diverse range of data distributions across interconnected nodes. DR-DSGD exhibits robustness in the face of data heterogeneity, graph non-regularity, and edge failures. We test DR-DSGD on a variety of real-world datasets and find it to be a more resilient alternative to standard decentralized methods. We also provide specific guidelines for selecting the hyperparameters that maximize performance. We derive theoretical justifications for DR-DSGD's convergence and empirical evidence supports its optimal performance. DR-DSGD is implemented in PyTROCR, an open-source decentralized optimization framework. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/huashuashua/trocr.

The way particles are produced in high-energy collisions of nuclei is influenced by two main processes: one that causes matter to expand and one that causes it to contract.  By analyzing data from the Large Hadron Collider, researchers discovered that, immediately after the onset of these collisions, the contraction process dominates and then gradually gives way to the expansion process.  To better understand particle production, they developed a simple theoretical model that includes the effects of expansion and contraction, thereby revealing the significant role that the initial conditions of these collisions play in the subsequent behavior of the colliding matter.  Notably, this model successfully captures the observed shift in the spectrum of particles produced in collisions of varying intensity without requiring any adjustments to model parameters.  By incorporating an additional component to simulate the movement of particles, the theoretical model becomes even more accurate, effectively reproducing the observed relationships between different types of particles and their momentum.  Overall, the outcomes of these tests confirm that a simple theoretical model, taking into account the effects of expansion and contraction, is well-suited to describe the phenomena observed in high-energy nuclear collisions.  This model provides new insights into the two processes governing matter expansion and contraction, thereby paving the way for further exploration of the initial conditions of these collisions.  Moreover, by applying a novel method to analyze the energy associated with these initial conditions, researchers estimated the amount of energy associated with them, thereby contributing to our understanding of the initial state of matter created in these collisions.  Finally, by combining the test results from multiple types of particles, researchers gained a deeper insight into the mechanism of matter contraction, thereby pulling theory and experiment closer together.  This research sets the stage for future applications and extensions of the theoretical model, including its application to the study of the interior of compact stars.  Based on the outcomes of these tests, it appears that nuclear matter is not as stiff as previously thought when subjected to extreme conditions of temperature and density.  This research also opens up the possibility of using high-energy collisions to explore the properties of the strong nuclear force, an effort in which the RHIC and LHC play a crucial role.  This research can be seen as a successful application of the principle of equiduality, thereby paving the way for a new era of research into the fundamental properties of matter, where nuclear physicists and solid-state researchers are working closely together to make new breakthroughs.  This research is a great example of how the findings of nuclear physics can be used to answer fundamental questions about the nature of matter, where novel experiments can be used

Using complex computer models, we examine how a fast protostellar jet interacts with its surrounding cloud, specifically how it affects the formation and movement of a second, slower-moving jet within the cloud.  After initializing the high-speed jet at an elevated level, we observe at what distances from the star both jets become visible and how they move.  Under the influence of the high-speed jet, the low-speed jet exhibits a non-circular cross-section and its movement is redirected, compared to a scenario where only gravity dominates.  However, when both jets are equidistant from the star, the low-speed jet does not show the same level of deviation from its expected path using only gravity alone.  Additionally, high-speed jets may not significantly impact protoplanetary disks as they move closer to the star, depending on the star's mass.  These results have implications for the observation of protostars and circumstellar material, using high-speed jets as a lens through which to view low-speed jets, which could explain discrepancies between modeled and observed outflow patterns.  This research may also explain why some jets appear to collide and create distinctive butterfly shapes, as well as their alignment when they reach the protoplanetary disk.  It sets the stage for future studies on how these jets affect the star's accretion rate and planet formation processes.  Based on our simulation, it is possible that high-speed jets can influence the movement of low-speed jets within protostellar environments, which may have implications for the observation of protostars and their surrounding circumstellar material.  This could be due to the high-speed jet's head disrupting the low-speed jet further out in the cloud, or its interaction with the surrounding material pushing the low-speed jet off its initial path.  This research sets the stage for future studies on the impact of high-speed jets on the movement of low-speed jets, and the potential effects on the star's accretion and planet formation processes.  It also highlights the complex interaction between high-speed jets, low-speed jets, and the surrounding gas in protostellar environments, which requires further investigation.  This research has far-reaching implications for the understanding of protostellar jets and the movement of low-speed jets, and their potential effects on the star's accretion and planet formation processes.  It also emphasizes the need for high-resolution observations of protostellar jets, using the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, to confirm our simulation results.  This would involve examining the movement of individual gas particles in the protostellar environment

This new characteristic seeks to identify groups with an abelian or nilpotent second quotient when divided by their commutator subgroup. We present the complete list of groups that fit this criterion when their quotients are nilpotent: specifically, the generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups, denoted $G(n, m)$, for specific values of $n$ and $m$. We also provide comprehensive descriptions of both torsion and non-torsion subgroups within the quotients of these groups, thereby achieving a definitive classification of the groups in question. We utilize a tool from group cohomology, referred to as $\mathrm{Ext}$-finiteness, in order to facilitate this classification. We further derive a method for calculating the abelian quotients of these groups, providing explicit numerical values in addition to a detailed theoretical framework. Finally, we present a guiding conjecture based on the groups' structures, along with a proposed classification of groups characterized by $R_\infty$ in relation to their rank and generators. We support this conjecture with explicit examples and a detailed theoretical structure. We also provide code that can be used to determine if a group can be characterized by $R_\infty$ and refer to existing software for additional computations. We investigate the nature of Gelfand-Shilov spaces with smoothness properties, specifically examining the Fourier transforms of functions within these spaces. Our work builds upon the research of Eschede and Berg, further extending their findings. In doing so, we provide a direct assessment of the non-ordinary characteristics of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, thereby gaining insights crucial for understanding the behavior of Toeplitz operators. Importantly, our results reveal the essential role of growth conditions in determining the operator's boundedness, a criterion that cannot be predicted by the smoothness of the Gelfand-Shilov space alone. To support this investigation, we develop a Fourier description of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, based on the decay and little L^p-admissibility of functions, with p ranging from 1 to 2. Furthermore, our analysis includes the examination of continuous symbols and bounded Toeplitz operators within Gelfand-Shilov spaces, particularly focusing on the survival of boundedness under the action of convolution operators. Predicting actions in future video segments is a task called action forecasting. This paper introduces a novel method for action forecasting by employing a feature mapping LSTM with a radial basis function (RBF) kernel, allowing for learning on the fly in an unsupervised manner. Leveraging the advantages of both kernel methods and sequence modeling, our approach outperforms existing techniques on benchmark datasets. Additionally, we propose a new dataset for the task, called Breakfast-V, which poses significant challenges due to its short duration and diverse contexts. Action forecasting finds practical applications in various domains such as video surveillance and human-robot interaction, making it a valuable problem for further research. A demonstration of our model's capabilities can be found at https://action-forecasting.github.io/. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/action-filtering/action-forecasting.

One of the most luminous stellar events observed in human history occurred on April 12, 1985, when the star AD Leo underwent a massive outburst. During this event, the star's energy output increased dramatically, exceeding its normal UV and visible light emission by several orders of magnitude. This outburst is notable for its extremely rapid variability, with fluctuations lasting just 20 minutes. Following up on earlier research, we created artificial versions of the star's UV and visible light spectra to match its abnormal behavior during the event. By comparing these simulated spectra to observations, we were able to see how the star's atmosphere behaved abnormally under extreme conditions. Using detailed computer models, we simulated two key types of energy movements in the star's atmosphere: electrical disruptions and intense particle showers. By adjusting various model settings, we were able to recreate the star's abnormal spectra and see which settings best match observations. This included mimicking the star's intense visible light emission and complex patterns of UV and visible light overlap. Additionally, our simulations helped us understand how the star's atmosphere behaved at high altitudes (around 2000 km below the star's surface) and allowed us to make an educated estimate of the star's abnormal energy distribution during the event. This includes a significant increase in the star's overall energy output and distinct changes in its UV and visible light emission patterns. Notably, our simulations conflict with some previous research over how the star's abnormal energy distribution spreads out in different parts of the spectrum. Moreover, our study suggests that the star's electrical disruptions are the primary driver of its abnormal energy behavior during the event, with other theories, such as high-energy particle showers, playing a much less significant role. Finally, our simulations help explain the star's rapid variability as a result of its own extremely fast-spinning core, triggered by the sudden release of energy from the initial outburst cause. This, in turn, causes the star's outer atmosphere to exhibit extreme and rapid changes in pressure, leading to its variable emission behavior during the event. This research provides the first evidence of electrical disruptions in the star's atmosphere, matching key observational features and shedding light on the star's abnormal energy behavior during the event. This includes distinct differences in its abnormal spectra under two distinct electrical conditions, featuring distinct patterns of UV and visible light emission, as well as the star's intense visible light emission and complex patterns of UV and visible light overlap. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets reveal that the proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance in object classification and semantic segmentation tasks. To validate the model's dependence on transformation and data variability, comprehensive ablation studies were conducted using multiple datasets. The findings from these studies confirm that the model's effectiveness is contingent on the specific coordinate transformation used and the data's complexity, as evidenced by the model's underwhelming performance on simpler datasets. These studies were placed in a distinct framework by Eberle and colleagues, who derived a spectral representation of entanglement based on interference patterns. In our research, we explore the application of this spectral concept to describe the combined interaction of two photons with atomic media that exhibit two-photon absorption. Building on Eberle's work, we propose a spectral model of entanglement that can be physically realized using quantum interference of photons. This model is exemplified through simulations of Hong-Ou-Mandel interference experiments that demonstrate two-photon absorption without prior entanglement. Additionally, we identify a limitation on the spectral representation of entanglement that arises when photons interact with diverse atomic media. These findings provide new perspectives for understanding non-separable states through quantum interference and potentially enhancing entanglement-based applications by optimizing spectral distributions. Furthermore, our work presents a feasible method for generating entangled states for practical use. This scheme could provide a substantial advantage over current methods for producing entangled photons, as it could achieve high efficiency and rate of entangled pairs through a single excitation of the intermediate state. Our research offers a meaningful connection between the abstract spectral representation of entanglement and real-world photon interactions, as exemplified by the proposed scheme for entangled photon production. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for predicting missing knowledge gaps in temporal datasets. Building upon successful results with static graph completion, this technique employs statistical models to fill in missing timestamped entity relations. However, current temporal knowledge graph completion methods are often hindered by their reliance on high-dimensional vector representations that become increasingly difficult to store and process as dataset sizes increase. In response, researchers have developed various techniques for scaling the representations without compromising performance. In this context, we introduce a novel method for temporal knowledge graph completion that utilizes low-rank and model-independent representations. Specifically, we modify traditional knowledge graph embedding formulas to produce representations of entity relations with a low degree of dimensionality. This modification enables more efficient use of model capabilities, and our results demonstrate that our approach can achieve substantial improvements in scalability and efficiency with minimal impact on performance. Additionally, we provide evidence of common knowledge graph embedding models' underlying independence from the specific details of the models themselves, and propose a method for evaluating and selecting individual model components that could be useful in future research. Our new approach offers several benefits over existing methods, and we verify its superiority through comprehensive testing with multiple datasets. In a flat band system, a single quantum phase can manifest in multiple ways, 
each corresponding to a distinct Hamiltonian configuration. By adjusting the 
strengthening of interactions within these systems, a transition can occur from 
non-confining to confining behavior. We demonstrate that in a two-dimensional 
lattice model featuring a non-confining flat band, increasing the interactions 
between neighboring sites causes a progressive shift towards a confining phase, 
even when interactions with long-range sites are introduced and varied. We show 
that in a two-dimensional model, a perfect flat band is never sufficient to 
induce confinement on its own. However, when coupled with a nearly flat band, 
modified by nearest-neighbor interactions, a confining phase can emerge. We 
also examine a system of bosons, where we find that in the two-dimensional case 
only a strictly flat band leads to condensation within a single Mott phase, 
contrary to a two-dimensional system where mixing flat and nearly flat bands 
supports condensation across multiple Mott phases. Lastly, in a real-world 
implementation using cold atoms in an optical lattice, a confining phase can be 
achieved through adjustment of a single experimental parameter alone. We suggest 
that a similar approach can be applied to other flat band systems to access 
confined phases. Additionally, this methodology may be useful in uncovering 
flat band compounds that exhibit unique quantum properties in actual materials. 
Our work presents an important insight into the relationship between flat bands, 
confinement, and interaction-strengthening, offering a unified understanding of 
this complex phenomenon. It also paves the way for a systematic exploration of 
quantum phases in systems that feature flat bands. Results derived from our 
research may find practical applications in experiments using cold atoms and may 
be relevant to the study of confining phenomena in general. Further analysis is 
required to determine whether these results can be extended to confining systems 
that feature multiple quantum valleys. It is also necessary to investigate whether 
these outcomes can be validly generalized to a broader framework of quantum 
confined systems in any dimension. Additionally, these findings may hold 
significant implications for flat band research and novel materials 
development/exploration. Precise numerical data was collected using 
precision computational methods such as iQDPy, and exact analytical results were 
derived using group theory techniques. We suggest that a similar approach could 
be used to identify and create novel quantum phases in systems that feature

Building upon this discovery, we introduce a novel concept, sectioning, which enables safe and independent distribution of execution across multiple threads while maintaining type accuracy.  Key features of sectioning include the ability to temporarily disable type checking and mark areas for execution distribution without locking.  Utilizing a compiler-assisted mechanism, types are re-established after each distribution event.  Additionally, we showcase the potential of sectioning by implementing a primitive distribution function and a concurrent data structure, specifically a queue, to demonstrate its practical applications.  The proposed sectioning mechanism offers a versatile framework for distributing execution and could serve as a foundational component for concurrent systems programming.  While our mechanism is presented as a library, it is anticipated that future compilers will be able to directly generate sectioning code.  The code for sectioning, including a queue, can be found at https://github.com/jzattenberg/execude.  Future research will focus on enhancing compiler support for explicit distribution hints to further optimize the performance of sectioning-based systems.  Ultimately, we aim to contribute to the development of programming languages with built-in concurrency distribution mechanisms.  It is also envisioned that sectioning can serve as a low-level foundation for concurrency distribution in high-level programming languages.  Specifically, we intend to investigate the design and implementation of a high-level language that can seamlessly integrate sectioning and distribution, enabling safe and efficient concurrent execution of arbitrary programs.  This high-level system will likely utilize a hybrid approach that combines the distribution of execution on a graph-level similar to GRAPA and the temporary disabling of types for safety.  The incorporation of sectioning will allow for the re-introduction of type safety without compromising performance, thus addressing a major shortcoming of previous graph-based distribution approaches.  The development of this high-level system will provide a viable alternative to the current compiler-assisted sectioning mechanism, thus further democratizing the deployment of concurrency distribution technology.  Conversely, we also plan to investigate whether the compiler-assisted sectioning mechanism can serve as a suitable replacement for existing concurrency libraries, thus enabling the efficient distribution of execution across multiple threads without the overhead of current libraries.  The ultimate goal is to demonstrate that concurrency distribution technology can offer comparable performance, safety, and portability relative to current systems, thus enabling the efficient distribution of execution and the development of concurrent systems

This study provides an in-depth examination of Leibnizian infinitesimal analysis within three modern mathematical contexts: Robinsonian nonstandard analysis, hyperreal number theory, and synthetic calculus. Leibnizian methodology is contrasted with Newtonian and Eulerian approaches, and its implications for Cauchy and Weierstrassian analysis are explored. A key focus lies on the derivative as a limit, and our analysis draws upon an extensively annotated translation of Leibniz's significant correspondence with Clarke and others. In particular, this correspondence includes the famous ten laws that encapsulate Leibnizian infinitesimal principles. These principles are examined in the contexts of hyperreal number theory, nonstandard analysis, and synthetic calculus, allowing us to offer a comprehensive interpretation of Leibnizian methodology and its implications for the development of real analysis. A critical aspect of our research examines the potential contradictions inherent in Leibnizian infinitesimals, and we argue that these can be resolved by adopting a distinct analytical framework. Furthermore, our study seeks to reconcile the perceptions that Leibnizian methodology is incompatible with a rigorous treatment of limits and that it oppositionally arises in response to such a treatment. Instead, we contend that Leibnizian infinitesimals can coexist harmoniously with a limit-based foundation for calculus. Moreover, we identify a critical turning point in the development of calculus, wherein the core methods and principles of both the Leibnizian and Newtonian schools were gradually abandoned in favor of Weierstrassian epsilon-delta methods. A notable conclusion arises from our analysis, namely that the ascent to the modern treatment of real analysis was facilitated not through an oppositional interplay between different schools of thought, but rather through a gradual and widespread adoption of epsilon-delta methods that was only fully realized towards the end of the nineteenth century. A related finding suggests that the failure to recognize the distinct analytical frameworks that underpinned the different approaches of Clarke, Leibniz, Newton, and Euler may have contributed to an unjustified dismissal of their approaches in favor of a more recent method for understanding real analysis. We seek to rectify this perceived injustice by providing a more equitable interpretation of the methodologies that underpinned the approaches of Clarke, Leibniz, Newton, and Euler. By leveraging bundle emission's capability to be reconfigured through dynamic adjustment of the parity gap, a series of mitigating strategies have been developed to overcome previous limitations.
