We investigate the problem of developing an algorithm to estimate a scale parameter in a small-world graph, representing a social network, that can handle malicious actors. The scale parameter is defined as the minimum distance between two nodes in the graph, and our goal is to create an algorithm that can accurately estimate this parameter without the assistance of a central authority or trusted parties. The algorithm we develop can operate efficiently, estimating the scale parameter quickly while also incurring low communication costs, even in the presence of malicious actors. Additionally, we demonstrate the accuracy of our algorithm, showing that its estimated scale parameter closely matches the actual value for both healthy and malicious nodes. Notably, we find that the accuracy of our algorithm increases significantly as the number of malicious actors decreases. The results of our investigation yield two important conclusions: first, we establish a lower bound on the communication costs required to accurately estimate the scale parameter; second, we construct an algorithm that surpasses this bound, effectively providing a solution that can efficiently estimate the scale parameter even under the influence of malicious actors. The accuracy of our protocol is quantified by bounding the difference between its estimated scale parameter and the actual value, and we find that this difference is directly proportional to the number of nodes and logarithmic in the actual scale parameter. The constant proportionality constant provides a valuable benchmark for evaluating our protocol's performance. Furthermore, we examine the behavior of our algorithm and find that it remains robust even in the presence of multiple malicious actors, and that it can efficiently operate at large graph sizes. The findings of our investigation offer insights into developing algorithms that can accurately estimate the scale parameter while limiting communication costs and efficiently operating at scale. The algorithms we develop provide a framework for estimating the scale parameter even under the influence of malicious actors, and our results yield valuable bounds on the accuracy of our protocol. The research offers a valuable contribution by examining the problem of distributed algorithm design for graph scale parameter estimation in the presence of malicious actors, and the findings provide insights into novel techniques for robust scale parameter estimation. The novel protocols developed can be useful in various real-world applications, such as decentralized cryptocurrency networks, and our research provides a valuable framework for investigating such problems. The algorithms we develop can potentially be applied to actual networks, and our results can provide practical benefits for operating such systems efficiently. In recent years, various models have been proposed to forecast time series data, but these models primarily focus on single locations or specific dimensions of multidimensional time series data. Furthermore, they typically do not consider connections between different dimensional nodes. To address these limitations, we present a new model called Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network (AdGCN), which combines the advantages of graph neural networks and traditional multivariate models. AdGCN dynamically builds relationships between nodes within individual dimensions as well as between nodes across different dimensions, taking into account the interconnectedness of temporal series data. To optimize model performance, we suggest an adaptive dropout strategy, which allows nodes with high predictive confidence to remain undropped. Experimental results demonstrate that AdGCN significantly outperforms existing models in terms of accuracy and predictive stability, while also providing a clear interpretation of model decisions through the capture of critical connections in multidimensional time series data. The effectiveness of AdGCN is empirically validated across three real-world datasets, offering a promising solution for multidimensional time series forecasting in diverse applications. The code for AdGCN is openly available on GitHub.

Astronomers using adaptive optics (AO) systems have manually calculated AO models off-site, but these typically don't account for local scattering effects seen on-site. A novel technique combines data from infrared cameras capturing the scattered light signal in various wavelengths. By analyzing the difference between ground-based and space-based data, astronomers can identify on-site scattering effects, even if AO models are inaccurate. This technique was applied to data from the Gemini Observatory's GRISM instrument, and AO models were corrected for 13 nights of observations. Scattering effects were consistently seen across different fields of view, and were more significant when the full moon was present, indicating that these effects are likely due to atmospheric conditions rather than intrinsic solar properties. Correcting the AO models led to improved reconstruction of the atmospheric phase, and resulted in better image quality and focal plane mapping in the mid-infrared. This technique, now referred to as the Infrared Atmospheric Scattering Effect (IASE) correction, could be adapted for use in other AO systems. A prospective approach to implement IASE corrections in real-time is also outlined. This has allowed users to apply the IASE correction to their own data, even if they didn't originally collect it through the Gemini Observatory. This method involves analyzing the changes in materials' shear modulus in response to pressure. Due to its high sensitivity, this method can potentially detect even tiny amounts of ultra-light dark matter particles collected within materials. In our analysis, we primarily consider the influence of non-Newtonian momentum dependence of the ultra-light bosonic dark matter particles' cross-section and the impact of pressure on this shear modulus. We found that a number of factors, such as specific materials properties, pressure levels, and the manner in which the momentum dependence of the dark matter particles' cross-section arises, influence the efficiency of this method. This paper explores the mathematical concept of basis pursuit, a technique used to solve sparse optimization problems. Given a positive definite matrix B and a vector b, basis pursuit seeks the unique vector x that minimizes the L1-norm while satisfying the equation B*x = b. However, this uniqueness may not always be the case. Our research reveals that if the matrix B has multiple columns with negative and positive signs in common, there may exist multiple solutions x that minimize the L1-norm. We provide geometric and geometric-algebraic methods to find these solutions, and demonstrate that these solutions are also optimal in various Lp-norm minimization problems for 1 < p < 2. We further extend our findings to the Euclidean space and the complex numbers, and provide a visual representation of our results using 3D and complex 2D plotting. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Ultimately, our study shows that, in the context of basis pursuit, uniqueness may not be a guarantee, and additional information may be required to find a unique solution. Our research expands the scope of basis pursuit and provides novel insights into finding optimal vectors x. It also identifies potential blind spots in the existing literature. We consider our contributions a starting point for further exploration and research. We explicitly construct solutions for specific matrices B and vectors b, and introduce a new concept - the CP-diagram, which becomes a valuable tool for solving basis pursuit problems quickly and easily. The CP-diagram is also useful for obtaining optimal solutions for various Lp-norm minimization problems for 1 < p < 2. We consider these findings an important contribution to the existing literature on basis pursuit. We study the behavior of CP-diagrams for randomly generated matrices B and the corresponding geometric structures. Our research reveals that these diagrams exhibit order and display unique properties. We observed consistent results in our experiments and provide a mathematical explanation for these findings. Our study also touches on the phenomenon of stochastic resonance, which may occur when using these matrices for basis pursuit. We provide a mathematical explanation for this phenomenon and demonstrate how it can be observed in the context of basis pursuit. We consider these findings unique and interesting. We study the ergodic and mixing properties of the transformation associated with basis pursuit. Our research reveals that these properties are not universal and may not apply in various situations. We provide a mathematical explanation for these findings and demonstrate how the behavior of the transformation can vary depending on the chosen matrix B. This study proposes the P416 compiler, an open-source, language-based tool for creating programmable packet processors. Designed for forward and switch elements, the compiler enables users to write in C-like code C416 instructions, mapping packet headers to C416 registers. The compiler automatically generates compile-time-readable configuration files for multiple packet processing platforms. The study examines current programmable hardware components and possible additions. An open-source version of the P416 compiler is presented, readable in Python, with examples illustrating its usage. Evaluation demonstrates that the P416 compiler produces compatible code with existing hardware components, and demonstrates a 30% increase in performance with custom instructions. The P416 compiler framework is released under the BSD license, allowing for free use and modification. Additionally, the study proposes three new instructions to enhance flexibility in packet processing applications. These instructions enhance P416's capabilities in dealing with irregular packets, supporting hardware implementation on the P4P16-based TeraFLOP processor and similar custom ASICs. However, these instructions cannot be implemented on hardware without modifications to the processor architecture. Possible future work involves incorporating these instructions and introducing supporting hardware. The P416 compiler framework can be used for creating flexible match-action table switches using existing hardware components, and can be adapted for custom hardware designs. A straightforward discretisation of the convection equation using lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements results in a sparse matrix representation, which implies a lower order of accuracy than its natural companion problems, such as the mixed formulation of the second-order convection-diffusion equation. We introduce a straightforward post-processing technique to improve the accuracy of the numerical solution, achieving a method that is comparable to the second-order convection-diffusion equation discretised using the Raviart-Thomas elements. This revised approach retains the same numerical properties as the underlying Raviart-Thomas discretisation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method through numerical experiments, comparing it with two alternative higher-order discretisation methods, notably a conventional Raviart-Thomas discretisation and a recently introduced "HTI" discretisation, also employing the Raviart-Thomas elements. The comparative assessment is carried out on a range of test cases, primarily designed to evaluate the performance of the methods under conditions of varying flow directions and non-uniform velocity fields. These experiments reveal that the proposed method exhibits superior convergence characteristics across all cases, particularly when the velocity field is not uniform, and that it outperforms the HTI discretisation when the flow direction is non-uniform, achieving a more consistent and accurate solution than the HTI discretisation in such scenarios. Nonetheless, the proposed method shows a slightly lower performance than the HTI discretisation when the velocity field is uniform, and only performs marginally better than a conventional Raviart-Thomas discretisation in all cases. Despite this marginal superiority of the proposed method over the HTI discretisation in uniform velocity cases, our method remains straightforward to implement and relatively easy to understand, and it displays a consistent and impressive performance in a wide range of scenarios, including cases with non-uniform velocity fields. Therefore, we recommend its use as a reliable and accurate method for solving the convection equation when the Raviart-Thomas elements are employed. Additionally, we propose four potential improvements to enhance the performance of the numerical methods, and invite researchers to tackle these challenges. Finally, we suggest that the proposed method could also be extended and successfully applied to solve more complex problems, such as the convection-diffusion equation, using the Raviart-Thomas elements. This potential extension is outlined in detail. Federated learning promises a balance between performance and user data protection, 
achieving this by gradually releasing aggregated model updates instead of sensitive data. 
Despite this, prior research has demonstrated that a FL model's updates can reveal 
important information about users' behaviors, potentially violating their anonymity. 
Considering the initial goal of FL to support empowering technologies that benefit 
historically marginalized communities, there is a clear disconnect between the process 
and a consistent objective of justice. This research explores the concept of justice 
within FL and specifically focuses on one aspect, cohesive justice, which it defines 
as ensuring the benefits and risks associated with algorithms affect people equally. 
A new evaluation framework, JFL, is introduced to assess this aspect of justice 
and evaluate various risks associated with different FL processes, 
ultimately finding that centralized training poses a more significant threat 
to users' confidentiality and anonymity compared to decentralized and semi-centralized methods. 
As a result, decentralized training appears to be the most suitable option 
for supporting empowering technologies and promoting a just distribution 
of risks and benefits, thus facilitating more equitable interactions 
between humans and machines that respect users' autonomy. This study provides 
the first evaluation of the risks and challenges associated with justice 
from a FL perspective and offers a novel approach for analyzing and addressing 
this issue. This research will be presented in a forthcoming paper titled 
"Federated Learning Meets Justice: A Novel Framework for Evaluating 
Censive Risks and Challenges," which will be presented at ICML 2022. ```ICML 2022``` was held July 18-24, 2022, in Vancouver, Canada, and the corresponding paper can be found on arXiv. ```arXiv:2205.12633```. A recently introduced method called Continuous-Phase Runge-Kutta (CPRK) has demonstrated higher accuracy and robustness in comparison to traditional Runge-Kutta algorithms when dealing with differential equations. This advancement over Euler-Ackleymer (RK4) methods can be observed in various numerical integration applications, such as signal processing, differential equations and ordinary / partial differential equations. Notably, CPRK outperforms RK4 in numerical solutions for Navier-Stokes equations and ensures stability in the case of the 2D rotating Stokes equations, even when strongly distorted, when used in conjunction with the Multistep-CPRK method. This level of performance is maintained across CPRK's various formulations, which share common characteristics of increased order and low discretization error with an $O(h^5)$ complexity. This makes CPRK a highly efficient method with $O(h^7)$ complexity when used in combination with interpolation. This research further develops the concept of Continuous-Phase Multistep Runge-Kutta (MPRK) methods, which exhibit even greater numerical stability and accuracy, reaching an $O(h^9)$ complexity. The stability and precision of these MPRK methods are confirmed through the analysis of the 2D rotating Stokes equations, where they demonstrate complete stability and precise results up to a level of $10^{-12}$ achievement level. Unlike two-dimensional scenarios, where increasing dissipation enhances Wada basins, experiments with smooth, non-overlapping spheres in three dimensions reveal an inverse trend. A vital concern for IoT devices activating wireless communication is resilience against various network assaults launched by malicious adversaries. Since IoT devices are often resource constrained, there's a need for efficient and accurate network attack detection methods that can be easily integrated into these systems. This paper introduces a novel intrusion detection system called NBcoded, which combines Naive Bayes and Classifier using Encoder to identify various network assaults on IoT devices, and can be effectively implemented using resource-limited IoT devices. To improve detection accuracy, NBcoded utilizes two improved Naive Bayes models, one utilizing Counterfactual Networks and the other combining Generator and Discriminator networks. Experimental results demonstrate that NBcoded achieves outstanding performance with high accuracy, specifically 99.94% for datasets transformed into binary form, and 99.90% for datasets employing Encoder. Furthermore, NBcoded shows substantial computational efficiency, specifically 0.91 seconds for binary datasets and 0.81 seconds for datasets transformed using Encoder, making it an ideal solution for resource constrained IoT devices. This paper also employs ACC as the performance metric for NBcoded models, and to validate the transformation of network data into binary form, or data transformed using Encoder, a binary classification model is used. Additionally, this paper confirms the validity of NBcoded through rigorous experimentation by comparing its performance with existing IoT intrusion detection systems, and verifies that NBcoded can effectively detect network assaults on IoT devices using wireless communication. The proposed NBcoded detection system offers a simple and effective method for detecting network assaults on IoT devices, utilizing wireless communication, and can be effectively implemented using resource-limited IoT devices. To support ongoing research in this area, the NBcoded dataset is made available on GitHub. This paper is structured as follows: related research is discussed in Section 1, and NBcoded is introduced in Section 2, with experimental results and a discussion of the findings in Section 3. Finally, conclusions are drawn in Section 4. Utilizing the Universal System, we identify inherent inconsistencies within the current framework of global physics. In the absence of experimental evidence to distinguish between different global physical models, we propose adopting the simplest option, which corresponds to quantum mechanics with gravity. Furthermore, our method encourages researchers to revisit and reinterpret basic concepts in physics, as well as to develop novel approaches for addressing long-standing challenges and unsolved problems. Precision calculations in physics, such as loop tree unitarity, espinosa, and top loop equivalence, heavily depend on complex integral calculations being accurate to at least $10^{-6}$ or $10^{-5}$. This level of precision is required for photon polarization accuracy ($\sim 10^{-5}$) and top quark production precision ($\sim 10^{-6}$) needed for the LHC and future colliders. Since many loop-level processes can be challenging to analyze, even with single-loop simulations, we examine the requirements for multi-loop simulations, such as those in four-loop electron anomalous magnetic moments, five-loop epsilon expansion calculations, and high-scale particle physics predictions. We find these scenarios frequently involve hundreds to tens of thousands of integrals and require accuracy in at least $10^{-6}-10^{-8}$. To meet these needs, we outline standard procedures for integral evaluation, including employing numerical values of parameters, avoiding complex parameter spaces, using internal variables for dimensionless expressions, and applying complex rotation for on-shell calculations. We also propose $10^{-6}-10^{-8}$ as the target accuracy for numerical integration, considering the behavior of scales in loop-level processes and anticipating future high-energy colliders' requirements. To achieve this, we recommend performing numerical integration over a fine grid with at least $10^6-10^8$ points, while also outlining best practices for numerical phase-space integration. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive list of recommended and available software tools for integral calculations that meet the requirements of $10^{-6}-10^{-8}$ accuracy. We utilize examples from loop-level processes, such as double-box calculations, to demonstrate how to meet these precision standards. Finally, we anticipate that future high-energy colliders will demand numerical calculations with an accuracy of at least $10^{-6}$ for thousands of processes. To meet these precision standards for both particle physics and amplitude-based calculations, we need to perform numerical calculations with an accuracy of at least $10^{-6}$. The Gromov-Hausdorff distance establishes a category structure on the set of all metric spaces, with distinct properties including the existence of a medial object that represents their category product. We introduce a method to describe and study subcategories defined by distance bounds in the Gromov-Hausdorff metric. Specifically, we identify a type of subcategory known as extensive, where the presence of a metric map from a given space to another's boundary does not imply it lies within that space's boundary. We demonstrate that the category of all extensive subcategories is vast and complex, with distinct size levels, while also proving that its first countable subcategories constitute a vast and complex category with distinct size levels. Furthermore, we define a type of subcategory known as central, where their elements contain a distance-measuring metric map to the space's center, and show that the categories of central and extensive subcategories are incomparable in terms of size. We achieve these results by introducing a method to describe the elements of subcategories using cloud-like structures formed from compactly generated spaces' boundaries, and establish a technique for obtaining a central subcategory from an extensive one involving these cloud structures. We define the concept of an element's heaviness with respect to a given space, and demonstrate that this heaviness determines whether an element lies within a particular space's boundary, thereby systematically describing the elements of numerous subcategories, and proving their abundance and diverse size levels in the category of all subcategories defined by distance bounds in the Gromov-Hausdorff metric. We define the concept of an element's inclusivity with respect to a given space, and demonstrate that this inclusivity determines whether an element contains a particular space within its distance metric. We achieve this by establishing a technique for obtaining a subcategory known as the category of all weakly expansive subcategories, and prove that its elements contain a distance-measuring metric map from the space's center, thereby covering a particular size level in the category of all subcategories defined by distance bounds in the Gromov-Hausdorff metric. We demonstrate a vast and complex relationship between distance metric maps and the size levels of a particular space's category, and establish a technique for obtaining a subcategory known as the category of all category-preserving subcategories, and prove that its elements contain a distance-measuring metric map from another space's boundary, thereby covering a particular size level in the category of all subcategories defined by distance bounds in the Gromov-Hausdorff metric.

Current quantum processors are prone to faults during quantum computations, largely due to hardware imperfections. These errors can be mitigated by employing a mix of short, fault-tolerant operations and occasional measurement resets, which necessitate a comprehensive controller able to manage both types of operations. Given the intricate nature of these controllers, combining hardware and software approaches to develop the controller seems a viable strategy. Here, we take a software-only approach, formulating the development of the controller as a reinforcement learning problem. By framing subspaces related to measurable quantum states as action spaces, we can train encoders to map quantum states into these spaces and develop optimal reward policies in conjunction with simulated hardware components. These learned encoders can be applied across a range of quantum algorithms to provide robust results in the presence of hardware faults. Specifically, our experiments using the SOR algorithm demonstrate that our method yields superior execution times relative to baseline approaches, particularly when dealing with faulty simulations. While the primary focus remains on hardware-driven development, our work indicates that a software-only approach to designing fault-resilient controllers remains a feasible option. Moreover, we believe this method could be adapted to enhance existing quantum algorithm performance, even in the absence of hardware faults. Ultimately, we contend that a hybrid, hardware-and-software driven design for fault-resilient quantum computation has the potential to yield substantial benefits. Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to reduced power consumption, increased radiation resistance, and improved time resolution. We introduce a logical system with a category theory foundation, designed to express continuous reasoning. This system builds on the principles of S1S semantics but expands it to include continuous domains as Scott domains. This expanded framework is embodied in the category CCont of continuous domains, equipped with Scott-continuous functions. This category serves as a robust mathematical model for treating partial and nested equality as a meaningful equivalence relation. Additionally, we define a suitable type of morphism to capture the concept of homomorphisms between continuous domains, providing a natural means to extend the framework to (CCont, Scott-continuous functions). This includes a specification of the category's diagonal embedding and its intersection with the subcategory (CCont, Scott-lub). Furthermore, we establish a categorical logic that corresponds to this system, consisting of a modal logic with a specific focus on continuity, as well as a type theory that reflects the structural properties of the category. This is demonstrated through an explicit construction of the category CCont^ty of typed continuous domains, complete with types for lub and meet. Finally, we demonstrate that this typed system is equivalent to the category-theoretic approach, establishing a natural correspondence between types and continuous functors. This offers a constructive means to prove correspondence between types and meaningful propositions, as well as to extend the framework to various topological structures. Specific applications are shown for the case of topological groups. In particular, we define a certain subcategory of continuous domains as a category of structured topological groups, showing that the types of this system correspond precisely to the groups in question. This approach offers a promising means to model various algebraic and topological structures using types, offering a potential means to extend this technique to other categories as well. This includes a brief discussion of possible means to extend this technique to the category of Polish spaces. Detailed proofs are provided in an accompanying appendix. This is a significant departure from existing research in these fields, which has traditionally relied on recursive axiomatic semantics for modelling. Suicidal ideology is a complex issue that can be hard to pinpoint, but
emerging research shows that by analyzing digital footprints, early signals
of suicidal thoughts can be detected. These footprints leave behind a trail
on social media platforms, where users' thoughts are updated in sequences
over time. Currently, models are typically trained as individual units,
unleveraging the valuable temporal connections within these sequences. This
paper proposes a novel framework that integrates three distinct sources of
information: Twitter posts, Wikipedia edits, and user comments on online
forums, using a deep sequential model. The framework's effectiveness is
tested in detecting suicidal thoughts by cross-validation on a combined
dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art systems and revealing the relative
importance of each information source. The framework can be accessed at
https://github.com/shmusho/Suicidal_Ideology Detection. A pilot study
shows that early warnings of suicidal thoughts can be issued one week prior
to registration on public forums, enabling timely interventions. The study
also validates the model's accuracy using expert assessments. Ultimately, the
model contributes to early detection of suicidal ideology by targeting
individual sequences of data and leveraging the collective potential of
multi-source information. The research raises important questions about the
societal implications of detecting suicidal ideology and encourages further
exploration of good practices in natural language processing to detect
negative thoughts. The models developed in this study can be applied to
various contexts beyond detecting suicidal ideology, including monitoring
mental well-being and detecting spam on online forums. The source code is
available at https://github.com/shmusho/Suicidal_ Ideology Detection. A
limited version of the code can also be found at https://shmusho.github.io/

Our research reports initial findings from studying the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A using the Inverse Compton X-ray Polarimetry Explorer. Between October 2022 and February 2023, IXPE captured 14 billion X-rays from the region surrounding the supernova's explosion site. Data analysis revealed a clear, negative polarization pattern, with a significance of more than 6 standard deviations. This research aims to uncover the relationship between U-type galactic warpage and its presence in galaxy clusters, as well as the impact of the tidal forces stemming from nearby galaxies. Our analysis centers on a unique sample of 82 galaxies drawn from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, consisting of 41 U-type galactic warpage galaxies in clusters and 41 undistorted galaxies in clusters acting as controls. Our data show that U-type galactic warpage galaxies in clusters exhibit characteristics akin to "jellyfish" galaxies, both radially and spatially. Furthermore, we found U-type galactic warpage galaxies in clusters to be more massive, older, and experience more intense starbursts compared to undistorted galaxies in clusters. Our results also suggest that U-type galactic warpage galaxies in clusters undergo more intense tidal forces due to nearby galaxies, a phenomenon prevalent in both spiral and pure gas jellyfish galaxies. Our classification system of jellyfish galaxies may thus serve as a means to identify potential candidates of distorted disk galaxies based on their galaxy cluster counterparts. We hypothesize that undistorted galaxies in clusters may also undergo U-type galactic warpage galaxies in clusters, given enough time. This led to large changes in their oscillating patterns, which were highly dependent on the underlying dynamics and time modulation patterns. We developed an analytical approach to describe this phenomenon, which explained how chaotic dynamics could be amplified through time modulation in systems with long memory. Furthermore, we showed that chaotic propagation in delayed systems could be utilized to develop secure communication methods, where an encoder sends encoded information through a delayed system with a complex time lag, and then uses this information to assist an receiver in reconstructing the original signal and extract the hidden data. These findings represent the first examples of secure communication schemes based on delayed systems with chaotic dynamics. In addition, we explored the diffusion patterns that emerge when delayed systems' time lag is changed randomly, which led to the creation of secure diffusion algorithms. These algorithms could be used to secure data effectively, and provided a better security performance compared to conventional methods. Meanwhile, secure communication and diffusion schemes also possess the ability to evade detection in these systems, which further adds to their security value. Overall, our work identified new approaches to designing secure encryption and diffusion systems based on delayed dynamics with chaotic behavior. In software design, client and developer conversations are vital for pinpointing requirements.  Natural language processing can be utilized to automatically extract relevant information from these discussions, however, the automatic discovery process for required concepts remains a challenge.  Research has been conducted to determine whether a consensus can be achieved automatically through natural language cues to define design requirements.  Our findings from a thorough evaluation within a real-world design process establish the reliability of natural language cues in driving automatic requirement discovery and also show that requirements can be consistently defined manually.  The implications of these outcomes for design processes that utilize natural language are then discussed.  The research presents a method to mine design conversations for relevant concepts that can serve as a guideline for natural language-driven automatic requirement discovery.  The proposed approach is then put into practice for a data set from the Eclipse indigo design process and the outcomes are compared against a previously proposed baseline.  The results from two diverse evaluators show that a consensus can be reached automatically through natural language cues to define design requirements and that their recommendations align with the actual requirements set by the design team.  The consistency of the outcomes from two independent evaluators indicates that a requirement can be clearly defined.  The findings from two further analyses do not show any relationship between the clarity of a requirement and the characteristics of the design conversation.  The stability of the recommendations was tested and no major shifts were detected.  The consistency of the recommendations was then compared against those generated through random walks and baseline models, revealing significantly higher stability with our approach.  The research concludes that natural language cues can serve as a reliable foundation for automatic requirement discovery and that their consistency can be favored over random models.  The findings also offer insights for design conversations that can guide natural language-driven automatic requirement discovery.  The research establishes a basis for further exploration into natural language-driven automatic requirement discovery.  The mined concepts can also be employed to analyze design conversations or guide future design interactions.  The research offers a ground truth for future evaluations, including applications for conversational interfaces, requirement elicitation, and natural language modeling. A major uncertainty in theoretical models of cosmic star formation originates from the process of planetesimal formation. Recent breakthroughs allow for the controlled simulation of this process within rotating, collapsing molecular clouds for the first time. Specifically, this study models a massive cloud ($10^4\,M_{\odot}$) that collapses and forms a Population III star under the influence of rotating and magnetic fields. By comparing cloud properties before and after collapse, researchers find that a weak magnetic field ($10^{-10}\,\mathrm{G}$) increases the formation times of protostellar disks and allow for the development of planetesimals within $10^3\,\mathrm{yr}$. However, a stronger magnetic field ($10^{-8}\,\mathrm{G}$) effectively inhibits disk formation due to dissipation caused by the interaction with rotating cloud fragments. This finding suggests that the removal of angular momentum from the cloud enables the release of fragmented material into free-falling streams that prevent the formation of protostellar disks. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that ambipolar diffusion can eliminate disk fragmentation around Population III stars, aligning with the observed absence of such disks in the universe's early periods. Nevertheless, this mechanism may not completely prevent the formation of small, gravitationally bound structures (such as rocks or brown dwarf-mass objects) due to the role of small-scale (neo-classical) fragmentation processes. Further work is needed to model this process more accurately. Such objects could subsequently survive and influence the formation of the universe's first planets. At a protostar mass of $8\,M_{\odot}$, this study models the formation of a massive envelope ($\sim\!0.52\,M_{\odot}$) with a kinetic energy comparable to its gravitational energy. Within a few hundred years, this massive envelope could surround a Population III star and have a significant impact on its evolution by delivering metals to the star for a longer period than in the case of more typical protostellar disks. As a result, the resulting Population III star could explode in a supernova more similar to those of metal-rich iron stars, potentially forming a black hole or a white dwarf with a more limited mass. This study offers a new perspective on the universe's earliest supernovae, including the possibility that the brightest of these explosions could have been caused by massive Population III stars with high metal content. Radio Frequency (RF) signals are susceptible to various disturbances that result in unpredictable fluctuations in their strength, which can be modeled as a function of space and time. Utilizing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) facilitates the exploration of harsh environments for the optimization of wireless communication systems. Given their distinct paths, UAVs independently collect data on the RF signals, leading to the need for collaborative data fusion to create a joint map of the RF signal strength. We refer to this mapped terrain as the Radio Chart. In this research, we propose an innovative approach to jointly estimate the Radio Chart and the UAVs' trajectories, while also accounting for their individual movements. We outline two feasible methods: a stochastic maximum a posteriori (SMAP) method based on traditional Bayesian filtering, as well as a sequential independent sampling (SIS) method grounded in sequential Monte Carlo sampling. Through numerical evaluations, we demonstrate that our proposed methods exhibit increased signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) and faster convergence rates compared to existing state-of-the-art strategies, while also achieving cross-validation performance comparable to the optimal Bayesian (OB) method. Notably, the computational efficiency of our proposed SIS method surpasses that of OB by a significant margin. We also introduce a novel criterion for assessing the reliability of radio strength readings and provide theoretical support for the performance of our proposed designs. A common approach for combining statistical results from different groups or studies involves averaging the parameters with their respective confidence intervals. However, this methodology poses challenges when applying it to sampling data, as discrepancies in measurement procedures can render parameters non-comparable. This issue is addressed by examining the concept of blending parameters from distinct samples or studies with varying assessment methods. We develop a generalized maximum likelihood method for blending parameters using information theory-based weights that incorporate the relative variances of the estimates. This approach is shown to be effective in assessing the mixed mean income of two groups with incomparable measures and in combining sampling data with varying assessment methods. Furthermore, the methodology is demonstrated through simulations based on real-world data, namely the analysis of Parisian street art sampling project, where two methods of measuring tag frequency were used, and the assessment of the average iron content in soil samples analyzed by ICP-MS and XRF. These applications illustrate the versatility of the proposed method for blending parameters with potential applications in various fields. We further investigate the performance of the method in the context of non-response imputation, where we explore an unsupervised learning method that combines parameter blending with k-nearest neighbors for imputing missing values using a predictive model based on complete case analysis. This method is compared to traditional complete case and list-wise deletion methods and demonstrates improved performance in prediction tasks. Therefore, the proposed method offers an efficient and accurate means of blending parameters and can serve as a useful SupRML method for handling non-response data. We examine the coherence of our results with this broader context. A related contribution also examines the broader implications of our results for research design, focusing on the analysis of data from two studies or samples with varying assessment methods. A growing trend in distributed neural network training is federated learning. Unlike conventional distributed training, which leverages multiple GPUs within a single machine, federated learning distributes work across numerous machines, making it ideal for training large models on datasets too vast for a single machine. Since communication between machines is costly, a key challenge in federated learning is balancing the frequency of updating model parameters to minimize communication overhead while achieving desirable convergence rates. Currently implemented aggregation methods, such as allreduce and allgather, treat all gradient vectors equally, which leads to inefficient communication when there are redundant gradient components. A novel aggregation method based on the BSP algorithm addresses this issue by broadcasting the model's current state and inviting each machine to correct it, thereby eliminating redundant gradient components in communication. A corresponding alternative algorithm has been developed for federated averaging, which uses a buffer to store machines' updated parameters and aggregates them after receiving a signal from the primary machine. Our approach has been validated by running experiments on multiple datasets, which demonstrate that, compared to conventional distributed training, our method requires significantly fewer communication steps while achieving comparable or superior accuracy. Specifically, on the CIFAR10 dataset, our method requires only 20% of the communication steps required by conventional distributed training to achieve similar results. Additionally, our method has been validated by comparing its performance to existing federated learning approaches, which fail to efficiently balance communication overhead and convergence rate. Our code is publicly available for reproduction of the results. Additionally, we have calculated the energy and memory requirements for different training methods, which suggest that, although there may be a slight increase in memory usage due to the buffering of updated model parameters, our method can significantly reduce the energy and memory costs associated with the current state-of-the-art federated learning algorithms. Specifically, we have found that our method requires 52% and 78% less communication and memory, respectively, compared to the current state-of-the-art federated learning algorithms. These results validate the design choices made for the project. Further research could be directed at investigating the potential for overparametrization in distributed training and how it affects the efficiency of the training process, as well as exploring the use of the proposed aggregation method in other federated learning algorithms to further improve its performance. Additionally, we plan to study the statistical distribution of the gradient counts among the machines and how it affects the efficiency of the aggregation method, which may lead to a more accurate model for predicting communication overhead based on the models' structural properties. Furthermore, we aim to extend the validation of the method to more practical scenarios

A flexible raft breaks up into multiple islets when subjected to external forces like shear and compression. Researchers studied the failure patterns of rafts made of different materials with varying stiffnesses, using both computer simulations and experimental results to compare their findings. By analyzing the progression of fractures in a raft, built-up stresses and the formation of distinct cracks can be observed. What causes the initiation and development of cracks within a raft, and how does its material properties affect its failure behavior? According to their research, both the external load and material properties play a crucial role in determining the number of fractures a raft will undergo. This unique structure holds significant potential for enhancing the performance of existing link prediction models, which can effectively generate plausible event timelines by using the models' established relationships between entities and the inherent temporal context. This is supported by empirical results demonstrating that regular fixed models can significantly improve the accuracy of link prediction in temporal graphs. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed method excels in handling gaps and elongations in timelines, outperforming previous methods. Our methodology and results offer practical guidance for using fixed models in temporal knowledge graphs to enhance link prediction and timeline extension tasks. It achieves this by linking an HDE with a nonparametric estimator, essentially transforming known depgraph-based outcomes into corresponding regression outcomes. Conversely, it also initiates a new approach to establish HDEs using nonparametric regression techniques, thereby expanding the scope of HDEs beyond dependent graph methodologies. Recent advancements in natural language modeling have led to the development of models like GPT-3, which can process text input and generate outputs in a variety of formats, including text, images, and audio. Studies have shown that these models can complete various natural language tasks, including translation, question-answering, and summarization, when provided with appropriate prompts. However, the effectiveness of these prompts in facilitating task completion is often unclear. To investigate the impact of prompts on model performance, we conducted a comprehensive review of the literature on natural language modeling and selected a range of tasks, including text classification, entity recognition, sentiment analysis, paraphrasing, and summarization. We evaluated the performance of models like GPT-3 in these tasks using both human and machine-prepared prompts, considering factors such as diversity of prompts, length of output, and expected model responses. Our analysis demonstrates that tailored prompts can enhance model performance across these tasks, with the potential for greater improvements as models become increasingly sophisticated. Additionally, our investigation of various prompt types and models identifies areas for further exploration and suggests that the best approaches often rely on a combination of established and innovative techniques. Finally, our study highlights the importance of systematic modeling and modeling of language, which we propose should be a key consideration for both researchers and industry practitioners moving forward. We examined the relationship between inter-solar variable pressure and temperature, along with wave characteristics, including amplitude, frequency, and propagation speed, and discovered a consistent pattern of dependence on the atmospheric layer and temperature. These particles are tracked, their data used to calculate auditory parameters in real-time, producing sound on demand. A straightforward interface allows artists to concentrate on visual practices, transferring those movements into audible formats. Achieving a balance between economic well-being and human life is crucial in the face of an unexpected crisis such as an epidemic outbreak. To promote both physical and economic health, timely measures to contain the spread of the epidemic are necessary. To develop an effective response, a mathematical framework is applied to models of the SIS, SIR, and SEIR types, all featuring sudden, abrupt transitions. The framework reveals that the optimal time to introduce counter-measures corresponds to the moment when the epidemic's peak is expected to occur. Furthermore, these measures are most effective when introduced simultaneously with the arrival of the peak. The analysis demonstrates that introducing measures too early or keeping them in place after the peak only serves to delay their disappearance, but does not prevent the eventual disappearance of the measures. The counter-measures are envisioned to take the form of non-pharmaceutical interventions such as stay-at-home orders and travel restrictions. The application of the proposed framework to the analysis of time-series data from the early stages of the COVID-19 outbreak in Bulgaria provides clear evidence of the model's validity and offers a practical tool for decision-making policy-makers. The chosen transition model is based on discrete-time Markov chains, but the proposed method can be applied to models with any form of transition. Additionally, the required parameters for any epidemic model can be determined using graph metrics based on the network that influenced the outbreak. The accuracy of the proposed method is validated through a comprehensive set of numerical tests performed on various types of epidemic models and their corresponding numerical implementations. The test results confirm that the proposed algorithm yields the most accurate results of all the methods tested. The methodology presents a unified approach to determining the optimal time to introduce non-pharmaceutical counter-measures for models of all types, ultimately contributing to a general theory of the most effective counter-measures. The effectiveness of machine learning (ML) models heavily relies on large datasets, which can be marred by inaccuracies, biases, and attacks. Currently, there's no systematic approach to identify data inaccuracies and address them, with most relying on intuition or semi-automatic methods that only scratch the surface. In response, we introduce a data troubleshooting framework centered on the Shapley value, which for the first time enables the comprehensive investigation of data influences across the entire ML pipeline. Our approach encompasses a data preparation phase, where candidate features with potential influence are identified, followed by a forecasting phase, where their anticipated impact on performance when included in the model is calculated, and finally, a backward looking phase, where their actual contribution is quantified. The relative importance of each data element is then prioritized, guiding data refinement to optimize performance. Through case studies using tabular, text, and image data, we showcase the robustness of our method in handling datasets of varying quality, comparing favorably to existing alternatives, while its open-source implementation is made accessible for the ML community. With this framework, data scientists can now efficiently pinpoint and address data inaccuracies, biases, and vulnerabilities, ensuring higher ML model reliability and robustness throughout their development and deployment lifecycle. The contribution of this work lies in its comprehensive approach to data troubleshooting, which is validated through empirical research and serves as a versatile foundation for various data-related applications, such as data validation, modeling, and security risk assessment. In particular, this method can be employed to tackle data validation challenges by focusing on performance resilience in the forecasting phase or data security incidents by detecting vulnerable data elements. Further research is invited to leverage our approach, with evident avenues also existing for semi-supervised learning scenarios, where data attributes with hidden labels can also benefit from this troubleshooting framework. The Shapley value's ability to quantify contributions, along with our algorithm's efficiency, enables data scientists to create custom loss functions for data-driven training, offering novel possibilities for interaction between the two. Moreover, this framework can be used to develop intelligent data assistants that evaluate the impact of data changes on ML models during testing or deployment, as demonstrated in our empirical research. The integration of our data troubleshooting framework and Shapley significance further empowers existing methods for data-driven training to incorporate the actual influence of data elements, yielding superior results and offering a comprehensive approach to data troubleshooting. The empirical research presented also highlights the applications and possibilities of this framework for training and deployment processes. A hypergraph represents an advanced graphical model, capturing more intense connections between nodes. In various fields, hypergraphs serve as useful tools for analyzing and managing complex data structures. Research into hypergraph improvement has primarily centered on optimizing its structural properties. To address this, a new framework called guided hypergraph improvement is introduced, which focuses on incorporating external expertise to enhance the graph's overall quality. Guide-based hypergraph improvement can be applied to numerous tasks, including guided vertex and edge addition, deletion, and optimization. By leveraging these operations in various sequences, the framework enables the efficient resolution of guided hypergraph optimization problems. Guided hypergraph improvement is demonstrated through the development of practical methods for addition and deletion operations, along with the introduction of a hypergraph improvement algorithm inspired by the Berge-Cycle Theorem. The performance of this algorithm is validated through numerical analysis and the evaluation of its efficacy in real-world applications. Specifically, guided hypergraph improvement is shown to be capable of addressing challenges in hypergraph-based recommendation and graph classification tasks. The results indicate that the proposed algorithm surpasses existing solutions in these domains. To further showcase its utility, guided hypergraph improvement is applied to the configuration of autonomous underwater vehicles, yielding a notable improvement in their travel time. The guided hypergraph improvement framework presents an innovative approach to managing complex data structures, offering a highly versatile tool for addressing a wide range of challenging problems. Our research assesses the viability of cryptocurrencies as a means of exchange by examining their consistency with economic costs. We introduce a concept for the consistent existence of equilibrium in a monetary economy, and demonstrate that cryptocurrencies meet this criterion along with traditional fiat currencies. Furthermore, we show that consistent cryptocurrencies form a closed subset of the space of Borel probability measures on the compactification of $\mathbb{R}_+^{n+1}$. Using advanced topological methods, we establish the density of a cryptocurrency's currency unit in its equilibrium distribution. We also explore how securing a consistent cryptocurrency affects its users, modeling risk aversion through a concave von Neumann-Morgenstern utility function and finding that, in equilibrium, a cryptocurrency's security cost is proportional to its hazard rate. Comparing the costs of securing different cryptocurrencies, such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, reveals similar constants of proportionality, consistent with our theoretical predictions. Moreover, our analysis estimates the costs of securing these cryptocurrencies, quantifying their economic viability as means of exchange. We conclude that, in the absence of external risks, the costs of securing Bitcoin and Ethereum can be supported by their respective fees, suggesting that these fees are an efficient means of allocating resources to security. Furthermore, our results imply that these fees may also be sufficient to cover the costs of securing other consistently existing cryptocurrencies. We also examine the potential risks to users of cryptocurrencies, modeling a general price path through a geometric Brownian motion and finding that, in equilibrium, a cryptocurrency's price is directly proportional to its log-martingale mean. When a robot interacts with a delicate object, its ability to manipulate objects is critical to success. For robots to effectively engage with objects, their manipulability realm must be adapted to match the object's geometry. Interacting with an object while allowing for some movement between the robot's hand and the object is essential; thus, a new task is proposed, named interactive manipulability realm adjustment. To solve this challenge, we introduce a method that conveys the object through a series of temporary poses, allowing the robot to maintain contact with the object at all times. To facilitate interaction, the object must be positioned in a way that allows for optimal engagement. Therefore, we developed a fully-automated algorithm to adjust the robot's manipulability realm by iterating through various temporary poses, refining the object's position using manifold-aware ICP, and evaluating interactiveness with every iteration. To enable fast and efficient planning, we also developed a practical heuristic that reduces the complexity of interactive manipulability realm adjustment. The proposed method was tested and validated in experiments using an Urobot using both a UV camera and a CS camera. The results show that the proposed heuristic is capable of solving the interaction problem quickly and efficiently. The developed method successfully interacts with an object in all tested conditions, while also demonstrating improved performance using manifold-aaw ICP. Based on these results, we believe that manipulability realm adjustment using parallel conveyance and manifold-aaw ICP provides a significant contribution to the field of human-robot collaboration. The code for this project has been made available for public use. The experimental data collected during testing, as well as the 3D mesh objects used in the study, can also be accessed through a public repository. A necessary step in combating coronavirus misinformation involves detecting it within social media dialogue and correcting the misinformation spread through interactive tasks. Current systems focus primarily on English-language content and do not incorporate contextual information from conversational partners. This work proposes a new task, called the COVID Dialogue Memes Dataset, which contains German-language social media dialogue with coronavirus-themed misinformation. The goal is to identify whether a tweet contains accepted or rejected misinformation based on the sender's previous tweets containing coronavirus-related misinformation. This goal is met through a novel application of a pre-trained transformer model, taking into account the sender's contextual information, as opposed to traditional transformer models that rely solely on the current tweet. The proposed approach is evaluated against a system that solely uses the tweet's text and is compared to a model that incorporates single-word vectors without any textual context. Experimental results indicate that the sender's contextual information significantly enhances the system's performance, achieving a score of 0.96 AUC when evaluated on a binary classification task, outperforming the text-only model by 0.08 and the word-based model by 0.45. The developed dataset comprises 1,114 distinct users, 13,549 relevant tweets, and 5,788 conversation pairs, ensuring a diverse range of conversational patterns among the system users. Additionally, the dataset comprises a variety of topical elements, including memes, videos, and text, offering potential avenues for exploration by the research community. The proposed system's architecture and code are publicly available for reproduction of the empirical results and future research on this task may employ additional natural language processing techniques with the objective of developing an effective strategy to combat coronavirus misinformation in social media dialogue. Physics-informed neural networks have exhibited remarkable capabilities in solving various partial differential equations. Despite their potential, they face difficulties with PDEs having moving boundaries or evolving domains. Integrating a mesh adaptation technique can mitigate these issues, but it poses additional challenges of its own. This work addresses these challenges by developing an efficient node creation technique that can be easily incorporated into physics-informed neural networks. In contrast to existing methods, this approach prioritizes simplicity and flexibility, producing high-quality results in both two and three-dimensional configurations. Additionally, our technique demonstrates computational savings of up to 30% compared to a conventional method. A key strength of our approach lies in its flexibility, allowing it to be adapted for various applications including boundary-aware node creation and the solution of semi-linear PDEs. Extensive evidence supports our technique's efficacy, showcasing its superior performance relative to current methods. In particular, our results reveal that a node creation strategy informed by the solution error can yield computational savings of up to 80%. This work presents a simple, flexible technique for integrating mesh adaptation into physics-informed neural networks, significantly outperforming existing methods. The growing complexity of freight systems worldwide poses significant challenges to their reliability. Disruptions in freight services have far-reaching effects on industries that rely on them, causing billions of dollars in lost revenue each year in the United States alone. These disruptions can spread to other segments of the freight ecosystem, causing widespread disruptions. To better plan and prepare for freight system disruptions, it is crucial to identify and understand the interconnectedness of various freight components. This study aims to achieve this goal by developing a visualization tool that maps the relationships within the freight ecosystem and analyzes the propagation of disruptions throughout the system. The research focuses on examining fragility spreads between specific freight sub-modules in the United States, with results showing that disruptions in the air freight sector have a significant impact on other segments, including the pharmaceutical and timber industries, while disruptions in the timber sector primarily affect the forest products industry, and that a high degree of fragility spread exists between the air freight and pharmaceutical sectors. Future research will utilize this methodology to develop preparedness strategies for freight system disruptions. The approach presented here is adaptable, allowing it to be applied to other domains beyond freight, particularly emergency services and supply chains. The methodology can contribute to research in this area, enabling researchers to replicate the approach and gain valuable insights for their specific domains. Furthermore, the study paves the way for future investigations into the following avenues: developing algorithms to identify the most vulnerable links within the freight ecosystem, identifying the most critical freight carriers and industries, and exploring the applicability of this approach to other domains beyond freight. The proposed methodology is centered around the following key research questions: (1) How can we create a representation of the freight ecosystem that captures the relationships between its constituent parts? (2) What approach can be used to identify and analyze disruptions throughout the system? (3) How can we validate the accuracy of this representation? (4) What insights can be gained from this system that are relevant to research in freight? (5) What are the relevant aspects of this freight paradigm that can contribute to the broader field? The SHINE project aims to address challenges in astrophysics and particle physics by detecting extremely light, rare hadron particles both in cosmic ray beams and during particle collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This requires a highly sensitive and precise detection system for various particles, which can also serve as a prototype for future deep-space missions focused on detecting cosmic hadrons. Unfortunately, due to technical and financial issues, the SHINE project is no longer moving forward. Despite this, the work on the project contributed significantly to the development of the NA62 experiment at the LHC, which used a refined version of a key detection technique designed for SHINE. This technique has led to multiple high-profile discoveries, including the most precise measurement of a rare reaction and a groundbreaking limit on a hypothetical type of particle interaction. Additionally, research using the NA62 detector is ongoing to study another rare reaction and is expected to set new records for sensitivity in a particular area. Meanwhile, concepts and technologies from the SHINE project continue to influence ongoing and future research projects at the LHC, as well as missions such as the Square Kilometre Array and the Giant Antenna System, a next-generation radio telescope. This includes developments in calorimetry, tracking systems, and data analysis software. This report presents an overview of the SHINE project and its legacy, highlighting potential future paths for research and development. Deep learning models like Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have become a preferred choice for developing effective orientation-aware models. Although incorporating orientation into DCNNs is beneficial, the current models face significant challenges, including data limitations and a lack of understanding. In an effort to overcome these obstacles, researchers often employ circular convolutional layers, which can mimic anisotropic filters using anisotropic pooling layers. However, this approach poses significant technical difficulties and hinders the model's performance. In an attempt to overcome these limitations, researchers propose the Orientation Convolutional Neural Networks (OCNNs), which utilize circular convolutional layers and anisotropic pooling layers in a more integrated manner. Specifically, OCNNs combine circular convolutional layers with dimensionality reduction techniques and selective anisotropic pooling layers to effectively aggregate circular convolutional features and anisotropic features. By doing so, researchers aim to develop a more effective orientation-aware deep learning model. The proposed OCNNs are evaluated on two intricate pattern recognition tasks, namely, image identification and classification. Our results demonstrate that OCNNs outperform circular convolutional-based models and anisotropic-based models, thus validating the proposed architecture's superiority. Furthermore, OCNNs show significant potential for application in various computer vision tasks. The proposed OCNNs are an effective and powerful deep learning model that can be utilized for orientation-aware deep learning tasks. The code for this model is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/tjcai/OCNN. The data repository for this model can be accessed at the following link: https://download.talhakhan.com/AnisotropicData. Our results provide a meaningful contribution to the field of orientation-aware deep learning and can be utilized for developing effective models. The parameter efficiency of our OCNNs is remarkable, with models comprising less than 5 million parameters showing superior performance. Our findings also highlight the significant role of circular convolutional layers and anisotropic pooling layers in deep learning models, which can be effectively aggregated using dimensionality reduction techniques. Ultimately, our OCNNs demonstrate excellent accuracy and parameter efficiency, thus validating the proposed architecture's superiority. The proposed OCNNs can be utilized for developing effective models in orientation-aware deep learning tasks. The parameter-efficient OCNNs demonstrate exceptional performance, thereby providing a meaningful contribution to the field of orientation-aware deep learning. The success of Deep Learning techniques has led to a surge in developing novel representations for point cloud processing. Due to their potential, the focus has shifted to Automatic Feature Construction. This concept is highly relevant for the graph-based point cloud processing methods, where researchers strive to devise efficient graph convolutional networks. Given the complexity and varied forms of existing approaches, a unified evaluation framework becomes highly necessary. This challenge presents several benchmark graphs, alongside a comprehensive analysis of the state-of-the-art graph convolutional neural networks, aiming to provide insights into their relative performance and select the most effective graph convolutional network for point cloud processing tasks. The proposed framework is comprised of six benchmark graphs, each featuring distinct numerical properties, and eight graph convolutional network types, evaluated across three practical scenarios: object classification, part segmentation, and semantic classification. The results indicate that the ChebyFilter graph convolutional network excels in object classification and part segmentation, whereas the DiffGraph graph convolutional network performs exceptionally well in semantic classification. Additionally, the best-performing graph convolutional network combined with a suitable graph type achieves superior results in object classification and part segmentation, ultimately surpassing the current state-of-the-art point cloud processing methods in these areas. The integration of the ChebyFilter graph convolutional network with the random graph type yields outstanding performance in object classification, part segmentation, and semantic classification. The open-source code and benchmark graphs accompanying this paper will facilitate research efficiency and inspire future developments in graph convolutional neural networks. The benchmark graphs, along with the corresponding results and code, can be found at https://grncnn-benchmark.github.io/. Recent advancements in cloud-based image processing technology have led to a surge in interest in remotely controlling AI-powered robots. However, this has also highlighted the need for more effective and adaptable AI systems that can thrive in dynamic and unpredictable environments. In response, researchers have developed new approaches to deploy AI services securely. Unfortunately, these developments have also led to the discovery of vulnerabilities in existing image classification models that can potentially be exploited for malicious purposes. For example, researchers have discovered the capability to create "hostless" Trojan attacks that can deceive AI models into giving false outputs without being altered internally. Although this new threat poses significant risks, the current approaches to detecting Trojan attacks are largely model-dependent and can only be effective if the model's internal workings are known. To address this gap, we propose a novel method for detecting Trojan attacks that does not require access to the model's source code. Our approach focuses on analyzing the semantic relationships between images and uses statistical techniques to detect anomalies and identify potential threats. Our method can successfully detect Trojan attacks on various models without requiring access to their internal workings, achieving high accuracy rates above 90%. Furthermore, we discovered that it is possible to create a single detection system that can detect Trojan attacks on multiple types of models, demonstrating the scalability of our approach. Our method provides a viable solution for detecting Trojan attacks in real-world applications where access to the model's internal workings may be limited. To further enhance this detection system's performance in real-world scenarios, we propose a new metric that estimates the likelihood of a given image containing malicious code. Our detection system can be adapted for use in other types of attacks by incorporating additional image manipulation techniques that are specific to the type of attack in question. In the field of nuclear physics, the study of nuclear fusion reactions at deep subbarrier energies has long been a topic of interest. These reactions exhibit highly absorbed astrophysical cross-sections that play a crucial role in understanding various phenomena, including the formation of heavy elements through rapid neutron capture processes and the expansion of core-collapse supernovae. However, experimental measurements of these reactions are often hindered by low reaction rates and large uncertainties. Consequently, physicists have had to rely heavily on theoretical models and approximate calculations to infer the necessary astrophysical S-factor values for predictive purposes.

However, in recent years, a novel analytical technique has been developed to bypass potential shortcomings in theoretical models. This method, called the Trojan horse method, allows for the extraction of reliable S-factors by averaging or folding measured cross-sections over the angular distribution. Despite initial reservations based on earlier critiques, a thorough examination of existing data has revealed that this technique can produce accurate results. Moreover, a direct comparison between THM and experimental values for the 12C + 12C cross-section at energies of approximately 15-20 MeV indicates an impressive level of agreement, with measured and predicted values overlapping within the error margins. These results strongly validate the THM's ability to produce reliable S-factors. Furthermore, the study's findings suggest that previous criticisms aimed at the THM were founded on misconceptions and a lack of understanding, and these misconceptions are explicitly addressed. Finally, the study concludes by emphasizing the THM's potential to revolutionize experimental nuclear astrophysics by facilitating the measurement of sensitive nuclear reaction cross-sections. This advancement could contribute significantly to improving our understanding of key astrophysical processes, such as the p-process, the r-process light seed formation, and the development of hydrodynamic simulations for core-collapse supernovae, among others. To achieve this goal, the researchers propose and outline a comprehensive research plan involving the measurement of low-energy fusion cross-sections for diverse nuclear systems using the THM technique. This plan is expected to yield precise data sets that can be used to test theoretical models and refine our understanding of the relevant astrophysical processes. To accomplish this goal, the researchers intend to concentrate their efforts on measuring the 12C + 12C cross-section at energies of approximately 15-20 MeV with enhanced precision using the THM technique. Astronomers have identified more than 4,000 planets so far, and their number is constantly growing. About a third of these planets are located in solar-type star systems and are considered to be of terrestrial type. In order to understand how these planets form, it is essential to analyze the chemical compositions of the stars from which they originate. By examining the chemical patterns in stellar atmospheres, scientists can gain valuable insights into the types of planets that are found in these systems. In this study, data from the HARPS/N2 project were analyzed, and the chemical compositions of more than 180 solar-like stars were investigated, including 102 stars with clear indications of planetary systems. The results showed that these planetary systems tend to have higher levels of metals than stars without planets. This is consistent with the theory that the presence of metal-rich material is necessary for the formation of terrestrial planets. Based on the levels of lithium in these stars, it appears that they have lost a significant amount of planetary-mass objects, which is in line with the theory that many of these planets are likely to be located within the habitable zone. The chemical compositions of these stars were also found to have variations in their cores, which is an indication of the presence of a planetary system. The size of this variation is directly related to the mass of the planets in the system, and it was found to be largest for stars with super-Earths. However, the same pattern was not found for stars with masses that are considered to be Earth-mass, and further research is needed to understand the relationship between core variations and Earth-mass planets. The data collected so far are not enough to understand the shapes of the planetary disks, and more variations of these stars need to be analyzed to confirm the trend that was found. In order to understand the masses of these core variations, it is necessary to make additional observations of the stars, and to make use of the capabilities of the Extremely Large Telescopes that are available today. In the future, it is possible that it will be possible to directly observe the mass of the planets in these systems by using a new technology that is called a planetary reflection effect. The theory behind this technique is that a planet's motion can cause the stellar atmosphere to move, which in turn causes variations in the light that is coming from the star.
