A key component in the location calculation process is the propagation delay, which is usually estimated using channel state information (CSI). Recent research introduced the use of machine learning (ML) models in Wi-Fi locationing by developing a dataset of labeled CSI data. This paper introduces a new method using attention-based neural networks to predict device location from raw CSI data, thereby eliminating the need to train separate models for different locations and eliminating the need for channel modeling. Compared to prior methods, our approach yields greater accuracy and faster computation, thereby facilitating more effective and efficient location estimation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves up to 25% improved accuracy relative to prior methods. By broadening the underlying framework, we are able to work with any modal logic that can be translated into bilinear modal logic, while maintaining compatibility with the original categorial interpretation.  Through the use of categories with stabilising functors, we are able to assign modal logics their intended topological meanings, thereby integrating different interpretations of modal logic by linking various topological categories through stabilising functors. It also facilitates result sharing and enables collaborative modeling within groups, allowing them to explore multiple scenarios and discuss results in real-time. ShinyCOPASI extends COPASI's capabilities to include tabular data import, plotting, and statistical analysis, enhancing users' experience and enabling model investigation and result sharing. In finite Markov decision processes, the most efficient method for solving the linear system $Ax = b$ when $A$ is a large, sparse, and symmetric positive-definite matrix is through the generalized minimum residual method. This algorithm iterates on the basis of an orthonormal basis generated from $A$ and an initial vector $x_0$. The basis is updated with each iteration, with each step depending on an approximation of $x$ that is also improved with each iteration. The GMRES method can be highly effective, but it has several drawbacks: it only yields an approximation of $x$, it is prone to instabilities, and it requires significant computational power. To overcome these limitations, we propose modifying the GMRES algorithm to iterate on multiple solutions at once through a Monte Carlo simulation. This change allows for an interval of possible solutions, rather than a singular solution, which in turn provides an estimate of the solution's precision and an option to terminate the algorithm once a sufficient level of accuracy is reached. This modification comes with an increased cost, but it offers the benefit of being memory-efficient as it only requires storing one vector at a time. We test this new approach on a dataset of large-scale Markov decision processes under two different simulation methods and find that it yields an accurate approximation of the solution within a reasonable computational cost. Furthermore, we observe that the algorithm can terminate the search for an accurate solution when a sufficient level of accuracy is reached. Our approach offers an efficient and efficient alternative to solving large-scale linear systems and finding optimal policies in extensive Markov decision processes. A weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, is used to form an edge ideal, which has its own set of Betti numbers and depth. This research investigates how certain parameters, such as the depth and Betti numbers, behave when we shift from a weighted directed graph $\mathcal{D}$ to its underlying undirected graph $\mathcal{G}$. Specifically, our findings show that changing the weights in $\mathcal{D}$ affects the depth and certain Betti numbers of the edge ideal for a particular class of graphs, which are the forest edge ideals. Moreover, this research provides examples to demonstrate that these patterns do not always hold for all graphs, as well as calculates the Lyubeznik numbers for the edge ideal of a weighted directed forest. This study also presents limitations and asks further questions about the relationship between the weights in $\mathcal{D}$ and the Betti numbers of the edge ideal. Finally, this research proposes an open problem about the change in the length of the edge ideal when we shift from a weighted directed graph to its underlying undirected graph.

The need to determine the optimal settings for complex computer simulations based on performance metrics is a common and significant challenge. This problem is known as an inverse problem. In fields such as medicine and materials science, scientists often encounter the issue of identifying the best parameters that yield desirable outcomes from various models. Due to the nature of such models, which often produce one- or many-dimensional continuous or discrete results, existing methods for solving inverse problems are limited. To address this issue, researchers have developed a multiple assessment approach on a dimensional time series contour basis. This methodology, which evaluates the closeness of predicted and actual time series using the Euclidean distance on a normalized scale, effectively integrates the results of multiple models. To efficiently handle large datasets, the approach includes a filtering mechanism for model comparisons. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this methodology in solving the inverse problem for various real-world and synthetic cases. Additionally, researchers have made available a comprehensive R package, called MultiConAssess, which enables other researchers to solve similar inverse problems and integrate the methodology into their existing workflows. Materials scientists may find the proposed methodology useful in determining optimal heat treatment conditions for materials, while biomedical researchers may employ it to identify the best medication dosages. This study introduces a data labeling technique, regional querying, for robust model training, involving asking labeled questions about data subsets from specific categories. Such queries can help enhance model performance by addressing issues like dataset contamination, but raise concerns whether regional queries are always advantageous. Through theoretical analysis and experiments, we investigate the benefits and drawbacks of regional queries and provide criteria for determining when they can improve learning outcomes. Empirical research confirms our findings, with notable effects observed in cases of heavy contamination and performance plateaus. Additionally, we demonstrate the practical application of regional queries in multi-class and ranking tasks. In Pb+Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV, the modifications to jet fragments caused by the medium are investigated using isolated-photon-tagged jets in both the central and peripheral collisions. After correcting for detector effects, the fragments' momentum is adjusted in a way that minimizes changes at high momentum. In central Pb+Pb collisions, an increased number of jet fragments below 0.5 GeV/$c$ and a changes in jet fragments' mean and mean square by 10-20\% are observed at 1-3 GeV/$c$ compared to peripheral events. Between 3-6 GeV/$c$, the modifications decrease with a larger jet momentum and are observed to be on the same trend as those found with inclusive jets. Additionally, the changes in jet fragments on the photon's side are greater than on the opposite side, indicating a response from the medium to the hard photon interaction. The measurements are compared to the theory and are in line with simulations of jets interacting with a quark-gluon plasma at 5.02 TeV, and are in the intermediate stage of thermal equilibrium. The findings cannot be fully explained by the radial flow and participate-in-full model currently. Furthermore, the data do not display any changes in the jet fragments that could indicate the medium inducing jet multiplication. Lastly, the data to this point do not show any dependence on the jet resolution parameter ($R$) as it is similar between inclusive and isolated-photon-tagged jets with $R$ = 0.4. Future research will focus on the application of the jet-peak tagging technique and the use of the jet logarithmic calibrator to further analyze the data and confirm whether the medium causes jet fragmentation changes. Additionally, the strategy includes comparing charged-particle spectra between Pb+Pb and $pp$ collisions to further investigate the medium's effects. Ultimately, the research aims to confirm whether the medium causes jet fragmentation changes and to further analyze the data with the aid of several theoretical models. In particular, the team plans to confirm or refute the participation of the medium in the jet fragmentation process through the comparison of peripheral and central Pb+Pb collisions. The research also aims to apply and test a new model that describes the medium as a thermal equilibrium in order to further analyze the data. Furthermore, the team plans to re-analyze the data using a new detection technique and to further investigate the medium's effects on jet fragmentation. In general, the research aims to further understand the medium's effects on jet fragmentation

Results are derived for the rapidity, transverse momentum, and multiplicity of these particles, both generally and specifically for several different initial conditions. These results are compared to predictions made using the SHM and HSM models. Additionally, the characteristics of particle production in Xe-Xe collisions are compared to those observed in earlier Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. It was found that particle production rates for a given energy and rapidity increase significantly with the size of the collided nuclei, and that this trend matches well with expectations based on thermal statistics. The data collected also exhibit marked symmetry between proton and antiproton production. The ratio of φ meson production to pion production in Xe-Xe collisions was found to be equivalent to the corresponding ratio in Pb-Pb collisions at a higher collision energy, and this was observed to be constant across a wide range of rapidity. The data collected also indicate that the produced particles are in a state of thermal equilibrium, and that this is true for collisions at both fixed-targets and with larger nuclei. Furthermore, the characteristics of particle production in Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV were found to be consistent with a quark-gluon plasma state at a temperature of approximately 92 MeV. Creating infrastructure on other planets is heavily dependent on locally sourced materials and specific construction technologies that utilize heat to form and bind substances. The success of these projects hinges on understanding how the processes affect the final material properties. In this research, various methods are used to analyze the effect of sintering temperature on the mechanical and surface properties of lunar and Martian regolith samples. The samples were subjected to different heat treatments, ranging from 900 to 1200 degrees Celsius, and then tested for compressive strength, Young's Modulus, and surface hardness. The results show that the sintering temperature significantly impacts these properties, with the compressive strength increasing at a rapid rate but leveling off at higher temperatures, the Young's Modulus increasing at a steady rate, and the surface hardness displaying a rapid and uniform increase. The sintering temperatures affected the samples' microstructures and surface shapes, with the lunar regolith samples displaying stronger and stiffer properties than the Martian regolith samples at high temperatures. Additionally, the sintering temperatures affected the samples' bonding mechanisms, shifting from atomic to granular bonding at higher temperatures. The findings provide crucial guidelines for selecting the optimal sintering temperatures and materials for constructing infrastructure on the Moon and Mars. The data collected can also be applied to other materials under similar environmental conditions. The research paves the way for further studies on the mechanical and thermal properties of these materials under atmospheric and vacuum conditions. The sintering temperatures and pressures can be tailored to develop temperature-resistant materials and to improve the mechanical properties of these planetary regolith materials. The research also offers a method for developing and processing infrastructure materials on other planets that are strong, stiff, and resistant to heat. Research has shown that a non-circulating liquid film on a fiber exhibits the Rayleigh-Plateau instability when subjected to external forces, resulting in periodic capillary instability and ultimately sticking of the liquid to the fiber. A theoretical model has been developed to explain the slipping behavior of liquids from fibers in the absence of external forces. The model reveals that a potential difference between the fiber and liquid can influence slipping patterns. Furthermore, the models for sticking and slipping have identified three newly observed phenomena: (1) partial sticking, where the liquid remains on the fiber except for a droplet at the liquid-air interface; (2) non-axial capillary instability; and (3) re-formation of liquid jackets on the fiber, allowing for an understanding of how these phenomena occur. The models have been validated using experiments of water and glycerin on fibers with various surface treatments. The research findings could contribute to improving the fabrication of liquid-filled microcapsules. The theoretical models provide crucial insights into factors that can promote or inhibit liquid accumulation on fibers, and suggest ways to enhance or prevent liquid sticking. The models also reveal strategies for controlling the formation of liquid jackets on fibers. By analyzing a sample of 382 starburst galaxies from the SINGS database, we evaluated the reliability of star formation rate estimates obtained through SED fitting using different models, against a measured bracket gamma line that is largely unaffected by obscuration. We found a strong linear relationship between the rates derived from the models and the line data, but the slopes and intercepts varied significantly based on the models used. After applying corrections for dust and nuclear emission, our results showed a more consistent relationship, with the coefficients converging towards a single value. Notably, the coefficients for the Chary & Elbaz model were significantly higher than the others, while the models of Charlot & Pei and Fiore et al. produced comparable outcomes. Furthermore, our study revealed that using gamma_4228 instead of gamma_3871 provides a better fit for the data, and that filtering out objects with extreme emission could produce a tighter correlation. Based on our results, we propose a new calibration for converting bracket gamma line data into star formation rates, which could be useful for observations with space-based telescopes that are unaffected by dust. This standard could provide a valuable alternative for estimating star formation rates in cases where other methods are not available or are influenced by dust. By comparing our data with other proxies, we also examined the relationship between bracket gamma line and other star formation indicators, and found a tight, linear relationship with UV colors and a negative correlation with mid-IR colors. We also used our data to estimate average star formation rates for broad-line active galactic nuclei with little or no host contribution. We derived a bracket gamma line based on SED fitting that is in good agreement with empirical predictions, including one by Shirazi & Tsai. Using our line data, we calculated the average star formation rates for a sample of type-I active galactic nuclei, and found them to be in agreement with empirical predictions. We also used our data to estimate the average star formation rates for a sample of active galactic nuclei with little or no host contribution. We derived a bracket gamma line based on SED fitting that is in good agreement with empirical predictions, including one by Shirazi & Tsai. Using our line data, we calculated the average star formation rates for a sample of type-I active galactic nuclei, and found them to be in agreement with empirical predictions. We explored the possibility of using bracket gamma line data to estimate black hole masses, and found it to be unfeasible due to the lack of bracket gamma line data in many samples of active galactic nuclei.

Comprehensive analysis of the results sheds light on the challenges of working with stylus input data and highlights the merits of combining mathematical expression recognition with context-driven retrieval. Furthermore, our research showcases the feasibility of developing groundbreaking interactive applications that seamlessly integrate mathematical expression recognition and other forms of input. Additionally, the detailed assessments provided can serve as a foundation for refining existing stylus-based mathematical expression recognition systems, thereby driving enhancements to current stylus-based applications and standards. We experimentally investigate how solid particles are incorporated into turbulent plumes rising from a heated bottom surface in a vertical column. By adjusting the temperatures at the bottom surface and the concentration of suspended particles, we study the incorporation process through qualitative observations and quantitative data. The incorporation process is divided into two distinct regimes, separated by a critical temperature gradient, with different underlying mechanisms. When the temperature gradient exceeds a certain threshold, hot fluid near the bottom surface expands, causing it to sink and mix with the particles in the plume. This interaction leads to the accumulation of particles at a specific height, forming a layer with a higher concentration of particles. In contrast, lower temperature gradients result in direct deposition of particles onto the bottom surface. The incorporation efficiency and its dependence on the temperature gradient and particle concentration are examined in detail. Additionally, the effects of particles on the turbulence of the fluid are assessed using a novel approach based on image analysis and specifically defined variables related to particle dynamics. The results reveal how the particles modify the turbulence characteristics, especially in terms of intensity and scale. This research provides new insights into the interaction between particles and fluid turbulence and may be applied to understand natural phenomena, such as particle incorporation in geological and planetary contexts. Furthermore, it has potential applications in industries involving suspension dynamics to improve the understanding of particle incorporation processes. Developing efficient and reliable multithreaded software is increasingly crucial.  However, the intricate nature of multicore operating systems and the potential for thread interference makes error detection challenging.  Traditional locking mechanisms are ineffective against synchronization bugs, such as data races.  To address this issue, this paper introduces McMini, a thread checker that employs a configurable technique to identify violations of thread safety principles during execution.  McMini is built upon a dynamic partial-order reduction algorithm and incorporates a versatile policy for reducing thread interference.  This research presents an overview of McMini's architecture, the design of its interference reduction policy, and experimental evaluation of its effectiveness in verifying multithreaded applications.  Additionally, a public release of McMini's source code is made available for enabling research reproducibility.  Experimental results demonstrate that McMini outperforms a established state-of-the-art thread checker by 2.3 to 4.3 times.  Furthermore, McMini is capable of detecting 12 additional synchronization errors in a public thread-safe library, encompassing 10 data race issues and 2 deadlocks.  To date, McMini remains the fastest model checker for verifying multithreaded applications.  This research addresses the gap in existing literature by providing an in-depth analysis of McMini's design, performance, and error detection capabilities.  Specifically, the paper investigates under which circumstances model checking might fail to identify synchronization errors.  Our study offers guidelines for developers in pinpointing the root cause of model checker failure and suggests strategies for efficiently detecting all existing errors.  Finally, the paper presents an evaluation of the practicality of model checking in verifying actual bugs encountered during the development of multithreaded applications.  An empirical analysis reveals that model checking can successfully detect the majority of synchronization errors if their thread creation sequences and the corresponding states are known in advance.  To prove this point, the source code of the thread-safe library, as well as the corresponding McMini execution files, are released in public.  Our study demonstrates that model checking can be employed as an auxiliary tool for actual software development, aiding in identifying synchronization bugs encountered during testing.  While McMini may not detect all synchronization errors, our results show that model checking can successfully capture a range of synchronization bugs.  To showcase this, the source code of the thread-safe library, along with the McMini execution files, are made publicly available. This research proposes a new theoretical framework for inflation that is based on locally supersymmetric field theories.  In this framework, the conventional kinetic terms of scalar fields are replaced by a nonlinear interaction characteristic of such theories.  A new class of models, including the type I and type II f(R) inflating theories, is derived from existing supergravity models.  Our analysis indicates that the standard model of cosmological inflation can be effectively described within this framework, and specific models are presented along with corresponding inflationary predictions.  Furthermore, several solutions to stabilize scalar potentials at their minima, ensuring de Sitter vacua with no supersymmetric matter fields, are discussed.  This includes the application of flux compactification and stabilization by a Lincoln-Poisson term.  In addition, some type I inflation models satisfy all criteria for stability, including potental metastaability, with a nearly scale-invariant spectral index.  This approach potentially offers a coherent extension of the Standard Model of particle physics to the early universe, linking it to the mechanism of moduli stabilization.  This connection is explored in the context of the Starobinsky model.  However, other models, such as type II f(R) inflating theories, also allow for a good fit to observation-corrected n_s values.  Several type II models with no supersymmetric matter fields meet stability criteria.  In this framework, cosmic strings might be expected to have a low amplitude due to the noncanonical kinetic terms, which could provide a plausible explanation for their nonobservation.  This supresses not only scalar perturbations but also gravitational waves.  Finally, applying the framework to the Higgs field, considering the minimum of the scalar potential at v=173.5 GeV, reveals that it can accommodate a spectrum of inflation consistent with cosmic microwave background radiation data.  This involves a characteristic nonlinear interaction scale of about 10^10 GeV.  This value can be linked to the minimum of the scalar potential in the type I models, and also to the nonlinear interaction scale of the type II models.  This research offers a unique extension of locally supersymmetric field theories to the early universe, and provides a potential link between the mechanisms of inflation and moduli stabilization.  This connection provides theoretical unity across different scales, spanning from the Planck scale to the cosmic microwave background scale.  This approach provides a general framework for models, including the standard model of cosmological inflation, and suggests that inflation should be understood within the context of supergravity or superstring theory.

This data is then used to identify closed commercial systems, providing valuable insights into potential targets for exploitation. To obtain this data, attackers can employ passive OSINT methods, including running NTP/SNMP queries, and actively gathering IPv6 data through various means, such as scanning or exploiting vulnerable systems. This research delves into the techniques used by adaptive protocol analysts to identify and target sensitive systems, exposing them to assault via adaptive protocol identification. Specifically, our findings stem from an in-depth examination of six major adaptive protocol analysis tools, which revealed various vulnerabilities when subjected to comprehensive testing, including instances of deserialization exploitation, shell injection, and privilege escalation opportunities. Moreover, our research illustrates how these vulnerabilities can be exploited to allow attackers to manipulate identified data, potentially leading to false positives or sensitive system exposures. This paper presents multiple scenarios of adaptive protocol-related attacks, and provides mitigation strategies for each tool to prevent assaults on adaptive protocol analysis. Additionally, our research offers recommendations for implementing secure red teams and network defenses to minimize exposure to these assaults. Finally, our research affords a vulnerability exploitation timeline, enabling defensive teams to assess and compare the risks posed by these adaptive protocol analysis tools. This information is shared in the hopes that it may aid adaptive protocol analysts in strengthening their tools to prevent assaults on adaptive protocol identification. Moreover, our research aims to educate and empower network defenders to evaluate the risks posed by these adaptive protocol analysis tools, and encourage them to take action to secure their use. Ultimately, our research seeks to promote a more adaptive and resilient network defense posture. The relationships among COVID-19 coverage, cases, fatalities, and the news consumption habits of U.S. regions were investigated in a study that analyzed data from multiple sources and perspectives. First, an open-access database of COVID news coverage for 393 U.S. metropolitan areas from January 2020 to April 2021 was created. An analysis of the correlations among news coverage, cases, fatalities, and population data revealed that areas with more COVID-related news coverage had higher mortality rates and case counts. A factorial latent variable modeling technique was used to examine the causal effects of news coverage on cases and fatalities, while accounting for the influence of population demographics. A significant positive impact of news coverage on fatalities was found, but no such effect existed for cases. Additionally, it was observed that areas with more COVID news coverage had lower death-to-case ratios, suggesting that news coverage contributed to earlier COVID detection. The news consumption habits of U.S. regions were characterized through a topic modeling analysis of Google News data, where it was discovered that areas with more COVID news coverage were more likely to have a "COVID" topic that reflected ongoing pandemic coverage, while areas with less news coverage were more likely to have a "declining COVID" topic. A linear regression model showed that region-specific population demographics, including age, race, and income levels, accounted for variability in COVID news coverage, whereas the news consumption habits of regions were largely unaffected by these demographic factors. The data also highlighted the pivotal role of legacy news sources, such as The New York Times, in driving national COVID news coverage trends, while exploring the implications of the findings for science communication. Furthermore, the study connected COVID news coverage to broader social and political dynamics, including media polarization, political partisanship, and public skepticism toward politics and science. The interplay between news coverage and COVID mortality rates raised questions about the impact of news exposure on public health, while also raising concerns about undercoverage in areas with critical COVID needs. The research concluded by highlighting the importance of a nuanced theoretical framework that accounts for variability in news coverage, as well as the challenges and limitations of measuring COVID news coverage, particularly in areas with limited resource and capacity. The study contributed to theoretical debates on the news coverage-penetration model, media salience, and science communication, while also highlighting practical considerations for enhancing pandemic news coverage in areas with critical COVID needs. The research also underscored the significance of supporting independent and alternative news sources, as well as fact-checking initiatives, to combat misinformation and promote effective pandemic communication. Strong deepfakes are highly realistic and undetectable video manipulations that blend existing images and videos to create authentic-looking footage. Unlike weak deepfakes discovered in 2019, strong deepfakes can deceive everyone, including individual observers, as they nearly always pass the human visual check. Our research introduces an innovative strong deepfake generator, demonstrating the method's efficacy in creating manipulations that can evade detection through human vision. Conversely, we also introduce a powerful deepfake detector, showcasing its ability to accurately spot 93% of strong deepfakes as manipulations on the Labeled Strong Deepfakes dataset. Moreover, our research reveals that current deepfake detectors struggle to detect strong deepfakes, but a simple majority voting algorithm among three state-of-the-art models significantly enhances detection rates from 82.5% to 93%. Our created generator and improved detector will contribute to the advancement of deepfake research, ultimately promoting transparency and trust in video content. The generated strong deepfakes can be found at www.strongdeepfakes.com, comprising over 50,000 manipulations, and our project code is available at https://github.com/MeTron7/UnrestrictedStrongDeepfakes. The presence of a liquid envelope, specifically its composition, plays a crucial role in determining the size of a planet's radius. For planets with masses similar to Earth and composed primarily of rocky materials, a liquid envelope would result in a larger planet radius compared to a dry rocky body. Identifying the composition of a planet's liquid envelope could provide insight into its interior structure and balance of solubility versus gas thermodynamics.

Researchers reanalyzed theoretical models of small, rocky planets with liquid envelopes to develop new relationships between radius, mass, and surface gravity based on how the liquid envelope interacts with solids. They found that distinct transitions within these relationships are indicative of the composition of the liquid envelope and can be used to infer this composition through analysis of planetary transit signatures.

By comparing observed transit signatures of various exoplanets to this new framework, scientists were able to identify evidence of soluble compounds in two planets with masses similar to Earth and radius measurements in the 1.3 to 1.5 Earth radius range. Notably, this is the first time such compounds have been detected in planets of this size range, and their existence suggests that soluble compounds can dominate the liquid envelope composition of planets with masses as large as 2-3 times that of Earth. Finally, this new technique allows for a more accurate and efficient use of data from upcoming missions, enabling the identification of soluble compounds in a larger selection of exoplanets.

Inspired by brain-like learning processes, spiking neural networks, which incorporate plasticity, enable machines to acquire new information. However, existing gradient-based learning methods for spiking neural networks often yield undesirable spike jamming, where neurons overreact to weak inputs. Furthermore, these methods typically require complete access to all network activity, which is impractical for large datasets. To address these limitations, we have developed a novel learning algorithm for spiking neural networks based on temporal difference learning, requiring only local information. This approach enables machines to learn without compromising network responsiveness and allows for robust learning from complex data sets. Additionally, we have found that our method facilitates biologically feasible learning processes by mirroring the learning dynamics observed in animal studies. To demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm, we have successfully applied it to learning temporal credit assignment weights in a model token-based memory system. This paper reports on the results of the Out-of-Lexicon Word Sense Disambiguation task, a sub-task of the Sense Text Reconciliation task, hosted by the Semeval 2021 program. The data collection process involved using the Wiktionary dictionary to gather non-lexically bound words that may have multiple senses within a sentence. The evaluation task required participants to identify the most suitable sense for each such word from a provided list of relevant senses, without disregarding polysemous baseline candidates. The task's scoring method incorporated both human and automated metrics, with human annotation scores determined through three anonymous annotations and automated scores calculated using both Chi-square Permutation and Conditional Random Fields algorithms. The winning system, submitted by Christian M. Meyer and Malte Ehlers, successfully demonstrated the ability to accurately determine the correct sense of out-of-lexicon words, achieving a 43.67% F1 score using the Wiktionary dataset and 41.91% F1 score using the AMR dataset, both of which surpassed the polysemous baseline's performance. Furthermore, the submitted system utilized a combination of transformer-based models, incorporating knowledge from the Wiktionary and AMR knowledge bases, to enhance its performance and achieve these results. A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. However, determining the precision of these expansions is challenging, especially in complex situations. To address this issue, we've developed a reliable method to assess the accuracy of these expansions outside their initial framework. By utilizing this method, we can determine if the approximations obtained are sufficient and identify areas where further improvement is needed. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we've applied the technique to four distinct cases, including one where the dynamics of a particle near a force field with uncertainty are studied, another looking at how a particle's motion is affected by uncertainty in its initial conditions, a study on Navier-Stokes equations with uncertainty, and finally an investigation of a reaction-diffusion equation also involving uncertainty. In each of these applications, we've tested the accuracy of our approximations against varying levels of precision in the numerical computations and explored the implications of our findings on what is known as the "uncertainty principle". Additionally, we've directly evaluated the remaining error in our approximations and demonstrated how our method can effectively analyze the precision of these approximations, reveal how the level of precision affects them, and provide insight into their limitations. Furthermore, we've tested the ability of our method to detect when the approximations become less accurate and explored its ability to effectively evaluate the precision of these approximations on different levels. We've also extended the method to higher-dimensional chaos expansions, revealed that the precision of these expansions can vary significantly in different parts of the space in which they are defined, and finally investigated how to effectively verify the precision of these expansions in complex situations. To accomplish this, we've created a fully implicit method that can effectively analyze the precision of these expansions in any part of the space and combined it with a fully implicit solver for the differential equations, providing a more comprehensive approach. Advanced safety-critical systems require dependable alteration detection to ensure proper operation, especially when experiencing partial or unpredictable changes in behavior. Although data-driven methods are effective for identification, they are often hindered by limitations such as sensor failures, missing or inaccurate data, and partial or unpredictable changes. To address these issues, a novel framework incorporates adaptive data validation and processing techniques to isolate and model system behavior before and after alterations. This is achieved through real-time and offline data analysis using robust statistical methods on a data structure that can handle inconsistencies, followed by dynamic modeling to capture system patterns. The proposed approach is demonstrated on aircraft collision avoidance systems and real-world flight datasets. Compared to existing methods, this approach offers significant improvements in alteration detection accuracy and system dependency, particularly in safety-critical situations. The associated code can be accessed via the GitHub repository. The concept of partially-observed alteration identification is introduced, which involves detecting changes in behavior without prior knowledge of when, where, or how they occur. Furthermore, partially-observed alteration isolation provides recognition of alterations themselves within ongoing sequences of system behavior. The integration of these techniques, termed Adaptive POAI, enables accurate extraction of alteration periods and identification of their individual instances, ultimately leading to the development of dependable dynamic models for safe system operation. The effectiveness of this approach is shown on aircraft collision avoidance systems and real-world flight datasets. The associated code can be accessed via the GitHub repository. We use data from multiple dwarf galaxy surveys and incorporate their compositions into the PARCELS simulation to establish a new reference for their stellar populations. By comparing observed data with simulated results, we address potential discrepancies and set boundaries for the simulation's parameters. Furthermore, we evaluate how well the simulation's models replicate the observed relationships between stars through a series of forward modeling. The examination of various elements in red giant stars reveals that the simulation's metallicity distribution functions generally match observed data, yet slight inaccuracies occur at the very metal-poor end. Nonetheless, the simulation's fast-producers of heavy elements align well with observations. As a result of the comparison between the simulation's predictions and the observed patterns of star formation, we determine that the time frame for the rapid growth of dwarf galaxies' stellar masses must have been longer than previously suggested. Subsequent analysis of the galaxies' structural evolution reveals that the rate at which their stars form does not depend on their distance from the galaxies' centers, yet this rate does correlate with their initial mass. By running the simulation in reverse, we can identify the underlying initial conditions of the galaxies based on their final stellar populations, thereby indicating that the galaxies we studied were initially rich in gas but had low levels of metallicity. Ultimately, the examination of the galaxies' chemical compositions provides evidence that the galaxies we studied experienced a single, extended period of star formation. Moreover, the galaxies' structure and the rate at which their stars formed do not vary based on their distance from the galaxies' centers. In a comparative analysis, we found that the galaxies we studied exhibit similarities to NGC 6681, an metal-poor globular cluster found in the galaxy NGC 6705. This comparison may serve as a standard against which other stellar populations can be measured. In contrast, the completely invisible galaxy Tucana II has a very limited life expectancy. For a profinite group G, an action spectrum is defined as a set of non-equivalent homotopy classes of G-actions on finite CW-complexes. The action spectrum for the profinite group G is denoted by Omega(G) and consists of orbits representing homotopy classes of G-actions on CW-complexes. Properties of Omega(G) are investigated when G is a compact abelian profinite group, including the structure of Omega(G) and its relationship with the spectrum Sp(G) for the category of compact sets, and both results are extended to the case of groups with surjectively profinite covers. Additionally, formulas for computing Omega(G) in terms of Sp(G) are established for groups with profinitely free profinite complements. These general results are applied to the case of groups isomorphic to the profinite completion of a free group on two generators. Finally, considerations for further research are outlined. The concepts and techniques employed in this work have the potential for application to other areas of mathematics. It is suggested that the development of Omega(G) could serve as a unifying framework linking diverse existing methods and providing new approaches to studying profinite groups. In particular, Omega(G) is argued to be a more natural and flexible analogue of the classical Borel spectrum. The relationship between Omega(G) and Sp(G) is likened to the relationship between homotopy classes of maps and the image of the Borel map in classical topology. It is conjectured that non-trivial elements of Omega(G) are always associated with free actions, and that a free profinite group has a CW-complex of a specific type that serves as a universal space for its action spectrum. The techniques employed in this work include methods from homotopy theory, along with analysis of the arithmetic and topological properties of numbers. The study of Omega(G) is grounded in a comprehensive study of the profinite groups admitting profinite complements with a nilpotent quotient. The groups in question are classified, along with the profinite groups that admit a complement with a nilpotent quotient that is also profinitely free. The methods used in the classification involve the application of arithmetic and topological principles, including a version of the Galois-Gauß map, the profinite Grothendieck ring, and Faddeev's theorem. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are increasingly being employed by researchers, yet their use poses significant challenges when it comes to model inference and training. Efforts to optimize models have primarily centered on pruning, which alleviates the resource constraints associated with memory and processing costs, but has failed to consider the impact of dimensionality reduction on training efficiency. Evaluating the effectiveness of training individual channels within a CNN, our analysis reveals that channel pruners, despite improving model compactness, actually degrade the model's performance. ClickTrain takes a novel approach to training effective and efficient CNNs by incorporating a new evolution strategy that selectively improves channel pruners during the training process. Additionally, our method reintroduces previously discarded information from channel pruned models via a novel cross-channel interpolation technique, resulting in improved accuracy with reduced computational cost. Our method surpasses current state-of-the-art models in various benchmark datasets, achieving substantial gains in accuracy, reduced computational cost, and model compactness. The code for ClickTrain is available at https://github.com/hjkmkg/ClickTrain. It has been validated on an NVIDIA A100 40GB GPU. Our method requires 0.5GB of GPU memory to train a model that achieves comparable performance to a pruned model trained using an A100 40GB GPU with an inference budget 3 times larger. Moreover, our method enables training of models that can fit entirely within the memory of an A100 40GB GPU, a feat previously impossible to achieve. Details on the memory requirements of various models can be found in Table 4. Our method has potential applications across a range of areas including resource-efficient CNNs, CNNs on edge devices, and CNNs on resource-constrained devices. Also, our method can be extended beyond CNNs and pruned models of other architectures, given that it centers on intermediate representations, a characteristic shared by various models of the Linear Model family. Therefore, our method can be applied to models like Linear Models, Linear Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Linear ODEs), and Linear Graph Convolutional Networks (Linear GCNs). More information on these potential applications as well as the specific details on evaluating and extending our method can be found at https://github.com/hjkmkg/ClickTrain/blob/main/extension.pdf. We introduce a primal-dual method for solving restricted Markov decision processes, offering a straightforward algorithm that achieves optimal value preservation under state restrictions. The method involves constructing a dual graph and performing a sequence of primal and dual computations, each resulting in a near-equilibrium state that maximizes or minimizes a particular metric. The algorithm has been successfully applied to various MDP variants, such as factored MDPs, probabilistic planning with intervals, and online MDPs with changing dynamics. The resulting policy exhibits robust behavior under changing conditions and can be easily obtained when the dual graph is part of a established structure, like trees or directed acyclic graphs. The method also facilitates the development of compact, infinite-horizon MDP models that can be solved efficiently. The proposed policy exhibits a range of beneficial epidemiological properties, such as optimal epidemic behavior, extended epidemic containment, and reduced outbreak frequencies. The primal-dual method has been successfully implemented and tested on various MDP variants, demonstrating superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art algorithms. Our research focuses on the dynamics of an interconnected system, where entities influence each other in multiple ways. By applying minimal models to robust algorithms, we examined how variations in network architecture and inter-entity interactions affect the collective behavior of the system. Using a simplified model of predator and Prey dynamics, we analyzed the impact of these changes on the system's stability. Specifically, we found that even minor alterations in the system's parameters can convert a stable pattern into chaotic behavior. Furthermore, we observed that converting a fully connected network to a more dispersed structure can initiate various patterns of behavior. Notably, our studies reveal that different interaction processes can yield distinct outcomes. While some interactions may produce identical results, others can lead to distinct patterns of behavior. Overall, our findings emphasize the importance of considering the underlying connectivity and interaction dynamics when analyzing and managing complex interconnected systems. By leveraging theoretical models and collective behavior patterns, we can gain a deeper understanding of the variability of interacting systems. Our research provides insights into the critical factors contributing to this variability, which can inform the development of theories and models for robust algorithms. Additionally, our studies demonstrate the feasibility of minimal models in tackling challenging problems, such as predicting and controlling the patterns of behavior in intricate systems. Lastly, our work highlights the necessity for precise and accurate representation of interaction dynamics and connectivity to ensure predictable patterns of behavior in such systems. Although our specific research focuses on predator and Prey dynamics, our findings and observations are generally applicable to the broader context of robust algorithms. We hypothesize that our observations will also apply to other scenarios of collective behavior, such as the determination of critical thresholds for tipping phenomena and developing early warning indicators for impending events. Additionally, our results may be relevant to the understanding of socio-economic systems, where variations in feedback processes can lead to distinct patterns of behavior, thereby affecting the very basis of modern economics. At last but not least, our studies illustrate the potential for leveraging simplicity and theoretical models to tackle challenging problems, thereby bridging the gap between basic research and real-world applications of robust algorithms. We hope that our insights will be useful in the further development of algorithms for collective behavior. We provide our results in an open-access manner, with the aim of facilitating the understanding and replication of our observations. We also offer our code, enabling researchers to extend our studies and fine-tune our models in accordance with their particular needs and research questions. We anticipate that our research will contribute to basic research in the field of collective behavior and provide valuable insights for the further development of algorithms. The Twin Prime Hypothesis asserts that there are infinitely many prime pairs $(p, p+2).$ We provide a straightforward proof of this hypothesis, adopting a concept from Liu and Yang's work \cite{Liu Yang 2019}, combining it with elementary principles. We start by defining a function $f(p)$ as $(\frac{p+1}{2})!$ and establishing the primality of $p+2$ when $p$ satisfies a specific condition related to its factorization. We aim to demonstrate that an infinite number of prime pairs $(p, p+2)$ exist, and in doing so, we introduce a general concept that may have broader applications. We also introduce the Notable Prime Hypothesis as a broader hypothesis, which asserts that there is an infinite number of primes $p$ for which $(\frac{p+1}{2})!$ is notable in the sense that it is not divisible by $p.$ We prove that if the Notable Prime Hypothesis holds, then the Twin Prime Hypothesis must also hold, utilizing this connection may provide insight into resolving the Riemann Hypothesis. We also explore potential examples of prime pairs $(p, p+2)$ derived from distinct regular polygons, specifically considering the cases of 12, 14, and 16 sides. Additionally, we introduce the Prime Pair Hypothesis, which asserts that there are infinitely many prime pairs $(ap, bq), $ where $a$ and $b$ are specific coefficients and $p$ and $q$ are primes satisfying a particular condition. We prove that if the Prime Pair Hypothesis holds, then the Notable Prime Hypothesis must also hold, establishing a relationship between these hypotheses. We also derive upper limits for the differences between consecutive primes, specifically $p-q$ and $q-p,$ based on the Notable Prime Hypothesis, which may provide insight into resolving the Prime Number Theorem. We conclude by exploring potential examples of prime triples $(p, q, t)$ for which $p,$ $q,$ and $t$ are primes and satisfy specific conditions, such as $p+1 \equiv q+1 \pmod{T},$ $q+1 \equiv t+1 \pmod{P},$ and $t+1 \equiv p+1 \pmod{T}.$ We utilize these regular patterns to discover prime quadruplets and propose a method for finding prime quintuplets. In recent years, salient item identification (SII) has garnered significant focus, which involves pinpointing objects with distinctive colors or textures, regardless of background clutter, as seen in everyday life and safety monitoring applications. This paper outlines a novel SII technique that integrates color and depth information from RGB and RGB-D images to effectively locate prominent objects. To ensure accurate detection, a cohesive framework is presented, incorporating two modules: a context awareness module and an object fusion module. The context awareness module utilizes a self-designed context awareness loss and contextual information to enhance shallow features, while the object fusion module employs a fusion module and deep supervision to combine fused object information. This framework is further divided into two implementations: RGB-based SII and RGB-D based SII. Comprehensive experiments were conducted on designed datasets, demonstrating the substantial performance improvement of the proposed framework over existing techniques. The UM-IU@LING system for detecting offensive tweets on the Basis of English content used a combination of BERT and Support Vector Machines. In the training process, BERT was applied to generate word-level embeddings, which were then combined with additional frequency-based information. These embeddings were subsequently fed into an SVM classifier to obtain the final prediction. Our team performed best in the data-only scenario, achieving an F1 score of 73.96 in the detection of offensive tweets. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in the medical and industrial sectors for creating detailed cross-sectional images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since X-ray machines can only produce X-rays of certain energies, CT reconstructions typically involve multi-energy CT (MECT) data to generate detailed images of objects composed of multiple materials. To overcome limitations imposed by non-uniform rotation angles, attenuations, and energy levels in MECT data, researchers have developed variational frameworks that utilize weighted least squares optimization. However, these frameworks are convex and can fail to accurately capture high-contrast objects, while simultaneously being sensitive to data corruption by background noise. To address these issues, we introduce a novel non-convex framework that integrates inpainting techniques into the variational formulation for enhanced image de-noising and object separation. Specifically, our approach demoses and dematerializes polyenergetic CT data while promoting a seamless and reliable reconstruction of internal objects, even in the presence of incomplete and noisy projection data. Our framework's validity and accuracy have been verified through simulations involving synthetic and real-world scanning data, where we successfully dematerialized objects, removed background noise, and produced high-quality reconstructions that match the original ground-truth images. Moreover, our method demonstrates significant improvements over state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in terms of preserving the structural integrity of the images and successfully de-noising and dematerializing the CT data. All of the code and data used in this study have been carefully curated and shared for the sake of transparency and facilitation of replication. Additionally, we have introduced a range of challenging problems designed to push the limits of future research in this area. Our approach holds promise for the development of novel CT scanning technologies, such as extended X-ray energies that can distinguish between various materials, and could potentially be extended to the analysis of optical imaging data. In conclusion, our non-convex variational framework offers an innovative solution to the problem of reconstructing and de-noising CT data while simultaneously breaking down objects composed of multiple materials, and this approach is now poised to influence the broader research community. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a new approach that generates single-character sketches during training on character-level datasets. This sketch-based representation enhances the model's ability to recognize unseen characters by allowing it to learn more general features. By incorporating the proposed method, we demonstrate a notable improvement in HTR performance on handwritten datasets, specifically the NNAIL dataset (formerly used by Pan et al., 2019) and the Tamil handwritten dataset provided by the ICDAR 2019 Handwritten Document Recognition Competition organizers. Our results reveal that the proposed method surpasses the state-of-the-art performance on the NNAIL dataset and achieves comparable results on the Tamil dataset, with the performance on Tamil dataset still unsealed at the time of writing this article. We demonstrate this method using the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, which exhibits a topological transition following alteration of its Hamiltonian.  By examining various wave functions representing key concepts, such as energy bands and edge states, we show that our approach effectively identifies both localizable and non-localizable sections.  Furthermore, we apply this strategy to discover hidden patterns within quantum systems, revealing the topology of the SSH model through accessible human interpretation.  This method also enables the detection of supporting legs for quantum topological defects, enabling equivalent representations of different topological events, and potentially enabling automatic defect engineering.  Additionally, we show that our approach enables accurate classification of topological properties in multi-orthogonal states without requiring a complete wave function, by focusing solely on localizable parts.  This strategy offers a versatile framework for extracting topological insights from wave functions in quantum systems.  However, it may not always generate displays with clear physical meanings; hence, the choice of wave function should be guided by the objectives of the study.  This novel method also enables the incorporation of additional resources, such as imaging experiments, for understanding topological properties of quantum systems with multi-body interactions.  Details of the implementation, together with the used code, are available at https://github.com/JuliaTopologicalQOC/Topological-QOC_jl/blob/main/src/topological_qocjl.math.fts.py. High-performance computing on CPUs, GPUs, and other co-processors heavily relies on memory allocation to support object-based programming. Although memory management on hardware other than CPUs is often overlooked, efficient memory allocation is essential for achieving optimal performance. In order to address this gap, we have developed DynaSOAr, a highly efficient memory allocator designed for use with GPUs. DynaSOAr utilizes a novel approach of dividing free memory into aligned blocks to facilitate efficient management and speed up memory allocation operations. By doing so, DynaSOAr not only provides rapid memory allocation, but also improves data integrity by reducing the risk of memory corruption caused by overlapping memory access. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's optimized memory management has led to a significant reduction of memory-related exceptions on GPUs, allowing for a notable increase in overall performance. Our experimental results show that DynaSOAr's average speed is 3.31 times faster than the current standard memory allocator, while its maximum error margin for data integrity is less than 0.0003%. Our study further reveals that DynaSOAr can achieve speedups of up to 1.87 times and 1.43 times compared to the current memory allocator when used with CPUs and TPUs, respectively. Additionally, DynaSOAr demonstrates exceptional resilience to soft errors, outperforming other allocators by at least 1.3 times in such scenarios. In Bayesian networks, uncertainty is represented through probability distributions, with credibility levels represented by deterministic constraints on distribution parameters. This work introduces a method to ensure robustness against possible changes in credibility assumptions by first identifying set approximations for the original probabilistic constraints, then capping these sets with stricter constraints. The resulting increased uncertainty levels are shown to provide valid bounds on posterior probability changes, effectively guaranteeing a minimum posterior confidence level in the face of uncertain prior assumptions. The proposed approach is applied to two scenarios: the first involves assumptions based on statistical theory, while the second considers limitations inherent in any form of credibility measurement. Experimental evaluations using standard machine learning datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. The presented methodology provides a suitability assurance for any Bayesian network-based system, ensuring a specified level of reliability against potential shifts in credibility assumptions. These electron groups are produced through multi-photon absorption that overlooks the material's absorptivity. A rate approach is introduced to describe the development and relaxation of electron groups, guided by the Keldysh perturbation model. The rate framework yields accessible mathematical formulas that facilitate the analysis of electron groups. A novel method called U reversible steganography is introduced, which allows the sender and receiver to engage in encrypted conversations while maintaining the ability to freely transmit plain texts without any restrictions.  The implementation of U steganography relies on converted data being transmitted through an encrypted channel.  The sender converts input plaintexts into plaintexts with higher dimensions, represents them using Bayesian Neural Networks, and then sends the expanded data through an encrypted channel.  The receiver reconstructs the original plaintext by applying the inverse operation provided by the Bayesian Neural Networks, based on previous knowledge.  The key characteristic of U steganography is that both the sender and receiver do not retain any secret key.  The main challenge to realize U steganography is to design a conversion mechanism that allows for error-free transmission of plaintexts, even if the channel quality is poor.  In this research, a conversion mechanism based on Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) was developed to fulfill this requirement, as BNNs can be viewed as reliable models that recognize their own uncertainties.  The implementation details of the U steganography scheme and the theoretical foundations of BNNs are discussed.  The presented U steganography scheme is further validated through experiments, which demonstrate that high compression ratios and high error rates can be achieved with superior quality.  Specifically, under an entropy-limited scenario, up to 16x compression ratios can be attained with less than 5% error rates, while under a fixed-lifetime scenario, up to 64x compression ratios can be achieved with error rates under 10%.  The research also proposes an algorithm to find the optimal trade-off between compression ratio and error tolerance.  Additionally, the maintenance of message integrity in the U steganography scheme is addressed using error-correcting codes.  The efficiency and robustness of the proposed U steganography scheme are further verified through comparisons with existing approaches. The existence of dark matter is unmistakable, yet its actual nature remains a mystery. Despite decades of research, the primary problem is that the laws of physics as we currently understand them enable the existence of either extremely massive but visible dark matter or extremely lightweight but non-interacting dark matter, yet observed data suggests that it is neither of these. This paper presents an innovative solution to this enigma, proposing that dark matter is composed of extremely small but magnetically charged particles called milli-magnetic monopoles. The interaction between these monopoles and normal matter via an exchange of a scalar field, as well as their charge in relation to other fundamental forces such as electromagnetism, is described in detail. The model presented here includes the mechanism by which these monopoles are produced and stabilized, as well as their potential impact on the behavior of normal magnetic particles in specific experiments. The study further examines the phenomenon of galactic magnetic fields, providing a new explanation for their enduring presence, where the balance between magnetic energy and that of ordinary matter is key. The explanation for dark matter composed of milli-magnetic monopoles offers a cohesive framework in which various observational evidence, such as galaxy rotation, large-scale structure, and the cosmic microwave background, can be reinterpreted. The proposed model also provides a potential means of observing or detecting dark matter by examining normal matter particles affected by galactic magnetic fields. The created milli-magnetic monopole-ordinary matter pair systems can serve as sensitive probes of dark matter properties at low energy intervals. The creation of a comprehensive model that fits observed data while complying with the laws of physics is the primary aim of the paper. A detailed model is offered where dark matter behaves in a non-liquid, solid state at the earliest stages of the universe, resulting in matter with both magnetic charge and rest mass. The minimum size of these milli-magnetic monopoles is estimated to be around $10^{-18}$ meters in size, and their relatively small mass is no more than two times that of normal protons. The proposed model suggests that dark matter exists in two states: an plasma state that existed during the earliest stages of the universe and a solid state that exists in our current galaxy. The interaction between these two states via normal particles allows for the phenomenon of galactic magnetic fields to persist, providing a new explanation for the enduring presence of magnetic fields in our galaxy. Climate forecasting holds significant value in both practical and monetary terms, but the intricate and continuous nature of climate patterns presents difficulties for prediction models. These models struggle to capture the topography's spatial and temporal variations accurately, which are crucial for reliable forecasting. In this research, we introduce a cutting-edge transformer network, denoted as TWCF-Net, that incorporates a unique cross-attention mechanism across differing window sizes. This innovative approach enables TWCF-Net to consider localized, region-specific, and broader contextual information when making predictions. As a result, TWCF-Net is capable of forecasting climate patterns with high precision. Our experimental results demonstrate that TWCF-Net significantly surpasses existing models in the literature, achieving outstanding performance with only half the parameters compared to these models. Additionally, a practical evaluation highlights TWCF-Net's ability to forecast climate patterns up to 20 time steps ahead with great accuracy. In brain tissue, the balance of nutrients and waste products depends heavily on a complex system of substance transport across the blood-brain barrier and the fine-tuned regulation of neuronal energy demands.
Due to the intricate morphology of neurons, traditional reaction-diffusion models are often insufficient for solving the branching problem, and are therefore adapted into an optimization framework that incorporates spatial awareness.
By formulating this problem as a constrained optimization problem, along with experimental data, the model is solved numerically using an interior-point method, and its effectiveness is evaluated in a simplified glial model.
This approach leads to the discovery of parameter sets that successfully demonstrate homeostasis and prevent the occurrence of substance buildup, providing a starting point for further exploration and refinement. 
Ultimately, this model serves as a preliminary effort towards developing optimized therapeutic strategies for treating metabolic disorders and other disturbances of brain energy metabolism. 
Due to its general applicability, this method may also be applied to other cellular systems where substance transport regulation plays a crucial role. 
In particular, the techniques established here merit consideration for applications in modeling retinal photoreceptor cells where substance transport across the cell membrane plays a critical part. 
It is hypothesized that such a model can contribute significantly to the development of sight-restoring therapies. 
This work is a direct outcome of the author's participation in the 2022 SIAM Conference on Mathematics of Data Science, where the problem is initially presented as a challenge, and the subsequent collaborative efforts with the mentioned co-authors. 
In particular, the problem is initially posed by Michael Hahnfeldt, and the numerical methods are contributed by Alan Antunes, while the model itself is refined and analyzed through the joint efforts of the author and Robert Gaudy. 
This collaborative research is a testament to the importance of interdisciplinary scientific interactions, and the cross-fertilization of ideas within the mathematics community. 
It is also noteworthy that this research is entirely independent of the COVID-19 pandemic, and serves as a microcosm of the various challenges faced by the scientific community during this period.

Despite GCNNs' success in various applications, their mechanism and the transfer of information through the network layers are not clearly understood. In contrast, the foundations of classical convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are well-established, allowing for the development of filtering methods that precisely match the convolutional operation in CNNs. Inspired by this, we introduce a novel matched filtering method for GCNNs, leveraging GCNNs' eigenfunctions to define filters that equate to the graph Laplacian's eigenvalues. This method illuminates the GCNNs' implicit assumptions about inter-node connectivity, node self-lookups, and the relative transfer of information between nearby and distant nodes. However, it becomes apparent that the matched filters incur high computational and memory requirements for common datasets such as Citeseer and Cora. In a surprising discovery, we find that the existing GCNNs, including the popular GCNNs, outperform the matched filters by a significant margin in performance and efficiency. Based on these findings, we suggest essential research avenues to further engineer and understand the graph convolutional neural networks' foundations. Deep neural networks have made significant advancements in natural language processing, 
particularly in dependency parsing for languages with abundant tree banks.
However, countries with limited resources face challenges in accessing expert annotations.
Our novel approach tackles this problem by leveraging an auto-pointer distribution 
to dynamically learn pointers for unknown sentences within minutes.
The network's inherent context awareness enables it to draw connections 
between sentences, thus enhancing syntax annotation with less expert involvement.
Our experiments on three diverse languages demonstrate that
our self-learning method can achieve comparable results with extensive tree banks.

The LFQM model incorporates mass and gauge boson effects using a instantaneous Schwinger method and incorporates radiative corrections through the interaction of quarks and light degrees of freedom within the $B$ and $D$ mesons and the $\ell
u_\ell$ leptonic system.  The study reveals that incorporating radiative corrections significantly improves agreement between theory and experiment, and suggests that effects related to the $b$ quark mass alone are insufficient to explain observed patterns in the data. This paper explores unique likelihood distributions that possess circular and
nontransitive properties. We start by clarifying the relationship between these
properties, establishing that any circular nontransitivity necessarily involves
a mixture of independent and identically distributed variables. We then
demonstrate that a specific class of models, which includes the Cauchy and
generalized Cauchy distributions, can give rise to nontransitive likelihoods.
Additionally, we examine the implications of symmetry for the third and fourth
moments, and discuss potential paradigms for testing the presence of
nontransitive effects in a likelihood context. Our investigation also considers
the distinct behavior of expectation and likelihood-based predictions. Further,
we analyze how to maintain a group's nontransitive property over multiple trials,
illustrating the method with a likelihood example. Lastly, we touch on the
connection between our discussion of likelihoods and the established framework
for utility functions in social welfare theory. Our analysis provides a fresh
perspective on the concept of nontransitivity in the context of likelihoods.

Computer systems' performance is heavily influenced by the efficiency of their software setup process, with many systems requiring setup options to be modified frequently. Optimizing a system's setup process often involves streamlining the sequence in which components are initialized to eliminate unnecessary dependencies. Typically, this optimization process relies on expert insights; however, advancements in machine learning and code transformation technologies now enable the automation of this process. Specifically, this research investigates the application of two advanced techniques - machine learning model pruning and static analysis - to three benchmark systems, demonstrating how their combination can surpass expert-designed setups in overall performance, with improvements averaging 5-10% across the benchmarks examined. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the stability of these optimized setups in diverse system configurations can be accurately forecast during the compilation process, resulting in a 2-3 times decrease in setup complexity for the benchmarks evaluated. The source code for our research is publicly available on GitHub. The technical contribution of this research involves developing a general-purpose framework for automated setup optimization, which can be applied to various systems by specifying context-dependent factors through a specialized programming interface. The study also presents an in-depth analysis of the challenges and complexities underlying the optimization of computer systems and encourages the exploration of new approaches to this problem. The findings of this research suggest that a comprehensive comparison of different performance optimization methods may be a valuable area of inquiry. The results of our experiments raise questions about the limitations of methods relying on heuristic algorithms and machine learning-based techniques, and offer an alternative perspective on the issue of responding to changing performance demands through software setup processes. The study offers a fresh perspective on the issue of when to apply heuristic machine learning and code transformation methods to improve system performance. This paper investigates the dynamics of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, where coupled photons and electrons interact in a two-level system and non-relativistic photon field.  We observe that without initial entanglement between photons and electrons, phenomena like Rabi oscillations, entanglement, and transmission behavior primarily rely on the detuning and photon occupation.  Notably, in the case of positive detuning, electrons tend to stay in a superposed state, whereas negative detuning causes Rabi oscillations to disappear.  In regimes of strong coupling, Rabi oscillations of electron spin and transmission exhibit contrasting behaviors.  Additionally, this system can enable quantum entanglement transfer from photons to electrons, with transmission serving as a measure to verify this process.  Our theoretical findings align with experimental observations using ultra-cold atoms, and we suggest an applicable experiment using cold atoms.  Such research has broader implications for anti-Jaynes-Cummings model applications. Heart rate variability or HRV is highly responsive to individual therapeutic interventions. To measure HRV, the inter-beat interval, or IBIs, must first be assessed from heart rate signals. Although mathematically straightforward, identifying IBIs can be computationally expensive due to signal noise. Current fast methods either simplify the assessment, reducing accuracy, or use machine learning, which incurs significant processing costs. We present an innovative approach utilizing a Tiramisu framework to simultaneously identify IBIs and estimate their corresponding confidence levels. In our research, we demonstrate that this new method outperforms existing techniques by accurately determining IBI durations, estimating their uncertainty, and doing so at a significant computational savings. We showcase the effectiveness of our approach through recordings from healthy individuals and patients undergoing therapeutic treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder. Furthermore, we provide an analysis of our code's efficiency, illustrating the Tiramisu framework's potential for real-time application in systems aiming to monitor individual responses to therapeutic interventions. We make our full code available for public review. We plan to expand our research by applying this method to various types of signal noise and incorporating multiple types of deep learning frameworks for comparison. Additionally, we aim to investigate its potential to monitor individual responses to treatments for various psychiatric conditions. We expect our work to have a positive impact on the field, providing an accurate and efficient method for assessing HRV and advancing therapeutic monitoring strategies. We anticipate an update on our progress within the next six months. We present a novel and efficient method for IBI assessment, which we believe will serve as a durable solution for evaluating heart rate variability. Due to the straightforward mathematical underpinnings of IBI identification, we anticipate our work to be of considerable value to researchers seeking to develop individualized therapeutic monitoring systems. The computational savings achieved by our approach, specifically a reduction of approximately 24 times, makes it an accessible and efficient method for various datasets.
